en: In this word-index (*śabdānukramaṇikā*), whichever word appears at its own head is to be sought in the commentary (*ṭīkā*). Although the word-index was originally composed by Cintāmaṇi Śāstrī, whose surname is Thatte, nevertheless, because certain words from the lexicon were not included therein, I—Bhaṭṭa Vāmanācārya, surnamed Jhalakīkar—have completed it by adding those missing words through the inclusion of terms found in variant readings (*pāṭhāntara*).

And it should be understood that [the text] has been fully expounded. Furthermore, it should be observed that the root text was collated with a handwritten palm-leaf manuscript from the year 4398 of the Kali Yuga (corresponding to the Christian year 1297), and the commentary was likewise compared with the commentaries of Rāmāśrama and others. Now, the introduction.

This lexicon titled *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana* was indeed composed by Amarasiṃha, as he himself has written at the conclusion of each section: "Thus [ends] the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana* composed by Amarasiṃha. However, regarding the question of when this Amarasiṃha lived, it is stated only after determining that he must have existed prior to the latter part of the eleventh century of the Śaka era (i.e., before 1100 CE).

For it has been stated by Mammaṭa, who lived in the aforementioned year, in the seventh chapter (*ullāsa*) of his *Kāvyaprakāśa* (page 328): "He took up the fragment of the *Amarakośa*: 'The [words] *devatāni* [and *puṃsi* are used] in the masculine. That Mammaṭa lived in the aforementioned year has been determined in the introductory section (*upoddhāta-prakaraṇa*) of our commentary on the *Kāvyaprakāśa* titled *Bālabodhinī*; therefore, it should be consulted there. Some, however...

It is said that this Amarasiṃha was a contemporary of Vikrama; this will become clear immediately hereafter. This Amarasiṃha was indeed a Buddhist. Regarding this, Paṇḍita Śivadatta Śarmā states in his commentary on the Amarakośa, titled *Vyākhyāsudhā* (better known as *Rāmāśramī*), composed by Bhānudīkṣita: "It is not certain when this Amarasiṃha lived, what his caste was, or which region of the earth he adorned."

By the enumeration of general names for gods—such as "rāḥ, vikṣarī, devāḥ, asidaśāḥ, vibudhāḥ, surāḥ"—and then beginning with the specific names of a particular deity through the writing of names such as "Mugataḥ, Buddhaḥ, Dharmarājaḥ, Tathāgataḥ, Samantabhadraḥ, Bhagavān, Mārajit, Lokajit" and so forth, his Buddhahood is established. However, some [cite]: "Dhanvantari, Kṣapaṇaka, Amarasiṃha, Śaṅku, Vetālabhaṭṭa, Ghaṭakarpara, and Kālidāsa... [and so on].

"Varāhamihira is renowned in the assembly of the king, and indeed Vararuci [is the ninth] among the nine jewels of Vikrama"—from this verse in the *Vaikramanavaratnamālā*, they say that Amarasiṃha was a contemporary of Vikrama. Others, however, on the basis of the verse: "Indra, Candra, Kāśakṛtsna, Āpiśali, Śākaṭāyana, Pāṇini, Amara, and Jainendra—these eight grammarians are victorious," maintain that he lived in the interval between Pāṇini and Samantabhadra.

In this regard, it should be understood that this does not indicate a chronological sequence, because Candrācārya—the author of the Cāndra-vyākaraṇa, which was completed at the same time as Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya—wrote his work prior to Pāṇini. His status as a grammarian is indeed established by the verse: "Amarasiṃha, however, surpassed the entire Bhāṣya," from which we perceive his mastery of the essence of the whole Bhāṣya (i.e., his complete knowledge of the Mahābhāṣya).

"The statement that this is said by way of a different interpretation is because, as a Buddhist position, it contradicts all Vedic [tradition]. Precisely because he is a Buddhist, Amarasiṃha employed the word *jina* in the first position in the verse from the section on various synonyms: "The two Dharmarājas are Jina and Yama. For instance, in the case of "Jinayamau," since rules such as "the shorter [word]" (Pāṇini 2.2.34) do not apply—as they do not in cases like "Tāpasaparvatī"—the *pūrvanipāta* (prior placement) of the word *jina* occurs by virtue of the Vārttika rule: "And that which is more important."

"Preeminence" (*abhyarhitatvam*) means being worthy of worship (*pūjyatvam*), and this is evident in the Buddhist view because the Jina—who is another name for the Buddha—is a specific type of deity. If Amarasiṃha were not a Buddhist but rather a follower of the Vedas, then, since in the Vedic tradition Yama is more preeminent than the Jina and there is no rule regarding the order of words in such compounds, he would have said "Yamajinau. Furthermore, if he were a Buddhist, many ancient commentaries on the Amarakośa also support this conclusion.

For instance, during the commentary on the first verse beginning with "yasya jñānadaya-sindhoḥ," [the author] provides a detailed syntactical analysis (anvaya) with the following intent: "O wise ones! [Let that Blessed One]—who, like an ocean, is an ocean of knowledge and compassion; who possesses faultless qualities; and who is unfathomable—be served and propitiated for the sake of prosperity and immortality. Furthermore, he states this in order to avoid the defect resulting from the failure to specify the subject (viśeṣya).

Rāyamukuṭīkāra states: "Even when not explicitly mentioned in a sentence, that which is to be indicated (lakṣya) is clearly perceived through [contextual factors] such as propriety (*aucitya*) and so forth. For example, in the verse: 'This one rises, breaking the seal of the lotus-beds—the young mandāra flower of the forest-grove on the mountain of sunrise'—the sun, though not mentioned, is indicated by the rising and by the breaking of the seal of the lotuses. Others, however, maintain that sometimes even a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) brings about the cognition of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), as in: 'She who has the ocean for her garment, like the earth containing treasures within'."

Thus, they say that here too, the qualifiers such as "with mountains, rivers, and oceans" serve to identify the qualified [subject], and so there is no fault. However, in this case, if the term "Buddha" and so forth were mentioned, the followers of the Southern Path (the Jains) would not be included; whereas if the term "Kṛṣṇa" and so forth were mentioned, because of their non-inclusiveness, the Buddhists—who are intoxicated by the power of their own time—would not be included. Therefore, for the sake of inclusion common to both, the primary [term] is mentioned subsequently.

It is also stated in the *Amaradīpikā*: "In the sense of the ocean, the gods (*devāḥ*) are called *dhīrāḥ* because they receive (*rānti*) and hold (*gṛhanti*) the intellect (*dhī*) characterized by all-knowingness. In the sense of the Buddha, O wise ones (*dhīrāḥ*), meaning scholars (*paṇḍitāḥ*), that Buddha should be served. It was also stated by Rāmanātha in the *Trikāṇḍarahasya*: "When this poet Amarasiṃha composed this work, there was at that time an abundance of pride among those who had strayed from the path of the Vedas."

"If [the name] Kṛṣṇa and others were mentioned, they would be unacceptable to those [of the North]; however, if Buddhapālita and others were mentioned, they would be unacceptable to those active in the Deccan (Dakṣiṇāpatha). Therefore, this opening verse possesses a profound hidden meaning intended so that both groups may accept it."

In the *Amarakośoddhāṭana*, Kṣīrasvāmin also stated during the commentary on the first verse: "Of that Blessed One, who is like an ocean (*sindhu*)—deep like the sea—of knowledge and compassion (*jñāna-dayau*), [there are] the thirty-seven faultless (*anaghāḥ*), sinless (*niṣpāpāḥ*) qualities (*guṇāḥ*) conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣyāḥ*), such as patience (*kṣānti*) and so forth. Then, he provided the introduction to the second verse: "Thus, at the commencement of another work, having recollected the Jina as the cause for the attainment of the desired goal, [the author] states the purpose of his own undertaking for the sake of encouraging the listeners..."

"By the initial statement beginning with *dheyam*, he says 'having saluted' (*samāhṛtya*). And thus, as for what Bhānudīkṣita stated—"But Svāmī (i.e., Kṣīrasvāmī) says that [the author] declares an auspicious invocation characterized by remembrance (*smaraṇa*) in the words 'having recollected the Jina' (*jinamanusmṛtya*); that is not so, because no word denoting the Jina is seen here.

Furthermore, it is improper for those following the Vedic tradition to interpret general terms as referring specifically to the Jina, and there is no evidence that the author of the Amarakośa (the author of the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana*) was a Jain"—that argument is indeed unacceptable.

Since the reason for employing words expressive of the Jina was demonstrated by ancient authors such as Rāyamukuṭin and others, and since even Vaidikas engaged in the commentary on Buddhist texts have accepted that general terms are to be explained as referring specifically to the characteristics of the Jina, and since the evidence for the authorship of this present work has already been established, those who are discerning should reflect upon this.

Although a certain poet, while enumerating the lexicons (*kośa*), stated, "This *Amarakośa* is eternal," for instance: "The *Medinī*, the *Amaramālā*, the *Trikāṇḍa*, the *Ratnamālā*, Rantideva, Bhāguri, Vyāḍi, and likewise the *Śabdārṇava*; the *Dvirūpa*, the *Phaliṅga*, Ramasa, Puruṣottama, Durga, the *Abhidhānamālā*, the *Saṃsārāvarta*, and the *Śāśvatī*; Viśva and Vopālita, as well as Vācaspati and Halāyudha; Hārāvalī, Sāhasāṅka, and Vikramāditya."

However, in that context, the meaning of the term "Sanātana" is that he is older than Viśva, Hemacandra, and others, but not older than Vyāḍi, Bhāguri, and so forth. This is because, relative to the lexicon under discussion, many other lexicons existed previously.

This is because Amarasiṃha himself clarified [the matter] by stating, "having struck down other treatises" (*samāhatyānyatantrāṇi*) on page 1. As for the evidence regarding Vyāḍi’s extreme antiquity, it is found in the *Mahābhāṣya* and other works composed by the great sage Patañjali and others. For instance, the *Mahābhāṣya* states: "In the *Saṃgraha*, this was examined primarily" (*saṃgrahe etatprādhānyena parīkṣitam*; *Mahābhāṣya*, 1.1.1). Regarding the word "in the *Saṃgraha*," Kaiyaṭa says, "in a particular work. He further specifies, "a particular work."

"The *Saṃgraha* composed by Vyāḍi is a work consisting of one hundred thousand verses (*lakṣa-śloka*); this is the well-known tradition," as stated in Nāgojībhaṭṭa’s commentary (*Mahābhāṣyapradīpodyota*). Furthermore, it should be noted that the statement of Śaunaka in the *Prātiśākhya*—"In the case of Vyāḍi, there is the elision of the designation [of the accent] everywhere"—also serves as authoritative evidence.

Now, those names of lexicons or lexicographers that are found in the commentaries on the *Amarakośa* and elsewhere are listed here in alphabetical order for the sake of beginners' understanding: 1. Ajaya; 2. Anekārthadhvanimañjarī; 3. Abhidhānacintāmaṇi.

O wise ones, may that ocean of knowledge and compassion, whose virtues are unfathomable, be resorted to for the sake of prosperity and immortality. (1) Having gathered from various other sources, this instruction on names and genders (*nāmaliṅgānuśāsana*) is here declared in its entirety through concise and refined groups of words (*varga*). (2) [The gender is determined] mostly by the difference in form, and in some cases by association (*sāhacarya*). (3)

It should be understood as feminine, masculine, or neuter, depending on specific rules in certain instances. (1.3) Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. I bow to that Supreme Bliss who is joined with Umā by his left half; from whose eyebrows the universe revolves like a wheel. Here, indeed, the illustrious Amarasiṃha composes at the beginning of this work—a lexicon (*nāmaliṅgānuśāsana*) intended to be composed—the following verse for the purpose of ensuring its flawless completion and for the instruction of his disciples: "yas... [etc. *Note: The text provided ends mid-sentence after "yas," indicating the beginning of the opening verse.*

O wise ones, he whose stainless qualities such as patience and the like exist within that ocean of wisdom and compassion—which is exceedingly profound even beyond the month of Māgha—is inexhaustible; for the sake of glory, prosperity, and the nectar of liberation, let him be served and propitiated. (1) He makes his intended purpose known by stating "He" (sa).

Having gathered together other treatises on that subject—namely, various *nāmaliṅgānuśāsanāni* (lexicons of nouns and genders)—and having condensed them into one, this work is called a *vyutpādaka-śāstra* (an etymological treatise) which provides instruction on the names, such as *svaḥ* and so forth, and on genders, including feminine and neuter designations; it is complete with all its primary and secondary parts (*sāṅgopāṅga*), composed in concise words that are not overly prolix, refined through the analysis of each word's root and suffix (*prakṛti-pratyaya-vicāra*) at every step, and arranged in groups of similar items. The word "by me" (*mayā*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 2 ||

Now, he states the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*) for the treatise that is about to be expounded in three verses, beginning with the word *prāyaśaḥ*. Here, *prāyaśaḥ* means "for the most part" or "generally," and it should be understood as neuter due to its specific form. For example: "Lakṣmīḥ patrālayā pagā" (Lakṣmī, the abode of leaves, the river); "pinākojagavaṃ dhanuḥ" (the Pināka and the Ajagava bow). Likewise, in some cases, it is to be understood through association (*sāhacarya*) or proximity to another word (*chanda*). For example: "aśvayugacinī" (Aśvinī and Citrā); "pramātmabhūḥ surajyeṣṭha" (Pramātman, the Self-born, the eldest of the gods); "viyadviṣṇupadam" (the sky, the station of Viṣṇu).

In this [section], words whose gender is doubtful and which do not deviate from their etymological derivation are listed alongside feminine, masculine, and neuter forms due to their association with the names of Aśvinī, Ātman, and Viṣṇupada. Furthermore: No *dvandva* (copulative) compounds, no *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), and no mixing of genders have been employed here for the purpose of expressing distinctions among unmentioned words of different genders that would otherwise disrupt the sequence. The term *triṣu* ("in all three genders") is used when a word possesses all three genders; the term *dvayoḥ* ("in two genders") is used for a pair of genders. When a specific gender is excluded, it serves the purpose of indicating the remaining genders. Words beginning with *anta-* or *atha-* do not apply to what precedes them.

5. *Kha*, *ravyaya*, *svarga*, *nāka*, *tridiva*, *tridaśālaya*, *suraloka*, *dyo*, and *div* [denote heaven]. The word *de* is feminine; *triviṣṭapa* is neuter. 6. In some cases, due to the prescription of a specific meaning for that term, a specific gender is stated, as in: "The *merī* is feminine, the *dundubhi* is masculine," and "In the neuter, *triviṣṭapa*. Regarding the word *bheda*: in this treatise (*alin*), for the purpose of explaining the distinctions between names that have not been mentioned or analyzed—namely those with dissimilar genders—a copulative compound (*dvandva*) has not been formed.

Just as one says "kuliśa, bhidura, paviḥ" and not "kuliśabhidurapavayaḥ," so too the *ekaśeṣa* (the grammatical retention of one term) has not been employed here; for only the meaning of the term being retained would be understood. For example, one says "namaḥ khaṃ śrāvaṇo nabhāḥ" and not "khaśrāvaṇau tu nabhasī. Likewise, without following the proper order—that is, without sequence—even a confusion (*saṃkara*), which is the mixing together of words with different genders, has not been committed; for that would result in the impossibility of determining the gender through association (*sāhacarya*).

However, feminine, masculine, and neuter genders are listed in their proper sequence; for example: "stavaḥ stotraṃ stutirnutiḥ," and not "stutiḥ stotraṃ stavo nutiḥ. In this regard, although the gender of those words whose derivation was explained according to the aforementioned method—namely, primarily by means of differences in form—is distinct, compounds such as *dvandva* are nevertheless formed with them in other instances. For example: "apsaroyakṣarakṣogandharvakinnarāḥ" and "mātāpitarau pitarau. [This concludes the section] regarding the three genders.

In the case of a collection of the three genders (*triliṅga*), the word *triṣu* is used; for example, "a spark (*sphuliṅga*) is a particle of fire in all three [genders]. The meaning is that the word *sphuliṅga* applies to all three genders. Similarly, in the case of a pair (*mithuna*), i.e., a woman and a man, the word *dvayoḥ* is used; for example, "the two bolts of the door of Agni. Likewise, when a gender is prohibited, it refers to the remaining gender; wherever a gender is excluded, there the safety of the remaining gender is established.

Just as in the rule "vyomayānaṃ vimāno 'strī," where the feminine gender is excluded, the masculine and neuter genders are prescribed for *vimāna*; likewise, *tuśabdaḥ* means that which has *tu* as its final member (*tuntam*), and *athaśabdaḥ* means that which has *atha* as its initial member (*athādi*). These two do not "partake of what precedes" (*pūrvabhāk*); they are not connected with what comes before. For example, in the verse "Pulomajā Śacī Indrāṇī, the city is Amarāvatī," the word *nagarī*, ending in *ī* (tvantam), is not connected with *Indrāṇī*, but rather with *Amarāvatī*.

Likewise, in the passage beginning with “*nityānavaratājastramapyathātiśayo bharaḥ*,” the word [“*api*”] does not precede the preceding term; rather, it is a synonym for *bhara*. Regarding the word *svaḥ*: *svaḥ* means heaven (*svargaḥ*), also called *nāka*. It is so called because there is no *aka* (suffering) there—*aka* being suffering (*duḥkha*) and *na* meaning that which does not exist. [This concludes] the first section, verses 6–10.

1] Amara, nirjara, deva, tridaśa, vibudha, sura, suparvan, sumanas, tridiveśa, divaukas, āditeya, diviṣad, lekha, aditinandana, āditya, ṛbhu, asvapna, amartya, amṛtāndhas, barhirmukha, kratubhuj, gīrvāṇa, and dānavāri are synonyms for gods. Vṛndāraka and daivata are masculine; alternatively, *devatā* is feminine. [7–9] The Ādityas, Viśvedevas, Vasus, Tuṣitas, Ābhāsvaras, Anilas, [Maruts, Aśvins, Rudras, and Ādityas constitute the twelve Ādityas. [10]

The Mahārājikas, the Sādhyas, the Rudras, and the Gaṇadevatās [are there]. (10) There is no elision of the *v* in *vāma*. There are nine names for heaven (*svarga*): *tridiva*, *tridaśālaya*, *suraloka*, *dyauḥ*, *dyauḥ*, *triviṣṭapa*, and so on. Among these, *svar* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) according to the rule "indeclinables such as *svar* and others are called nipātas. This means it lacks gender, number, and case-role (*kāraka*). The two forms *dyo* and *divau* are feminine. *Dyo* is like *go* (cow), etc.; *dyauḥ*, *dīvau*, *divaḥ*, *dhubhyām*, and so forth, constitute the other form.

*Triviṣṭapa* is exclusively neuter (*klība*). Terms such as *tridaśālaya* (abode of the thirty) are indicative of synonyms like *surasadana* (dwelling of the gods). Similarly, in what follows, other synonyms may be inferred by oneself based on semantic equivalence. There is also a reading: *triyau klīve*. *Amarāḥ*, *nirjarāḥ*, *devāḥ*, *tridaśāḥ*, *vibudhāḥ*, *surāḥ*, *suparvāṇaḥ*, *sumanasaḥ*, *tridiveśāḥ*, *divaukasaḥ* (also *divokasaḥ*), *āditeyāḥ*, *diviṣadaḥ*, *lekhāḥ*, *aditinandanāḥ*, and *ādilāḥ* [are synonyms for the gods].

The *Ṛbhus*—those who have no horses (*asva*), no homes (*amā*), and subsist on the nectar of immortality (*amṛtāndhas*). [Verse 8] *Barhimukhas*: those for whom the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is the mouth. *Ṛtubhujs*: those who enjoy the seasons. *Gīrvāṇas*: "Those who delight in speech" (*gīr*); the gods who are the enemies of the *Dānavas*. *Vṛndārakas*, *Daivatāni*, and *Devatās*—these are twenty-six names for the gods. The plural form is used because of the multiplicity of individual deities. Optionally, the word *daivata* may be masculine; for example: *daivatam idam* (this deity) or *daivato 'yam* (this is a god). A *deva* itself is called *devatā*; the suffix *-tal* is added in the sense of identity (*svārthe*). [Verse 9] Now, he speaks of those who move in groups:

Regarding the term *āditya*: "The Ādityas are said to be twelve; the Viśvedevas are remembered as ten; the Vasus are reckoned as eight; the Tuṣitas are considered to be thirty-six. The Ābhāsvaras are sixty-four; the Vātas are forty-nine; those named Mahārājikas are two hundred and twenty. The Sādhyas are renowned as twelve; the Rudras are remembered as eleven. The Ādityas are twelve; the Viśvedevas are ten; the Vasus are eight; the Tuṣitas are thirty-six; the Ābhāsvaras are sixty-four."

The Anilas are forty-nine; the Mahārājikas are two hundred and twenty; the Sādhyas are twelve; the Rudras are eleven. These are the *gaṇadevatās* (group deities). Here, the groups beginning with the Tuṣitas should be consulted in Buddhist, Pātañjala, and other sources. [The author] states the divine births (*devayonayaḥ*): "Vidyā... and so forth. *Vilāsa* (grace) is a particular excellence of the limbs manifested upon the attainment of a beloved or in sitting and other postures. *Vivoka* (affected indifference) is a lack of regard due to pride even when the desired object has been attained. *Viśrama* (rest) is considered to be the instability of mental states caused by fear and the like. *Lalita* (sportiveness) is a natural gesture of love not taught by a teacher. *Hāva* is a sign of internal feeling (*bhāva*), while *helā* (playfulness) is its manifestation; or, *helā* is defined as mature desire for sexual union. *Helā* is also the imitation of a beloved through speech, dress, and gestures. From the word "iti," which signifies "manner" or "kind," others [of this class] are also to be understood.

"Līlā, vilāsa, vicchitti, viśrama, kilakiñcita, moṭṭāyita, kuṭṭamita, vibhrama, vivvoka, and likewise lalita, as well as vihṛta—these ten are to be understood as the natural graces of women," so says the *Nāṭakaratnakośa*. *Vicchitti*: The careless application of ornaments out of pride in one's own beauty is *vicchitti*. *Kilakiñcita*: A mixture of song and other expressions arising from joy is *kilakiñcita*. *Moṭṭāyita*: The manifestation of a smile upon remembering a beloved is *moṭṭāyita*. *Kuṭṭamita*: [The text here provides the term *kuṭṭamita*.]

The simulation of pain even when there is pleasure is *kuṭṭamita*. Joy arising from delight is *pramada*. Playful sport, jesting, amusement, pastime, dalliance, and mirth are synonyms. A pretext, instruction, a target, play, sport, and leaping are also related to play. *Dharma* (heat), *nidāgha*, and *kheda* denote fatigue; *salaya* is the state of having lost one's composure. *Avahitthā* is the concealment of one's true feelings; *saṃvega* and *saṃbhrama* are synonymous, meaning agitation.

A slight smile accompanied by a playful display is *sthādācchuritaka* (the "brushed" laugh). A moderate laugh that causes the hair to stand on end is *romaharṣaṇa*. Weeping, crying, and wailing are synonyms; while *jṛmbha* is the act of yawning, it is used in three genders (*triṣu*). *Vihata* refers to a speech that appears as if interrupted under the pretext of conversation. *Drava*, *keli*, and *parīhāsa* denote playfulness or jesting. In the word *parihāsa*, the lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule *upasargasya pani* (Pāṇini 6.3.93), which applies diversely (*bahulam*).

*Krīḍā* (sport) and *līlā* (play)—regarding *līlā*, some say it means *khele*—are nouns denoting mere play. *Keli* is masculine, because there is no *dvandva* compound of words with different genders. (32) *Vyāja* (pretext) is the performance of another action for the sake of achieving a desired object. [The suffix] *ghañ* is used; there is no substitution of *i* for *e*. In this context, *vyāja* means a pretext (*apadeśa*) or a target (*lakṣya*). This is a concealment of one's true nature. It is also a target (*lakṣa*). As it has been said: "The word *lakṣya* is used in the sense of a pretext and also as a target (*śaravya*), and it is neuter."

And in the commentary [on the lexicon], Rāmāśrama states that *nā*, *lakṣa*, and *vyāja* end with the retroflex nasal (*ṇ*) and mean "guise" or "pretext. *Krīḍā*, *khelā*, and *kardana*—these three refer to the play of children. *Dharma*, *nidāgha*, and *kheda*—the latter meaning "that by which one is excessively tormented"—these three refer to exhaustion. *Pralaya* and *naṣṭaceṣṭatā*—these two refer to the loss of movement. (33) *Avahitthā* and *ākāragupti*—these two refer to the concealment of outward appearance, such as the fading of the face caused by grief and the like.

*Saṃvega* is agitation; it is the hastening in actions due to joy and the like. *Sotmāsa* is laughter accompanied by intention, or alternatively, laughter accompanied by excessive excitement (*utsāsa*) or suppression (*kṣapaṇa*). Regarding *ācchuritaka*, it is said: "It is the laughter of another that produces indignation and is accompanied by sound. That laughter is called *īrisita* when it is slight (*manāka*) or minimal (*īṣat*). It is described thus: "Laughter with slightly opened teeth, accompanied by grace, and with the corners of the mouth and the teeth slightly revealed, is called *īrisita*. (34)

When that smile (*sahāsa*) consists of moderate sensation with a slight excess, it is then called *vihasita* (the gentle laugh). They say that *vihasita* is like nectar, arising from a preliminary musical introduction (*prastāva*), accompanied by affection, and characterized by the drawing back of the cheeks and eyes, as well as the sound of the breath. (1) *Tremor* (*romāñca*) is the bristling of the hair. *Pulaka*, *kaṇṭhaka*, *romavikriyā*, and *romodgama*—these two are synonyms for the rising of the hair. (2) *Krandita*, *rudita*, and *kuṣṭa*—these three are synonyms for weeping. (3) *Jambhā*, *jammaṇa*, and *de*—these are for yawning (*jambhikā*), which is known as *jāmaī*. (4)

In this regard, concerning *ammaliṣu* (in the case of women): *vipralambhaḥ* means deception or a contradiction; it refers to speaking something improper or the failure to fulfill what has been promised. *Riṅgaṇam* (also *rihaṇam*) means stumbling or wavering from one’s own duty and so forth. [From the Pātālavarga of the Amarakośa with Commentary: *Vipralambhaḥ*, *visaṃvādaḥ*, *riṅgaṇam*, and *skhalanam* are synonyms. *Nidrā*, *śayanam*, *svāpaḥ*, *svapnaḥ*, and *saṃveśaḥ* are also synonyms for sleep. (36)

*Tandrī* (lassitude), *pramīlā* (drowsiness), *bhraṃkuṭi*, *kuṭi*, and *dhrukuṭi* are feminine terms for a frown. *Adṛṣṭi* refers to an ungracious or displeased look. *Saṃsiddhi* and *prakṛti* denote the natural state or innate disposition; likewise, *svarūpa* and *svabhāva*. *Vepathu* and *kampa* mean trembling. *Kṣaṇa*, *uddharṣa*, *maha*, *uddhava*, and *utsava* all signify a festival or great joy. Thus ends the section on miscellaneous terms (Nānārthavarga). The nether world is called *adhobhuvana*, *pātāla*, *balisadma*, and *rasātala*. It is also known as *nāgaloka*. Furthermore, *kuhara*, *suṣira*, *vivara*, and *bila* denote a cavity, hole, or chasm.

*Chidra*, *nirmathana*, *roka*, *randhra*, *śvana*, *vapā*, and *suṣi* [are synonyms for hole]. Others say they refer to the openings for the hands, feet, and movement of elephants; the term *rāṇe* is well-known in common vernacular usage. *Nidrā*, *śayana*, *khāpa*, *svapna*, and *saṃveśa*—these five are the names for sleep. *Tandrī*, *sandriḥ*, *tandrā*, *pramīlā*—these two [names] refer to that lassitude which occurs at the beginning or end of sleep, or which consists of the incapacity of all the senses due to extreme fatigue and the like. *Akuṭi*, *śruṭi*, *dhūṭi* [are synonyms for a frown].

*Dhruva*, *kṛti*, and *kauṭilya* [mean crookedness]. Because it belongs to the *udārādi* group, there is also the form *bhūpaṭī*. This refers to the state of being bent (*bhūvakratā*) produced by anger and the like. *Bhairūpya* means deformity (*akasavat*). *Adṛṣṭi* is one term for an ungentle or angry eye—that is, an ungentle or unsightly, contrary gaze; the meaning is a cruel look (*krūradṛṣṭi*). *Saṃsiddhi* and *prakṛti* [mean nature]. (37) *Kharūpa*, *kha*, *rūpa*, *nisarga*: these five are synonyms for *svabhāva* (nature). It is stated that these two [terms] are feminine in order to indicate their female gender.

*Vepathuḥ* means trembling; *ve* is the prefix for trembling. *Kṣaṇaḥ*: "A *kṣaṇa* may mean a specific point of time, a festival, an opportunity, intoxication, the state of being incapacitated by activity, or dependence on another," according to Hemachandra. *Uddharṣaḥ*, *mahaḥ*, *uddhavaḥ*, and *utsavaḥ*—these five denote a festival. *Mahaḥ* ends in a short vowel (*adantaḥ*). [End of Section 7] The section on the theater (*nāṭyavarga*) is concluded. *Adhomukham* means downward-facing; it is both *adhas* (down) and *bhuvanam* (the world). *Pātālam* is the subterranean realm of Bali; it is the *rasātalam*, the world of the *nāgas*, and the place where *pātāla* resides.

*Kuhara*, *supīra*, *tālavyādi* (beginning with the palatal *t*), *vivara*, *bila* ||1|| *Chidra*, *niyanthana*, *roka*, *randhra*, *va* (the last being *tālavyādi*). *Vapā* is that in which something is sown (*upyate*); from the root *vap* with the suffix *aṅ* due to its inclusion in the *midādi* group; it is feminine. *Supis* and *śuṣis*—these eleven denote a hole or cavity. *Supis* is feminine. That which is a pit (*gartā*) in the earth is called *avaṭa*; this [term] refers to a hole in the ground. [From the *Amarakośa*, First Book: "Garta" and "avaṭa" refer to a pit in the earth; "suṣira" refers to anything having a hole or cavity, and is used in three genders. ||2||

*Andhakāra*, *dhvānta*, *tamisra*, *timira*, and *tamas* are synonyms for darkness (the last being used in all genders). In dense darkness, it is called *andhatamasa*; when the darkness has diminished, it is *avatatamasa*. (3) When it is pervasive, it is *saṃtamasa*. The Nāgas are the sons of Kadrū; their lord is Śeṣa, also known as Ananta. Vāsuki is the king of serpents. Then, *gonasa* (4) refers to the *tilitsa*. Both *śayu* and *vāhasa* denote the *ajagara* (boa constrictor). *Alagarda* and *jalavyāla* are synonyms for the water-snake. *Rājila* and *ḍuṇḍubha* are equivalent terms. (5)

*Māludhāna*, *mātulāhi*, *nirmukta*, and *muktakacuka* refer to a snake that has recently cast its skin. *Sarpa*, *padāku*, *bhujaga*, *bhujaṅga*, *hiri*, and *bhujaṅgama* are synonyms for a serpent. According to Hemachandra, *avaṭi* and *kukundara* denote a hole or pit; *gartā* is also used. As stated by Ramasena in the section on masculine and feminine genders, "śaṭhaka-saragarta-śuṅgāḥ" [are masculine]. *Avaṭi* may also end in a long vowel (*avaṭī*). *Suṣira* is a single term for anything possessing a cavity or being perforated. *Aṣira* is also used for this; it is triliṅga (of all three genders) when used as an adjective. 2–6. *Avaṭe kukundare*—Hemachandra. *Gartā* is also used. "Śaṭhaka-saragarta-śuṅgāḥ"—from Ramasena’s section on masculine and feminine genders. *Avaṭi* also ends in a long vowel. *Suṣiram* is one word for a hollow or a thing endowed with a hole. *Aṣiram* is also used; it is triliṅga (in all three genders). 2.

*Andhakāraḥ*, *dhvāntam*, *tamisram*, *timiram*, and *tamaḥ*—these five are synonyms for darkness (*andhakāra*). Among them, *andhakāraḥ* is used in both the neuter and masculine genders. When the darkness is dense and excessive, it is called *andhatamasam* (one term). When the darkness has diminished, it is called *avatamasam* (one term). Pervasive darkness that spreads everywhere is called *sattamasam*. The words *andhatamasam*, *avatamasam*, and *saṃtamasam* end in the vowel *a*; the suffix *aC* is applied here according to the rule "from *ava*, *sama*, and *andha*" (*avasamandhebhyaḥ*) to form the compound ending. This is one [term].

"Nāgāḥ" and "kādraveyāḥ"—these two denote serpents (*nāga*). "Vadīśvaraḥ," "nāgānām īśaḥ," and "śeṣaḥ" or "anantaḥ"—these two denote Śeṣa, the lord of serpents. "Vāsukiḥ" and "sarparājaḥ"—these two denote the king of serpents (*nāgarāja*). "Gonasaḥ" (the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa* states: "gonāsa" and "gonasa")—[denotes the same]. || 4 || "Tilitsaḥ" and [another term]—these two denote the snake known as *pāṇasa*. "Ajagaraḥ," "śayuḥ," and "vāhasaḥ"—these three denote the boa constrictor known as *āra*. "Alagardaḥ" (also "alagarddhaḥ") and "jalavyālaḥ"—these two denote the water-snake.

*Pānasarpa* (pānasarpa), *viroleṃ* (viroleṃ), and so forth, are names for the well-known [venomous snake]. *Rājila* (rājila)—also spelled *rājīla*—and *iṇḍama* (iṇḍama), beginning with the third letter of the dental class (*tavarga*), are two names for the non-venomous, two-faced snake known as *māluṇḍa*, *mahāndula*, or *dutoṇḍe*. This is according to the lexicon which states: "A non-venomous snake is called *nirmukta*, *rājila*, and *parikīrtita*. *Mālughāna* (mālughāna) and *mātulāhi* (mātulāhi) are two names for the variegated snake shaped like a bedstead, known as *ādholeṃ* or *divaḍa*.

*Nirmukta*: "Nirmukta" means one who has abandoned attachment; it is also found in another lexicon (*kośāntara*) as "nirmukta, muktaka, śuka, bhogin. *Muktaka* and *śuka*—these two denote one whose slough (*kabuka*) has been cast off; here, *kabuka* refers to the skin. *Sarpa*, *pradāku*, *bhujaga*, *bhujaṅga*, *ahi*, and *bhujaṅgama* [denote a snake]. [It is called] *bhujaṅga* because it moves with its body (*bhuja*) in a crooked manner (*kauṭilya*). *Āśīviṣa* (also *āśīrviṣa*): the *āśī* is the palate... [The rest of the verse continues: *āśīviṣa*, *viṣadhara*, *vakra*, *vyāla*, and *sarīsṛpa*.

Kuṇḍalī, gūḍhapāt, cakṣuḥśravas, kākodara, and phaṇin; || 7 || darvīkara, dīrghapṛṣṭha, daśana, bileśaya, uraga, pannaga, bhogin, jihmagā, and pavanāśana. || 8 || ("Le lihāna, dvirasana, gokarṇa, kañjakī, as well as kumbhīnasa, phaṇadhara, haribhogadhara, and likewise [others]. || 1 || 66: The body is called *bhoga*; the fang of a snake is *āśī* or *ahidaṃṣṭrikā*.")

1 || (1) Poisonous bone and so forth belong to the three [categories]; however, the hood (*phaṇā*) belongs to two [of them]. *Kañcuka* and *nirmoka* are synonyms for the sloughed skin. *Kṣveḍa*, *garala*, and *viṣa* denote poison. || 9 || *Kākolaka*, *kālakūṭa*, *hālāhala*, *saurāṣṭrika*, *śauklikeya*, *brahmaputra*, *pradīpana*, *dārada*, and *vatsanābha*—these nine are varieties of poison. [In the section on Pātāla, group 64: "The fang (*daṃṣṭrā*) has gone; one pierced by it does not live."]

In this context, regarding the term *viṣama* (poisonous), it refers to a venomous snake (*viṣadhara*), a hooded snake (*cakrin*), or a serpent (*vyāla*). According to the *Viśva* and *Medinī* lexicons: "The word *vyāla* denotes a wicked elephant, a serpent, a villain, a beast of prey, and a lion. [Also] *vyāḍa*. *Sarīsṛpa*, *kuṇḍalī*, *gūḍhapāt*, *cakṣuḥśravas*, *kākodara*, *phaṇī*, *darvīkara*, *dīrghapṛṣṭha*, *daṃdaśūka*, *bileśaya*, *uraga*, *padmaga*, *bhogī*, *jilaga*, and *pavanāśana*—these twenty-five are synonyms for a snake. *Lelihāna* and *ayaṭa* refer to snakes in general.

*Bhoga* (the body) is one term for the serpent’s body. *Āśīḥ* and the following two terms refer to the serpent’s fangs. That which consists of the poison-fang and so forth is called *āheya* (belonging to a snake); this is one term. In the feminine, it is *āheyī*. *Sphaṭā*, *phaṭā*, and *phaṇā*—these two [latter] terms refer to the hood; both are used for both genders. *Kabukaḥ* and *nirmokaḥ*—it is shed (*mucyate*) by means of the skin; these two refer to the serpent’s slough. *Kṣveḍaḥ*, *garalam*, and *viṣam*—since it is stated that *viṣam* is used in the masculine as well as when neuter, and that it is connected with the word "poison" (*viṣeṇa*), these three terms denote poison in general.

9–10. Kākola, kālakūṭa, halāhala, saurāṣṭrika, śauklikeya, brahmaputra, pradīpana, dārada, and vatsanābha—these nine are the varieties of stationary (sthāvara) poisons. Among them, the first three beginning with kākola are [toxic] for both women and men. Kākola is black like a crow; kālakūṭa arises from the blood of the Daitya Pṛthumālī; halāhala has the shape of a palm leaf.

*hālāhala*, *hālahala*, and *halāhala*—these are also its names. [Note: This half-verse is not found even in the palm-leaf manuscript. 11. A physician of poisons is a *jāṅgulika*; one who catches snakes is an *ahituṇḍika*. Thus ends the section on the underworld and serpents (Section 8). 1. *bhāraka*, *naraka*, *niraya*, and *durgati* (feminine) denote hell. Its specific varieties are *tapana*, *avīci*, *mahāraurava*, and *raurava*.

The *Saṃghāta*, *Kālasūtra*, and so forth are the names of the hell-beings (*nāraka*). The *Pretas* are the river *Vaitaraṇī*. *Nirṛti* is *Alakṣmī* (misfortune). [Note: *Hālāhala*, *Hālahala*, and *Halāhala* are synonyms for poison, according to the *Dvirūpakośa*: "They call it Hālāhala, Hālahala, and also Halāhala. The *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa* states: "Gonāsa and Gonasa; Hālāhala and Hālahala are poison. That which originates in the country of Surāṣṭra is *Saurāṣṭrika*; it is also called *Sāroṣṭrika*. That which comes from *Śuklikā* is *Śauklikeya*.

*Somala* is well known [as a type of poison]. A *brahmaputra* is the son of Brahmā; for instance, Yājñavalkya said: "O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in truth and righteousness. That which inflames the stomach is *pradīpana*. *Dārada* is that which originates in the Darada country, namely *vatsanābha*, well known as *bacanāga*. A *viṣavaidya* and a *jāṅgulika* are two terms for a physician who removes poison—one who studies or knows the *jāṅgulī*, the science of poisons. And it is said:

"Parīkṣit was attended by physicians who ate together with him and were skilled in finger-medicine. A *vyālagrāhī* is a snake-catcher; *ahituṇḍika* means one whose mouth (*tuṇḍa*) is directed toward snakes (*ahi*). [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "one who deals with that. These two terms refer to a snake-catcher, known as a *gāruḍī*. There is a reading *vyālagrāsāhituṇḍika*; in that case, *āhituṇḍika* [is used]. Thus ends the section on those who move in the underworld (*pātālamogivarga*). 8. *Nāraka*, *naraka*, *niraya*, and *durgati*—these four are synonyms for hell. He now states the subdivisions of hell.

*Tapana*, *Avīci*—where no *vīci* (pleasure) exists; for the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *vīci* may mean a very small wave, an opening, or pleasure. *Mahāraurava*, *Raurava*; *Saṃghāta* (also read as *Saṃhāra*), *Kālasūtra*, and others such as these are the various types of hells beginning with *Tapana*. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), *Āmisra*, *Kumbhīpāka*, and so forth are included. It is called *Tapana* because beings are tormented (*tapyate*) therein. Although appearing like water, it consists of a surface of stone where there are no waves (*vīci*); thus it is *Avīci*.

The *Raurava* hell is so named because it is connected to the *ruru*, which are extremely cruel flesh-eaters (*ṛvyāda*). The *Mahāraurava* is a great hell related to those same beings. A single term, *vṛkṣavāṭikā*, refers to the private grove belonging to ministers or courtesans. (2) A grove intended for the king’s recreation together with his common women or others is called either an *ākrīḍa* or an *udyāna*. Regarding this, the *Amaramālā* states: "This [grove] is known as an *ākrīḍa* or an *udyāna*," thus indicating that *ākrīḍa* may also be used in the neuter gender.

Therefore, if it is suitable for the sporting of the queens of the harem, it would be a *pramadavana* (pleasure grove). [The rule] "In the case of *chāyā*, there is shortening in technical names and Vedic usage" applies here; thus the vowel is shortened. (1) A *vīthī* (path/row), *āli*, *āvali*, *pati*, and *śreṇī*—these five are synonyms for a row. [The rule] "The feminine suffix *ḍīp* is optional; otherwise, it is also *vīthi*. Regarding *āli* and the following three, they may also end in a long vowel when *ḍīp* is applied. *Śreṇī* may also end in a short vowel. (2) *Lekhā*, *rekhā*, and *rājayaḥ*—these two refer to lines. A *pati* is a row with intervals; a *lekhā* is one without intervals. (3)

As [stated] by Bhāskara: "The collection of forests is *vanya*—this is one term. Regarding the newly sprouting fresh shoot, *aṅkura* is one term; Halāyudha states: "*Aṅkura* is so called. (4) 46. Tree (*vṛkṣa*): *mahīruha*, *śākhī*, *viṭapī*, *pādapa*, *taru*, *anokaha*, *kuṭa*, *śāla*, *sāla*. Regarding *sāla*: "The word *sāla* refers to the *sarja* tree, as well as a tree in general and a rampart," according to [Halāyudha]. "The word *sāla* may denote a tree in general or a rampart," according to the *Medinī* and *Viśva* lexicons.

*Palāśī*, *druma*, and *agama*—these three are for a tree [in general]. (5) A tree characterized by flowers and produced fruits is a *vānaspatya*; this is one term for the mango tree (*āmra*) and others. A tree characterized by fruits produced without flowers is a *vanaspati*; this is one term for the jackfruit (*panasa*), the fig tree (*udumbara*), and others. The term *vanaspati* may also be used for any tree in general; as the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *vanaspati* applies to any tree, except for a fruit-bearing tree that does not flower. Those plants whose life ends precisely with the ripening of their fruit are called *oṣadhi*.

One [name] is for rice, barley, and so forth. Alternatively, there is the reading: "An *oṣadhi* is that which ends with the ripening of its fruit. With the feminine suffix *ḍīṣ*, it becomes *oṣadhī*. [From here begins] the second section (*kāṇḍa*). Plants that end with the ripening of their fruit are called *oṣadhyaḥ*. *Avandhyaḥ*, *phalegrahiḥ*—these two denote a tree that bears fruit. *Vandhyaḥ*, *aphalaḥ*, *avakeśī*—these denote a barren or fruitless tree. *Phalavān*, *phalinaḥ*, *phalī*—these denote one possessed of fruit. *Praphulla*, *utphulla*, *saṃphulla*, *vyākośa*, *vikaca*, *sphuṭa*, *phulla*—these denote that which has blossomed or opened. The words beginning with *avandhya* (barren) apply to all three genders (*triṣu*).

A *sthāṇu* is a fixed wooden stake; a *kṣupa* is a shrub that has no branches or roots. (8) A *stamba* and a *gulma* refer to plants without a trunk. A *vallī*, *vratati*, and *latā* denote a creeper. A *pratāninī*, *vīrudh*, *gulminī*, and *ulapa* also signify a spreading creeper. (9) The height of trees and the like is called *ucchrāya*, *utsegha*, and *ucchraya*. (3-4) One that bears fruit is called *aphala* or *phalegrahi*; it is termed *phalegrahi* because it "grasps" (*gṛhṇāti*) fruits.

By the rule *phalegrahirātmabhariśca*, the substitution of *e* for the final vowel of the upapada and the suffix *in* are applied irregularly to the root *grah*. These two [terms] refer to one who bears fruit at the proper time. (6) Thus ends the section on *vandhya*. *Bandhya*: that which is fit for binding; it refers to three things: one that is fruitless and barren (*avakeśī*), even during its season. *Phalavān*, *phalina*, and *phalī*: these three denote that which possesses fruit. An example is *phalino dantaḥ* ("a tooth with a pulp-cavity"). *Praphulla*, *utphulla*, *saṃphulla*, and *vyākośa*: [these denote a flower that has blossomed].

“Or ending in *mūrddhan*”: *vikaca*, *sphuṭa*, *phulla*—these eight denote that which has blossomed or flowered. Words beginning with *avandhya* (such as *avandhya*, *aphala*, etc. and ending with *vikasita* belong to all three genders (*triṣu*). *Sthāṇu*, *dhruva*, and *śaṅku*—these three refer to the trunk of a tree that has been cut; or else, the word *sthāṇu* optionally denotes a male (*pumān*). Due to the difference in form, it is neuter (*napuṃsakatvam*). Alternatively, there is the reading *sthāṇur astrī*. “*Sthāṇu* is masculine in the sense of a peg or the god Śiva.”

According to the *Medinī* lexicon, *dhruva* is not feminine (*astrī*). A branch (*śākhā*) is well known. A root (*śiphā*) is the base of a tree. That which has short branches and roots is called a shrub (*kṣupa*); this is one term [for such a plant]. That which lacks a trunk (*prakāṇḍa*) is a bush; for that, there are two terms: *stamba* and *gulma*. A creeper is *vallī*, formed by the suffix *in* added to all roots. Thus, *vallī* and *vellī* are both used. Vācaspati states: "The creeper is *vallī*, *vellī*, and *saraṇa*. A spreading vine is *vratati*. Ilāyudha states: "*Pratati*, *vratatī*, *pratati*, and *vratati* are synonyms."

*Latā-trayam* refers to three terms for a creeper. *Vīrut*, *gulminī*, and *ulapa*: these three denote a creeping plant that spreads by means of branches and the like; this is the meaning. Among them, the word *vīrut* ends in a dental *t* and is feminine. (9) *Nagādyārohaḥ*: the height of trees and such; there, *ucchrāyaḥ*, *utsedhaḥ*, and *ucchrayaḥ*—these three [denote it]. Regarding *ārohaḥ*, it is used in the sense of length. As Hemacandra states: "Āroha denotes length, height, the hips of a woman, a specific measure, and also a staircase or the mounting of an elephant."

By the phrase *nagādhāroha* ("climbing a mountain") and so forth, there is the inclusion of mountains, temples, and the like; as well as *utse-dham*. According to the *Medinī*: "The word *utsedha* is not feminine; it denotes height (*ucchraya*) and also firmness (*saṃhanana*). *Prakāṇḍa*: *Prakāṇḍa* is not feminine; it is synonymous with *skandha*. It refers to that part of a tree which extends from the root up to the beginning of the branches. (10) *Śākhā* and *latā* are synonyms. *Skandhaśākhā* and *śālā* are synonyms for the main branch. *Śiphā* and *jaṭā* are synonyms for the aerial roots. (11)

A shoot that grows from a branch or a root is called *śiphā-ruha*; a creeper that has gone from the root to the top is a *latā*. The word *śiraḥ* or *śikharam* (neuter) means the top; *mūlam* or *buvaḥ* (masculine) means the root. *Sāraḥ* or *majjā* (masculine) means the pith; *tvak* (feminine) means the bark, as do *valkam* and *valkalam* (both neuter). *Kāṣṭham*, *dāru*, and *indhanam* mean wood or fuel; *edhmaḥ*, *medhaḥ*, *samit* (feminine), and *idhmam* (neuter) refer to sacrificial fuel. *Niṣkuhaḥ* or *koṭaram* (neuter) means a hollow or cavity in a tree; *valarī* and *marīciḥ* (both feminine) mean a fissure. *Skandhaḥ* refers to the portion of a tree beginning from the root and extending to the branches.

There is also a reading: "of a tree from the root up to the branches. The space between the root and the trunk of a tree is called the *prakāṇḍa* (10). *Śākhā*, *latā*, and *deśākhā* refer to a branch. *Skandhaśākhā* and *śālā* are two terms for the principal branch; the meaning is a branch produced first from the trunk. *Śiphā* and *jaṭā* are two terms for the root of a tree, commonly known as *pāla*. The root of a branch is called *avaroha* (singular), commonly known as *pārogā* or *pāranī*.

A creeper, such as *guḍūcī* and others, that extends from the root—that is, starting from the base of the tree up to its tip—is called an *avaroha*; this is one [synonym]. It is also said: "A *śiphā* or *latā* is that which has grown upward from the root. (11) That which is at the head [of the tree] is called a *śikhara*. Some maintain that *śiras*, *agra*, and *śikhara* are all synonyms. The meaning is that *śikhara* may be used in the masculine gender as an alternative. *Mūla* and *budhna* (also *adhna*) are names for the base of a limb; they are synonymous with the term *pāda*.

There are three [terms] for the root of trees and the like: *sāra* and *majjā*. These two refer to the hard part of trees and the like, known as *gābhā* and *nāra*. Among them, *majjā* ends in a nasal (*-n*). In the masculine (*nari*), it is used; though in some places it is seen ending in *-t* as well. The reading is: "Sāra and majjā are synonyms; *tvak* is feminine. "Synonyms" means they share the same gender. *Tvak*, *valka*, and *valkala*—these three denote the bark. Among them, the pair beginning with *valka* is both neuter and masculine. (12) *Kāṣṭha* is wood; elsewhere it is called *dāru*. Since it is stated that *dāru* is both masculine and neuter.

Two terms refer to a piece of wood: *indhana*, *edha*, *ima*, and *eṣa* (the latter five) denote dry grass, wood, and so forth; the first three denote dry grass, wood, and so forth that are being ignited—that which is commonly known as *jalaṇa*. It is held that the last two refer to the sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) and such being offered at sacrifices and the like. Among them, the first word *eṣa* ends in *s* and is neuter; the other ends in *t* and is masculine. *Samiddha* is the end [of the series]. *Niṣkuha* and *koṭara* are two terms for a hollow or cavity within a tree; *koṭara* may be feminine or, in another view, masculine.

*Vallarī* and *mañjarī*—according to the *gaṇasūtra* "kṛdikārādaktinaḥ," they also appear as *vallarī* and *mañjarī*. These two terms refer to the fresh sprout of *tulasī* and other plants, specifically that which is known as *kaisara*. *pallava* (masculine/neuter) and *kisalaya* denote a young sprout; *vistāra* and *viṭapa* (not feminine) denote the spreading branches of a tree. The fruit of trees and other plants is called *phala*; the stalk that attaches it is *vṛnta*. The term *śalāṭu* refers to an unripe fruit, while *vāna* refers to a dried one; both [the latter two] apply to three genders. *Kṣāraka* and *jālaka* (neuter) denote a cluster of buds; *kalikā* and *koraka* (masculine) denote a bud. *Gucchaka*, *stabaka*, *kuḍmala*, and *mukula* (not feminine) denote a cluster of blossoms. *Sumanas* (feminine plural), *puṣpa*, *prasūna*, *kusuma*, and *suma* denote a flower.

13–16: According to Hemacandra, *parṇa* and *patra* both mean "leaf. *Pallava* and *kisalaya* (the latter also being *kiśalaya*) are two terms for the joint (*parvan*) of a branch that is covered with leaves and so forth; among these, *kisalaya* is used in both the masculine and neuter genders. Vyāḍi, however, states: "The word *pallava* is used in both the masculine and neuter genders. *Viṭapa* is said to be one term for the expanse (*ābhoga*) characterized by the collection of branches and shoots (*śākhā-pallava*). This is supported by the Medinīkośa: "The word *viṭapa*—not feminine—is used for a clump, a branch, an expanse, and a shoot."

According to the *Rabhasa* lexicon: "The word *viṭapa* is used for a branch (*śākhā*), a sprout (*pallava*), a trunk (*stamba*), and a spreading mass (*vistāra*)," and it is not feminine. Alternatively, these four terms beginning with *pallava* may have a single meaning. Regarding this, Kātya has stated: "That which is above the trunk of a tree is a branch (*śākhā*); a *kaṭaka* is considered a *viṭapa*. (14) The phrase "of trees and so forth" also connects with what precedes. The fruit of trees and so forth is called *sasya*. [It is] one term, though some say it begins with the *tālavya* class of consonants. That by which flowers and such are bound is called *vṛnta*; that is one term.

"Deṭha" is known as "ḍeṅkha. Kātya says that the stalk (*vṛnta*) is the support for flowers. *Śalāṭu* is the single term for an unripe fruit. *Vāna* is the single term for a dried fruit. Both *śalāṭu* and *vāna* are used in three genders when referring to the three genders [of the objects they qualify]. (15) *Kṣāraka* and *jālaka* are two terms for a fresh bud; some say they refer to its stalk. Among these, *jālaka* is exclusively neuter. *Kalikā* and *koraka* are two terms for an unblossomed flower, known as "kalī."

*Gucchakaḥ* (guccha) and *stabakaḥ* (stabaka)—these two terms refer to a cluster of young shoots (*pallava*) covered with buds and the like; some say they refer to a bud about to blossom. Rudra, in his list of words ending in dental consonants, states: "The word *gutsa* is said to mean a cluster, a type of necklace, and also a stalk. Rantideva, in his list of words ending in palatal consonants, states: "*Guccha* refers to a cluster of flowers and the like. *Kulaḥ* and *mukulaḥ*—these two terms refer to a bud that has slightly opened. *Sumanasaḥ*, *puṣpam*, *prasūnam*, and *kusumam* are synonymous. || 16 ||

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "In the case of all things that are equally good, it should be treated as if it were the object of expression. There are four names for a flower; *kusuma* and *sumam* are also found in the readings. Among these, there are five names for a flower: according to the *Ratnakośa*, "the word *sumanas* is feminine"; according to the *Medinīkośa*, "*sumanāḥ* [is used] in the feminine for a flower and the *mālatī* jasmine. *Makaranda* and *puṣparasa* are two terms for the nectar of a flower. *Parāga* and *sumanorajaḥ* are two terms for the pollen of a flower.

*Parāga* refers to the pollen of flowers (the dust of blossoms). *Makaranda* is the nectar of the flower; *parāga* is also the dust of the *sumanas* (flower). (17) In the case of fruiting, all terms are declined in the neuter gender, except for *harītakī* and others, which remain feminine. The words *āśvattha*, *vaiṇava*, *plākṣa*, *naiyagrodha*, and *audumbara* denote the fruit of those respective trees. (18) The word *bārhatam* denotes the fruit of the *jambū*; *jambū* is feminine, while *jambu* and *jāmbavam* are neuter. Words such as *jātī* and others denote the flower according to their own specific gender; however, words like *vrīhi* (rice) denote the fruit according to their own specific gender. (19)

The group beginning with *vidārī* is feminine even when referring to the root; *pāṭalā* is also neuter when referring to the flower. *Bodhidruma*, *caladala*, *pippala*, and *kuñjarāśana* [are synonyms] for the *aśvattha*. Furthermore, *dāḍhitya*, *prāhi*, and *manmatha* apply to the *kapittha*; they also apply to *dhūli* and *khāniya*. According to another lexicon: "[They are] famous as a type of mountain, as a type of eclipse, and as sandalwood. (17) All [these terms], including those to be mentioned hereafter, denote trees and creepers that are distinct from [the categories of] gendered nouns, even though they possess masculine and feminine genders.

The designation of trees such as the *aśvattha* and *kapittha* applies to their offspring—namely the flower, fruit, and root—but it should be understood as being devoid of those [specific parts]. The meaning is that the neuter gender is "devoid of two," namely female and male; for example: *camparka*, *āmra*, *sūraṇa*, and so forth. Regarding this, he states a specific rule: the fruit of the *harītakī* is called *harītakī*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one includes *kośātakī*, *karkaṭī*, *drākṣā*, and so on. The fruit of the *aśvattha* is *āśvattha*; the fruit of the *veṇu* is *vaiṇava*.

The fruit of the *lakṣa* is *plākṣam*; the fruit of the *nyagrodha* is *naiyagrodham*; the fruit of the *ikudī* is *aikudam*; the fruit of the *bṛhatī* is *bāītam*. Each [of these takes the suffix] *-aṇ*. This is because of the re-enactment of the rule for *-aṇ* by the sūtra "lakṣādibhyo’ṇ" (Pāṇini 4.3.167). The meaning is that there is no elision (*lup*) of the suffix after words such as *aśvattha* when referring to the fruit. *Jambūḥ*, *jambu*, and *jāmbavam*—these three denote the fruit of the *jambū*. Words such as *jātī*, *yūthikā*, and *mallikā*, when denoting flowers, are feminine only and not neuter.

Likewise, the flower of the *jāti* plant is called *jātī*, as is a woman [of that name]. Grains (*vrīhi*) retain their own gender when referring to their fruit; for example, the fruits of *vrīhi* are called *vrīhayaḥ* in the masculine. In this same way, *māṣa*, *udumbara*, and others should also be understood. For example, the fruit of *māṣa* is called *māṣāḥ*. (19) Plants such as *vidārī*, *bṛhatī*, and *aṃśumatī* also retain their own gender when referring to their root; for example, the root of *vidārī* is called *vidārī*. By the use of the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that they also retain their own gender when referring to their flower; for example, the flower of *pāṭalā* existing in its feminine form is *pāṭalā*; for instance, the flower of *pāṭalā* is called *pāṭalam*.

Because of the word *api* (also), it is also feminine (*svaliṅgā*). According to the *Śāśvata* lexicon, it is also masculine: "The *pāṭala* is a flower, a color, and also the *āśuvrīhi* rice; it is *pāṭala*. *Bodhidrumaḥ*, *caladalaḥ*, *pippalaḥ*, and *kuñjarāśanaḥ* [are synonyms]. It is eaten by an elephant (*kuñjara*); from the root *as* in the sense of "eating," with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*). These five names belong to the *pippala* tree. *Aśvatthaḥ* [is another name]. "Dvandvāni express a state [of being] through action. A pair (*yugma*), a couple (*yugula*), a pair (*yuga*), and a triad (*traya*) belong to the category of pairs. (40) The remainder of the definition is that the various types of groups (*vṛndabheda*), which are specific kinds of collections, will now be described.

The words *jaghanyaja*, *kaniṣṭha*, *yavīyas*, *avaraja*, and *anuja* denote one born later (the younger brother). *Amāṃsa*, *durbala*, and *chāta* mean weak. *Balavat*, *māṃsala*, and *aṃsala* mean strong or muscular. *Tundila*, *tundi*, *bhastaṇḍi*, *bṛhatkukṣi*, and *picaṇḍila* mean having a large belly. Two terms for old age (*jarā*) follow: *vikhasā* (that by which one trembles) and *jarā* (that by which the limbs decay). *Uttānaśayā*, *ḍimbhā*, *stanapā*, and *stanaṃdhayī*—these four refer to a suckling infant. The following three terms will be explained in the masculine; they are here indicated in the feminine form.

This is for the purpose of showing the difference in form when [the suffix] *strītva* (femininity) is applied. Although the word *ḍimbha* is mentioned in the section on the lion and other [animals], it is stated here again to demonstrate that it takes the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. *Bāla* and *māṇavaka*—these two denote a child (*bāla*). One is a child until the age of sixteen. *Vayastha*: [it is so called because he] "stays in his youth" (*vayas*). [The Viśvakośa states: "In the sense of a bird, *vayas* refers to childhood and so forth; in its primary sense, it refers to youth. *Taruṇa*, *yuvan*—these three denote a young man (*yuvan*).

*Pravayas*, *sthavira*, *vṛddha*, *jīna*, *jīrṇa*, *jaran*, and *pakva* refer to one who is old; [the forms] *pravayasau* and *jarantau* are dual endings. (42) *Varṣīyān*, *daśamī*, and *jyāyān*—these three refer to one who is very old. One who is exceedingly old is *varṣīyān*; the dual forms are *varṣīyāṃsau*. One who possesses the tenth stage of life is called *daśamī*; the suffix *-in* is added to a numeral to denote age. The dual forms are *daśaminau*. *Jyāyāṃsau* is the dual form. *Pūrvaja*, *agrya*, *agrīya*, and *agraja*—these three refer to an elder brother (*jyeṣṭha-bhrātṛ*).

*Pūrvaja* means one born at an earlier time; *jaghanyaja* means one born later, as does *kaniṣṭha* (also *kanīyān*), *yavīyān*, and *yaviṣṭha*—the latter being formed with the suffix *iṣṭhan* according to the rule for expressing excellence (*atiśāyana*). *Avaraja* and *anuja* constitute a group of five terms for a younger brother. One born at a later time is *jaghanyaja*; one born at a subsequent time is *avaraja*. *Amāṃsa*, *durbala*, and *chāta*—these three denote one who is weak. *Chāta* begins with the letter *ca* (as in the *cavarga*). [The root] *cho* means "to cut. There is also a reading *śāta*.

*Balavān*, *māṃsalaḥ*, and *aṃsalaḥ*—these three denote one who is strong. One who possesses strength (*bala*) in the shoulders (*aṃsa*) is called *aṃsalaḥ*. *tundilaḥ*, *tuṇḍilaḥ*, *tundikaḥ*, *tunditaḥ*, *tundibhaḥ* (or *tuṇḍibhaḥ*), *tundī* (or *tuṇḍī*), and *bṛhatkukṣiḥ*—these five denote one with a large belly (*bṛhadudara*). One who has a protuberant belly (*tunda*) is *tundilaḥ*. The suffix *ilac* is added to words beginning with *tunda* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). From *tunda* with the suffix *bha*, we get *tuṇḍibhaḥ*. [Dual: *tuṇḍibhau*]. 44.

44–47. *Avaṭīṭa*, *avanāṭa*, and *avaṭa* refer to one with a sunken nose. *Keśava*, *keśika*, and *keśin* refer to one with abundant hair. *Balina* and *balibha* are synonyms for one who has wrinkles on the abdomen. *Apogaṇḍa* refers to one with deficient limbs; he is also called *vikala*. *Kharva*, *hrasva*, and *vāmana* refer to a dwarf. One who has a drooping lip is called *eḍe-badhiraḥ*; one with a crooked arm is *kuṇiḥ*. (142) [The section on humans, 44] *Avaṭīṭaḥ*, *avanāṭaḥ*, and *avabhaṭaḥ* refer to one with a sunken nose—these four denote a person with a flat nose. The word *narta* is used for the nose itself; thus, because his nose is sunken (*avanāṭa*), the man is called *avaṭīṭaḥ* (using the suffix *ac* after the sense of *arśas* etc.). *Keśavaḥ*, *keśikaḥ*, and "one possessing hair" (*keśavān*) or *keśī*—these three denote one with beautiful hair. He is called *keśavaḥ* because he possesses beautiful hair (*praśastāḥ keśāḥ*).

*Balinaḥ* and *balibhaḥ* are two terms for one whose skin has become wrinkled due to old age. One who possesses a contraction of the skin (*tvaksaṃkoca*) is called *balinaḥ*. (45) *Vikalāṅgaḥ* and *apogaṇḍaḥ* are two terms for one who is deficient in limbs from birth. He is called *apogaṇḍaḥ* because he goes (*gacchati*) in a deficient manner (*apakṛṣṭam*); it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group of compounds. His single part (*ekadeśa*) is *pauṇḍa*, thus he is *pogaṇḍaḥ* or also *paugaṇḍaḥ*. The *Ratnakośa* states: "A *pogaṇḍa* is one with deficient limbs. And Halāyudha says: "A *paugaṇḍa* may be one with deficient limbs."

*Kharvaḥ*, *iṣvaḥ*, and *vāmanaḥ*—these three denote one who is short, known as "khujā. *Kharaṇāḥ* and *kharaṇasaḥ* (ending in *s*) are two terms for one with a sharp nose, known as "saraḷanākīla. *Vigraḥ*, *visraḥ*, *viduḥ*, and *vikhyaḥ* are synonyms. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "one whose nose (*nāsikā*) has departed"; here, the word *nāsikā* is replaced by *khya*. Rabhasa states: "The words *vigraḥ*, *visnuḥ*, and *vināsikaḥ* [denote the same]. *Gatanāsikaḥ* and [the preceding term] are two names for one whose nose is gone, known as "nakṭā."

46. *Khuraṇas* ends in a vowel (*sāntaḥ*), while *khuraṇasaḥ* ends in a consonant (*adantaḥ*); these two refer to one with a deformed nose (*vikaṭanāsikasya*). *Jaḍala*, *jaṭhula*, *kālaka*, and *piplu*—these three refer to a black-colored, specific mark on the body known as *lāsa*. *Tilaka* and *tilakālaka*—these two refer to a bodily mark that, by both shape and color, resembles a black sesame seed (*tila*). *Pratiśyāya* and *vīnasa* (two words) are names for the disease of the nose known as *pīnasa*, commonly called *paḍasa*; this is characterized by the frequent discharge of nasal mucus. According to the *Rabhasa* lexicon: "The word *pratiśyā* may be feminine or masculine. *Strī* (feminine), *kṣut*, *kṣutaṃ*, and *kṣavaḥ* (masculine) denote sneezing. *Kāsaḥ* and *kṣavathuḥ* (masculine) denote coughing. *Śophaḥ*, *vyathuḥ*, and *śothaḥ* denote swelling. *Pādasphoṭaḥ* and *vipādikā* denote cracked feet. *Kilāsa* and *sidhma* denote leucoderma. *Kacchūḥ*, *pāmā*, and *vicarcikā* denote scabies or itchy skin eruptions.

Itch (*kaṇḍū*), scratching (*kharju*), the act of scratching (*kaṇḍūyā*), a pustule (*visphoṭa*), and a pimple (*piṭaka*)—the last being feminine. Ringworm (*koṭha*), circular skin spots (*maṇḍalaka*), leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), and vitiligo (*śvitra*) are synonyms. Hemorrhoids are called *durnāman* and *arśas*. *Kāsaḥ* and *kṣavathuḥ* (two) refer to the disease of cough, known as *khokalā*. *Śophaḥ*, *śvayathuḥ*, and *śothaḥ* (three) refer to swelling, known as *sūja*. *Pādasphoṭaḥ* and *vipādikā* (two) refer to the cracking of the feet, known as the disease of *khoṃṭā phuṭaṇyā*. *Kilāsam* and *sidhmam* (two) refer to *sidhma*, known as white leprosy (*śvetakuṣṭha*). *Kacchūḥ*, *pāmā*, *pāmā*, and *vicarcikā*—this group of four feminine nouns refers to a specific type of itch (*kharjū*).

Regarding the term known as *olī kharūja*: here, *pāmā* is one form ending in a nasal (*n*), as in *pāmānau*; the other ends in *ṭāp*, as in *pāme*. *Kaṇḍūḥ* and *kaṇḍuḥ* [are synonyms]. According to Hemacandra: "*kharjūḥ*, *kharjūrī*, and *kīṭakaṇḍūḥ*. *Kharjūḥ* refers to itching; these three are feminine, as in *kharjūḥ*. *Sukī* and *kharūjā* refer to the plant known as *sukī kharūja*. *Visphoṭaḥ* and *piṭakaḥ* are two terms for what is known as *phoḍa*. In the feminine gender, *piṭakā* and *kṣipakā* are like [the previous terms]. *Vraṇaḥ*, *īrma*, and *aruḥ*—these three denote an ulcer (*vraṇa*). *Īrma* and *aruṣī* [are also used]. That ulcer which constantly oozes is called *nāḍīvraṇa*; this is one term. The mention of "masculine" (*pumān*) is for the purpose of specifying the masculine gender. *Koṭhaḥ*, *maṇḍalakaṃ*, *kuṣṭhaṃ*, and *śvitraṃ*—these four denote leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). Some say that the pair beginning with *koṭha* refers to leprosy in the form of circular patches (such as the unestablished *gajakarṇa*), while the pair beginning with *kuṣṭha* refers to white leprosy (*śvetakuṣṭha*).

*durnāmaka* and *arśas* (two terms) refer to the disease of hemorrhoids, known as *mūlavyādhi* or *arśa*. [Note: "The word *arśas* is also neuter elsewhere.
