There are various types of necklaces (*hāra*), such as the *yaṣṭi*, *guccha*, *gucchārddha*, and *goṣṭana*. An *arghahāra* consists of sixteen strings; a *māṇavaka* consists of twenty-four; and an *ekāvalī* consists of a single string. That same single-string necklace becomes a *nakṣatramālā* when it consists of twenty-seven pearls. An *āvāpaka*, *pārihārya*, *kaṭaka*, and *valaya* are terms for a bracelet (used in the feminine). A *keyūra* and *añjada* are synonyms for an armlet. An *aṅgulīyaka* and *ūrmikā* are synonyms for a ring. A *sākṣarāṅgulimudrā* is a finger-ring engraved with letters. A *kaṅkaṇa* is an ornament for the wrist. For a woman’s waist, the terms *mekhalā*, *kāñcī*, *saptakī*, and *raśanā* are used.

A *sārasana* is for a eunuch, while a *śṛṅkhala* is for a male; these two terms apply to all three genders. Two terms refer to a long necklace hanging down from the neck. That same necklace, when made of gold, is called a *prālambikā* (one term). That same *lalaṃtikā*, if fashioned with pearls, is called an *uraḥsūtrikā* (one term). A *hāra* (necklace) is so called because it captivates (*hiyate*) the mind, or because it causes the mind to be captivated (*hārayati*). A *muktāvalī* (pearl necklace) consists of two types. When that *muktāvalī* has one hundred strings (*yaṣṭikā*) or one hundred strands (*latikā*), it is called a *devacchanda* (one term).

There are two types of divine necklaces (*devacchanda*). Due to differences in the number of rods (*yaṣṭi*) and differences in the types of strings (*latā*), there are various varieties of necklaces such as *guccha* and others. [Note: There is also a reading: *gutsa-gutsārdha-gostanāḥ*. They are as follows: a necklace of thirty-two rods is a *guccha*; one of twenty-four rods is a *gucchārgha*; one of four rods is a *gostana*; one of twelve rods is an *ardhahāra*; one of twenty rods is a *māṇavaka*; and one of a single rod is an *ekāvalī*. That same *ekāvalī*, when composed of twenty-seven pearls, is [the *saptaviṃśati-muktikā*]. *Oṃ.*

A *nakṣatramālā* (star-garland) consists of [twenty-seven] individual [beads]. *Āṣāḍha*, *pārihārya*, *kaṭaka*, and *valaya*—these four denote an ornament for the forearm, known as *poṃcī* and so forth. *Keyūra* and *aṅgada*—both denote an ornament for the upper arm (*pragaṇḍa*), known as *bāhuvaṭe* or *bājubaṃda*. It is called *keyūra* because it joins (*yauti*) the head of the arm (*bāhuśiras*); [the root] *yu* means "to mix. *Aṅgulīyaka* and *ūrmikā*—both denote an ornament for the finger, known as *āṃguṭhī*. || 106–107 ||

If it consists of a single ring joined with syllables such as *rāma* or *nābha*, it is called an *aṅgulimudrā* (finger-ring). A *kaṅkaṇa* is an ornament for the hand; it refers to the ornament for the wrist known as *kāṃkarṇe*. The *Ranakośa* states: "A *kaṅkaṇa* is a *pratisara* (bracelet). A *mekhalā*, *kāñcī*, *saptakī*, and *raśanā*—the latter also having its *ṛ* sound in the middle—are terms for the girdle worn by women, known as *dāba* or *kaṃbarapaṭṭā*. It is an ornament for the waist. *Sārasana* and *pattra* are also names for this.

The tip of the foot is called *pādāṅguṣṭha*, *tulākoṭi*, *majīra*, and *nūpura* (the latter not being feminine). A *haṃsaka* is an anklet (*pādakaṭaka*), and a *kiṅkiṇī* is a small bell. Bark, wood, insects, and wool—these ten are the sources of cloth and are used in the three genders. Cloth made from bark is *vālka*; that from flax and the like is *kṣauma*. Cloth made from cotton is *phāla*, as is that from the *bādara* (jute) plant. Silk (*kauśeya*) arises from the cocoon of insects; cloth made from the hair of wild animals is *rāva*.

*Anāhata* (unbeaten), *niṣpravāṇi* (woven on a shuttle), and *tāntraka* (made of threads) refer to new cloth. That which consists of a pair of washed garments is called *udgamanīya*. *Patroṇa* is washed silk (*dhautakauśeya*), which is very costly and of great value. [From the section on humans: A girdle with a single rod is a *kāñcī*, while one with eight rods is a *mekhalā*. A *rasanā* is known to have sixteen [rods], and a *kalāpa* has twenty-five; these distinctions have not been mentioned here.]

*Śṛṅkhalam* is one term for a man’s waist ornament known as *dorā*; it is also called *śṛṅkhalā* (feminine) or *śṛṅkhalaḥ* (masculine). *Pādāṅgada*, *tulākoṭiḥ*, *mañjīraḥ*, and *nūpuraḥ* [are synonyms]. *Isakaḥ* and *pādakaṭakaḥ* are two terms for the anklet known as *ṣaṅka* or *toraḍyā paiṃjaṇa*. It is held that the pair beginning with *haṃsakaḥ* refers to the foot-ornament known as *vāle*. *Tulākoṭiḥ* is feminine; *mañjīraḥ* is not used in the feminine.

*Kiṅkiṇī* and *kiṅkiṇiḥ* mean *kaṅkaṇī*. Bhāguri states: "The *kaṅkaṇa* is a *pratisara*; the *kaṅkaṇī* is a small bell (*kṣudra-ṣaṇṭikā*). The term *kṣudra-ṣaṇṭikā* refers to two things known as *ghāgarī* or *ghuṃgura*. The group of four beginning with *tvak* (bark) constitutes the source or cause of garments; the meaning is that because there are four types of causes, there are four types of garments. With the exception of the group beginning with *kṣauma*, the ten terms starting from *bālkaja* and ending with *niṣpravāṇi* apply to all three genders.

Regarding the term *tatrakam*: because of the word "and" (*ca*), it is the eleventh [item] among those three; and since it is mentioned in association with the *dukūla* (silk) which is about to be described, *kṣauma* (linen) is exclusively neuter. Among the three [types of garments], these have been stated in the order of their origin from bark and so forth. Garments such as *kṣauma* and others are to be known as *vālka* (made of bark). *Kṣumā* is the flax plant (*atasī*); its derivative product is *kṣauma*. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), *śāṇa* (hemp) and so forth are included. This is one [term for] that. *Phālam*, *kārpāsam*, and *bādaram*—these three refer to the cotton garment, which is a derivative of the fruit.

*Kṛmikośaja* (silkworm-cocoon-born) refers to *kauśeya* (silk), which is a cocoon shaped like a bud produced by silkworms from their anus. *Bhṛgaromaja* (deer-hair-born) is one term for a garment made of wool; here, the word *mṛga* includes all animals, thus it also refers to blankets (*kambala*) and the like. *Anāhata* (unbeaten), *niṣpravāṇi* (without a loom), and *tatra* (freshly brought)—the latter meaning recently acquired—are four names for a new garment, commonly known as *koraṃ vastra*.

That from which the *pravāṇī*—the shuttle for weaving threads—has been removed is called *niṣpravāṇi*. A pair of washed garments (*vatra*) is termed *udgamanīya*, though the word "pair" (*yuga*) is not intended to be emphasized here. [112] Second Book: 159. Washed silk is *kauśeya*; linen is *kṣauma*; and fine cloth is *dukūla*. The two terms *nivīta* and *prāvṛta* apply to three genders (masculine, feminine, and neuter). In the feminine gender, when used in the plural, they denote the fringes of a garment; in the dual, they refer to the two folds of the lower garment. Length is called *dairghya*, *āyāma*, or *āroha*; while circumference is *pariṇāha* or *viśālatā*. [113]

*Paṭacara*, *jīrṇavastra*, *naktaka*, and *karpaṭa* are synonyms for a worn-out garment. *Vastra*, *ācchādana*, *vāsas*, *vasana*, and *aṃśuka* denote clothing in general. *Sucelaka* and *paṭa* (the latter not feminine) refer to a fine cloth; *dharāśi* and *sthūlaśāṭaka* refer to a coarse blanket. *Nicola* and *pracchadapaṭa* are synonyms for a bed-covering; *ralaka* and *kambala* are synonyms for a woolen blanket. *Antarīya*, *upasaṃvyāna*, and *paridhāna* refer to the lower garment (*aghoṃ'śuka*). [The term] *tatpatrorṇa* refers to one [type of such cloth]. That which is of great value, such as fine cloth and the like, is called *mahādhanam*; this is a single term used in all three genders.

*Kṣāma* and *dukūla* are two names for fine silk cloth, known as *pāṭāva*. *Nivīta* and *āvṛta* are two names for a wrapped garment. (113) *Daśāḥ* refers to the fringes at the two ends of a garment; this term is always feminine and plural. However, according to the reading *vastayo dvayoḥ*, *daśāḥ* and *vastayaḥ* both refer to the two ends of a garment. In that context, when feminine and plural, it is *daśāḥ*; when feminine or masculine and plural, it is *vastayaḥ*.

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *daśā* refers to the wick of a lamp, the end of a garment, the earth, and a woman; it is used in the dual for an enema (*nirūha*), and in the plural for the states of life. *Dairghya*, *āyāma*, and *āroha*—the latter being defined as *ānāha* by the author of the *Rāmāśramī*—these three denote the length of cloth and similar objects, known as *lāṃbī*. *Pariṇāha* and *viśālatā* are two terms for width, known as *ruṃdī*. (114) *Paṭṭadhvara* and *jīrṇavastra* are two terms for a worn-out garment.

*Naktaka* (also *laktaka*), *karpaṭa*: these two denote a piece of worn-out cloth, known colloquially as *phaḍaka* or *chāṭī*. *Vastra*, *ācchādana*, *vāsa*, *cela* (*cela*; according to the *Viśva* lexicon: "the word *cala* means 'low' in three genders; in the neuter, it means 'garment'"), *vasana*, *aṃśuka*: these six denote a garment. Regarding *aṃśuka*, the *Rabhasa* lexicon states: "The word *aṃśuka* refers to a white garment, a mere strip of cloth, or an upper garment. *Sucelaka*, *paṭa*: these two denote a fine garment. Among them, *paṭa* is not feminine.

*Varāśiḥ*, *barāsiḥ*, and *barāsiḥ* refer to a coarse cloth (*sthūlaśāṭaka*). Rabhasa states in his lexicon on words ending in dentals that "*varāsiḥ* means a coarse cloth. *Sthūlaśāṭaka* and [the others] are two names for a thick garment. *Nicola* and *nicula* are also used; Medinī states, "*nicula* may mean a cloak (*nicola*). *Pracchadapaṭa*—these two refer to that with which a lute, a cradle, or any such object is covered. *Rallaka* and *kambala* are two names for a woolen blanket. || 116 ||

*Antarīya*, *upasaṃvyāna*, *paridhāna*, and *ardhāṃśuka*—these four terms refer to a lower garment worn around the body. *Ardhāṃśuka* refers to the cloth covering the lower part of the body. *Prāvāra*, *prāvara*, and *bṛhatikā* (117) denote an upper cloak. *Uttarāsaṅga* (117–121) [is also used]. The two terms *prāvāra* and *uttarāsaṅga* are synonymous, as is *bṛhatikā*. *Saṃvyāna* and *uttarīya* refer to an upper garment; *cola* and *kūrpāsaka* (the latter being feminine) refer to a bodice.

*Niśāra* refers to a covering used to ward off cold winds. (118) *Ardhoruka* is a garment for excellent women; *caṇḍātaka* is a synonym, not feminine. *Āprapadīna* applies to all three genders and refers to that which reaches down to the tips of the feet (*āprapadam*). (119) *Vitāna*, *ulloca*, and *dūṣya*—the latter being neuter—are terms for a clothed pavilion or tent. *Pratisīrā*, *javanikā*, and *tiraścī* (or *tiraṣkarī*) refer to a curtain or screen. (120) *Parikarma* is the grooming or refinement of the body; *mārṣṭi*, *mārjanā*, and *mṛjā* are synonyms for cleansing. *Uddharṭana* and *utsādana* are both terms for rubbing or massaging; *ālāva* and *āplava* refer to bathing.

121. *Saṃvyāna* and *uttarīya* refer to that upper garment (*uttarīya*) which is worn over the left shoulder. It is called *uttarāsaṅga* because it is fastened to the upper part of the body (*uttarasmin dehabhāge āsajati*). *Cola* and *kūrpāsaka* are two terms for the bodice (*kañcukī*) known as such, which covers the breasts and other parts of women; the form *colī* also occurs due to the application of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the *gaura*-class. It is called *kūrpāsaka* because it rests upon the elbow (*kūrpara*); it is used in both the masculine and neuter genders.

The *Hārāvalī* states: "A *kūrpāsa* is a half-sleeved bodice (*ardhacolaka*). A cloak (*prāvaraṇa*) that serves as a protection against cold winds and snow is called a *nīśāra*; this is one term for what is commonly known as "rajaī," "dulaī," or "dulaī-lepa. It is so called because one is thoroughly protected (*nitarāṃ śīryate*) from cold winds by means of it. There is a usage such as: "Like a cow that has put on a *nīśāra*. (118) The garment of excellent women which covers the thighs up to the middle is a *caṇḍātaka*; this refers to what is commonly known as "parakara" or "lahangā."

*Ūrdhvorardha* (half of the thighs) refers to the *ardhorū*; by metaphorical extension (*lakṣaṇā*), because it is situated there, the garment is also called *ardhorū*. The suffix *kan* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). That which reaches as far as the toes—that is, up to the end of the feet—is *āprapadīna*, such as a garment or similar item. This one term applies to all three genders. (119) *Vitāna* and *ulloca*: these two refer to the cloth known as *candraka* (lit. "moon"), spread above for the purpose of warding off heat and so forth; it is commonly known as *cāndavā*. In the masculine, it is *vitāna*. *Duṣya* and other such terms refer to a single thing: a tent or a dwelling made of cloth, a house constructed of fabric.

The word *dṛśya* may also have the palatal *ya* (*dṛśyā*). From the first [root], we have *paṭakuṭī*, *ḍerā*, *rāhuṭī*, *taṃbu*, and so forth. *Pratisīrā*, *javanikā*, *yamanikā*, and *tiraskariṇī*—the latter being derived as "that by which something is concealed" (*tiraskriyate 'nayā*)—are three names for a curtain (*javanikā*), known colloquially as *paḍadā* or *kanātha*. (120) *Parikarma* and *aṅgasaṃskāra* are two terms for the mere decoration of the body with unguents and the like. *Parikarma* is an action performed for the purpose of removing foul odors.

The reading *pratikarma* occurs in some versions. *Māṅgalya*, *mārjanā*, and *mṛjā* refer to the cleansing of the body through sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other means. *Udvartana* and *utsādana* (two words) refer to rubbing with ground substances. *Snāna* (bathing), *carcā*, and *cārcikya* refer to anointing or smearing. *Sthāsaka* refers to a mark or paste. Now, *prabodhana*, *anubodha*, *patralekhā*, and *patrāṅguli* are synonymous terms for decorative leaf-designs on the face. *Tamālapatra*, *tilaka*, *citraka*, and *viśeṣaka* refer to forehead marks; the second and fourth of these are not feminine. Furthermore, *kukuma* (saffron).

123–125 || *Kāśmīraja*, *amiśikha*, *vara*, *bāhrīka*, and *pītana* refer to saffron. *Lohitacandana* (red sandalwood) is characterized by its firmness and its indication of the contraction of blood. *Lākṣā*, *rākṣā*, and *jatu* (the latter in the neuter gender) denote lac; it is also called *yāva*, *alakta*, and *brumāmaya*. *Lavaṅga*, *devakusuma*, and *śrīsaṃjña* denote cloves. Then there is *jāyaka*. [Note: Verses 122–125 describe substances for the removal of bodily impurities. *Āplāva* and *āplava* mean bathing. *Snāna*—these three terms denote the act of bathing. 121 ||

*Carcā*, *cārcikya*, and *sthāsaka*—these three refer to a specific type of body anointing with sandalwood paste and other substances, commonly known as *uṭī*. [The term] *cārcikya* is derived from *carcikā* with the suffix *pyañ* added in the sense of the base word itself (*khārthe*). *Prabodhana* and *anubodha*—this pair refers to the re-manifestation of fragrance in that which has lost its scent, such as the application of wine and other liquids to musk and similar substances. *Patralekhā* and *patrāṅgulī*—these two denote the leaf-patterns drawn on the cheeks and other parts of the body using musk, saffron, and so forth. A line in the shape of a leaf is a *patralekhā*.

This [term] is well known in regions such as Kaliṅga and others. *Tamālapatra*. Like the leaf of the *tamāla* tree, it is called *tamālapatra*. According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *tamālapatra* refers to the *tāpiccha* tree, a sectarian mark (*tilaka*), and also to a small leaf. There are four names for the sectarian mark made with musk and other substances on the forehead: *tilaka*, *citraka*, and *viśeṣaka*. Furthermore, according to the *Viśva* lexicon—"The *tamāla* is found in the sense of a sectarian mark and a sword"—the term *tamāla* is also used elsewhere.

In this context, the two terms *dvitīyam* (meaning "the second") and *tilakam*, as well as *turīyam* (meaning "the fourth") and *viśeṣakam*, are not feminine but rather masculine and neuter. *Kuṅkumam* || 123 || [is also neuter]. *Kāśmīrajanma* (born in Kashmir), *agniśikham* (having flame-like tips), *varam* (excellent), *bāḍīkam* (or *bāhikam*), *bāḍhīkam*, and *bāḍikam*—according to the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*, the word *dhīra* refers to asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and not to horses or countries. *Pītanam* (yellowing), *raktam* (red), *saṃkocam*, *piśunam*, *dhīram*, and *lohitacandanam*—these eleven are synonyms for saffron (*kuṅkuma*). According to Hemachandra: "The word *rakta* refers to that which is dyed with indigo and the like, as well as to saffron."

According to the *Viśva* and *Medinī* lexicons: "The word *saṅkoca* refers to a species of fish and to contraction; it is neuter when it means saffron. According to the *Medinī*: "The word *piśuna* also refers to saffron. (124) *Lākṣā*, *rākṣā*, *jatu*, *yāvaḥ*, *alaktakaḥ*, and *drumāmayaḥ*—these six names refer to lac. It is called *alaktaka* because one does not become stained (*lakta*) by it. It is called *drumāmaya* because it is a disease (*āmaya*) of trees (*druma*). *Lavaṅga*, *devakusuma*, and *śrīsaṃjña*—these three names refer to clove. It is the flower of the gods (*devānāṃ kusumam*). Or, it is like a god among flowers (*kusumeṣu deva iva*). Or, it is a flower worthy of the gods (*devayogya kusumaṃ*).

*Śrī-saṃjñam* is a synonym for *lakṣmī*. *Jāyakam* (125). *Kālīyakam*, *kālānusāryam*, and *jāyakam*—these three names refer to the fragrant substance known as yellow sandalwood (*pīta-candana*). *Kālīyakam*, *kālānusāryam*, and *samārthakam* are synonyms. *Vaṃśikā*, *aguru*, *rājārhā*, *loham*, *kṛmijam*, and *joṅgakam* (126) are names for black aloe-wood (*kāla-aguru*). That which is auspicious and has the fragrance of jasmine is called *aguru*.

Yakṣadhūpa, sarjarasa, rāla, sarvarasa, bahurūpa, vṛkadhūpa, kṛtrimadhūpaka, turuṣka, piṇḍaka, siha, yāvana, pāyasa, śrīvāsa, vṛkadhūpa, śrīveṣṭa, and saraladrava [are synonyms] for the well-known [incense]. Jayati, gandhāntara, and jāyaka [are synonyms for another fragrant substance]. Vyāḍi states: "Kālīyaka, kāleya, varṇaka, and kāntidāyaka [are synonyms]."

*Vaṃśika*, *vaṃśaka*, *aguru*, *rājārhā*, *loha*, *kṛmija*, and *joṅgaka*—these seven constitute the group known as *kālāguru*. This means they are synonyms for black aloe wood (*kṛṣṇāguru*). It is called *aguru* because it is not heavy (*na guruḥ*). According to Hemacandra’s lexicon, which states "aguru is used for *joṅgaka* and *laṣu*," *aguru* can also be masculine. In some places it appears as *agaru*. According to the *Medinīkośa*, which states "loha is used for a weapon, iron, *joṅgaka*, and all that is brilliant," *loha* can also be masculine. The word *aguru* is connected with the relative pronoun *yat*.

The word *syāt* (it may be) connects with what follows because it stands at the end [of the preceding phrase]. "That which is *aguru* and has the fragrance of jasmine (*malligandhi*) is auspicious (*maṅgalyā*)"—this is one [definition]. Here, *joḍa़kāntāni* refers to varieties of *aguru*. The pair beginning with *kālāguru* refers to black *aguru* (*kṛṣṇāguru*). Regarding the reading *tvitya taditi*, the meaning is: "that *aguru* which has the fragrance of jasmine is auspicious. *Yakṣadhūpa*, *sarjarasa*, *rāla*, and *sarvarasa* [are synonyms]. (127) *Bahurūpa*—these five are names for the incense known as *rāla*; or it is called *arāla*.

According to the *Rabhasa* lexicon: "rālaḥ, sarjarasaḥ, arālaḥ, dhūpakaḥ, vahnivallabhaḥ. *Vṛkadhūpaḥ* and *kṛtrimadhūpakaḥ* (two) refer to incense made from various ingredients. *Turuṣkaḥ*, *piṇḍakaḥ*, *sihaḥ*, and *yāvanaḥ* (four) are names for the fragrant substance called *siha*, known as "ūda" or "lobāna. The *Viśva* and *Medinī* lexicons state: "turuṣakaḥ [is used] for *siḍaka*, for a Mleccha tribe, and also for another country. *Pāyasaḥ* || 128 || *śrīvāsaḥ*, *vṛkadhūpaḥ*, *śrīveṣṭaḥ*, and *śrīpiṣṭaḥ*.

Regarding the verse beginning with "saraladravaśrīpiṣṭadadhikṣīraghṛtādike," the *Rabhasa* lexicon states: "Saraladrava" refers to the resin of the *sarala* tree—specifically known as the incense named after it—and "pāyasa" is a derivative of *payas* (milk) or *tum* (rice), meaning rice cooked in milk. *Saraladrava* is the liquid extract of the *sarala* or *devadāru* tree. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *pāyasa* is used in the neuter for 'fragrant ointment' (*śrīvāsa*) and in the masculine for 'boiled rice' (*paramānna*). *Mṛganābhi* and *mṛgamada* both mean musk; these three terms refer to musk, though *mṛganābhi* is used in the masculine.

"Mṛganābhiḥ, mṛgamadaḥ, mṛgaḥ, and kastūrikā also [denote musk]," according to Mādhava. "Madaḥ [is used] for semen and for musk," according to the Medinī lexicon. "Nābhiḥ is masculine when it means the navel or the center; [it is also used] for musk. [In this second section: Mṛganābhiḥ, mṛgamadaḥ, and kastūrī [are synonyms for musk]. Now, kolakaṃ, kaṅkolakaṃ, and kośaphalaṃ [denote the kakkola fruit]. Furthermore, karpūraṃ (masculine and neuter), ghanasāraḥ, candrasaṃjñaḥ, sitābhraḥ, and himavālukā [are synonyms for camphor]. 129–130.

Gandhasāra, malayaja, bhadra, śrī, and candana (in the masculine) denote sandalwood. Tailaparṇika and gośīrṣa denote yellow sandalwood (haricandana), which is not feminine. Tilaparṇī and patrāṅga denote the red sandalwood known as rañjana or raktacandana. Kucandana is another name for it. Furthermore, jātīkośa and jātīphala are synonymous terms for nutmeg. Yakṣakardama is a fragrant paste made from camphor, agallochum, musk, and kaṅkola. [Note: According to the Rabhasa lexicon, the word *prāṇya* occurs in two genders; *kastūrikā* and *madā* refer to musk, while *kastūrikā* is also used for the center of a wheel or something preeminent, and in the feminine gender.]

*Kolaka* means *koraka*. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *koraka*—which is not feminine—is used for a bud (*kuḍmala*), as well as for *kaṅkolaka* and the lotus stalk (*mṛṇāla*). (129) *Kaṅkolaka*, *kośaphala*, and *kaṅkola*—these three names refer to the plant known as *kaṅkola* or *gavalā*. *Karpūra*, *ghanasāra*, *candra*, *sitābhra*, and *sitābha*—these five names refer to camphor. The term *candra*, which is synonymous with the moon, is masculine when referring to camphor. (130) *Gandhasāra*, *malayaja*, and *bhadraśrī* [refer to sandalwood].

*Candana* has four [synonyms]. *Candana* refers to that which is known as *Malayāgara* or *Mailāgiri*. *Bhadraśrī* is one [name] for a specific white and cool sandalwood. *Gośīrṣa* is one [name] for sandalwood with the fragrance of a blue lotus (*utpala*). *Haricandana* is one [name] for tawny-colored sandalwood. Thus, there are three varieties. *Tailaparṇī* is produced from a specific tree called *tilaparṇa*; the suffix *kan* is used here in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*). According to Svāmī, "The mines of this [sandalwood] are the *tailaparṇa*, *gośīrṣa*, and mountains. (131)

*Tilaparṇī*, *patrāṅga*, *rañjana*, *raktacandana*, and *kucandana*—these five are varieties of red sandalwood (*raktacandana*). Regarding *tilaparṇī*: it means "that which has a river as its source" (*nadī ākaro 'syāsti*); [the suffix] *ac* and [the feminine suffix] *ṅīṣ* are applied. *Jātīkośa* is *jātīphala* (nutmeg). There is also a reading *jātikośaṃ jātiphalam*. [The word] *jāti* or *jātī* [is used], and *kośaṃ* [means] *phalaṃ* (fruit); these may also be used separately. Rāmāśrama states: "The word *jāti* is also used for *jātīphala*. Medinī and Viśvaprakāśa state: "'*Kośa*' is used for an earring, a leaf, a divine object, the sheath of a sword, and *jātīphala*."

"Phala [is used] in the sense of 'gain,' 'the seed-vessel,' 'the tip of an arrow,' and 'a shield,'" says Rudra. These two [terms] refer to what is commonly known as *jāyaphala*. (132) A specific type of ointment made by combining equal parts of camphor and other ingredients is called *yakṣakardama*; this is one term. Vyāḍi states: "Camphor, agallochum, musk, *kakola*, and saffron—all these combined together are desired as *yakṣakardama*. *Ghusṛṇa* means saffron (*keśara*). The rest is as follows: "Saffron, agallochum, musk, camphor, and likewise sandalwood..."

That which is called *mahāsugandhi* by name is a fragrant substance; it is also known as *gātrānulepanī*, *varti*, or *varṇaka*. *Ālepana* is an ointment for the body. *Vāsayogāḥ* are perfuming powders. That which has been treated with perfumes is called *bhāvita* or *vāsita* (in all three genders). The preparation consisting of perfumes, garlands, and so forth, is termed *adhivāsana*. *Mālya* is a garland worn on the head; *khaja* is one worn amidst the hair. A *garbhaka* is one that hangs from the crest-lock (*śikhā*). One placed in front is a *lalāmaka*.

135–136. That which hangs straight down from the neck is a *prālamba*; when it is thrown across the chest, it is called *vaikakṣika*. A *śikhā* (topknot), *āpīḍa*, and *śekhara* are terms for hair-ornaments worn on the crest. 137. *Racanā*, *parisyanda*, and *ābhoga* denote arrangement or fullness. *Upadhāna* and *upabarhaṇa* refer to a pillow; *śayyā* and *śayanīya* both mean a bed. "Yakṣakardama" [is a specific type of fragrant paste], according to Dhanvantari.

*gātrānulepanī*, *vartiḥ*, *varṇakaḥ*, and *vilepanam*—these four refer to fragrant substances ground and rubbed [into powder], known as *uṭaṇe*, which are suitable for anointing the body. According to the *Rasamañjarī*: "The first two are as already explained; the pair beginning with *varṇaka* refers simply to an ointment such as ground sandalwood and the like. There is also a reading: *karpūrāguru*. (133)

The preparation of perfumed powder (*cūrṇavāsayoga*) consists of two types, such as the powder for perfuming cloth (*paṭavāsa*) and so forth. "Vāsayoga" is a compound meaning a method (*yoga*) or means (*upāya*) for making something fragrant (*vāse sugandhikaraṇe*). "Bhāvita" and "vāsita" are two terms for an object that has been perfumed with a fragrant substance; they apply to all three genders. That refinement (*saṃskāra*) by means of perfumes, garlands, incense, and the like, which imparts fragrance to garments, betel, and so forth, is called *adhivāsana*. This is one term. (134)

*Mālya* and *mālā* are two terms for a garland worn upon the head by one whose strength of flowers is great; this usage applies elsewhere as well through figurative extension (*upacāra*). A garland worn amidst the hair is called *garbhaka* (one). That garland which hangs from the crest-lock (*śikhā*) is called *prabhraṣṭaka* (one). That which is placed in front, extending to the forehead, is called *lalāmaka* (one). That garland which hangs straight down from the neck is called *prālamba* (one).

A garland worn as a side-sash, cast across the chest in a straight line, is called *vaikakṣika*; this is one term consisting of four syllables. [The commentary notes: "Since it is on the *vikakṣa* (the chest), it is also called *vaikakṣaka*. *Āpīḍa* and *śekhara* are two terms for a garland merely placed upon the crest of the hair. *Racanā* and *parisyanda* are two terms for the arrangement of garlands and the like. [The commentary notes: "There is also a reading *parispanda*. *Ābhoga* and *paripūrṇatā* are two terms for the completeness of all ritual offerings.

*Upadhāna* (pillow) and *upabaī* (bolster) are two names for what is known as *ucchīrṣastha*, namely the "uśī" (head-pillow). That upon which the head is placed or supported is called *upadhāna*. *Śayyā*, *śayanīya*, and *śayana*—these three denote a bed. [The word *baī* is used here to indicate its equivalence with the following terms. *Mañca*, *paryaṅka*, *palyaṅka*, and *khaṭvā* are synonymous terms for a bedstead. *Genduka* and *kanduka* refer to a ball. *Dīpa* and *pradīpa* refer to a lamp. *Pīṭha* and *āsana* refer to a seat. || 138 ||

A small box, a casket, a recipient, a spittoon; a comb, a hair-pin, a scented powder, a cloth-perfume. (139) A mirror, a hand-mirror, a looking-glass; a fan, a palm-leaf fan. Thus ends the section on humans. (6) Lineage, clan, progeny, family, noble descent, ancestry, race, and lineage; these are synonyms for *saṃtati*. The social orders (*varṇas*) are the Brāhmaṇas and the others. (1) 137.139.

165. *Paryaṅkaḥ*, *palyaṅkaḥ*, *khaṭvā*—these four are synonyms for the bedstead known as *palaṅga* or *bāja*. *Gendukaḥ* (also spelled *geṇḍukaḥ* or *gaṇḍūkaḥ*) and *kandukaḥ*—these two denote the ball used as a plaything, known as *ceṃḍū*. Some say it refers to what is known as *giradī* or *gālauśī*. *Dīpaḥ* and *pradīpaḥ*—these two denote a lamp. *Pīṭham* and *āsanam*—these two denote a seat. According to the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*, "the word *viṣṭaraḥ* is a masculine-feminine neuter synonym for *pīṭha*. (Verse 138)

*Samudbhaka* and *saṃpuṭaka* (two) refer to a casket, commonly known as a *ḍabā* or *cauphulā*. *Pratigrāha* and *pratigraha* (two) refer to a water-dipper; according to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *pratigraha* is used in the sense of acceptance, the rear of an army, a water-dipper (*patadgraha*), that which is to be given to Brahmins according to rule, and another planet. *Patadgraha* (one) refers to what is commonly known as a *pikadāṇī*. *Prasādhanī* and *kaṅkatikā* (two) refer to a comb made of ivory and other materials, known as a *phaṇī*, used for cleaning the hair.

"Kaṅkata is an ornament," according to the Amaramālā in its section on neuter nouns. Piṣṭāta and paṭavāsaka are two names for the specific powder known as *bukā*. (139) Darpaṇa, kura, and makura [are synonyms]. According to the Medinīkośa: "Makura may mean a mirror, like mukur; it also refers to the Bakula tree and the potter’s rod. Some authorities also give *makara*. Ādarśa—these three denote a mirror, known as *ārasā*. Due to its association with other masculine terms, *darpaṇa* is used exclusively in the masculine.

"Ādarśa" is said to mean a mirror (*darpaṇa*), according to the *Amaramālā*. "Vyajana" and "tālavṛntaka" are two terms for a fan made of palm leaves or similar materials; it is called *vyajana* because the wind is fanned (*vyajati*) by means of it. Thus ends the section on humans (verse 6). *Santati*, *gotra*, *janana*, and *kula* [denote lineage]. According to another lexicon: "The word *kula* is used in the sense of a country, a lineage (*gotra*), a group of those belonging to the same caste, a dwelling, and the body; it is neuter. *Abhijana*, *anvaya*, *vaṃśa*, *anvavāya*, and *saṃtāna*—these nine denote a lineage (*vaṃśa*).

In this context, *saṃtati* means lineage (*strī*). The castes (*varṇa*) beginning with the Brāhmaṇa are one [category]. (1) Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra constitute the four castes, known as *cāturvarṇya*. (1) A member of royal lineage is called *rājabījī*, *rājavaṃśya*, or *bījya*; these terms refer to one born of a noble family. (2) *Mahākula*, *kulīna*, *ārya*, *sabhya*, *sajjana*, and *sādhu* all denote a person of high birth or good character. (2) *Note: The verse regarding the four castes is cited from the Amarakośa, Brahmavarga, verse 1.*

The student (*brahmacārī*), the householder (*gṛhī*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) constitute the four stages of life (*āśrama*). [The term] *āśrama* is not feminine. A twice-born man (*dvijāti*) is called a *janman*, a *bhūdeva*, or a *vāḍava*. This *brāhmaṇa* is also known as a *viśva*; he is endowed with the six duties (*ṣaṭkarma*) such as sacrifice and the like. A learned man is called *vidvān*, *vipaścic*, *doṣajña*, *sanskṛtadhī* (or *sansudhī*), *kovida*, *budha*, *dhīra*, *manīṣī*, *jña*, *prājña*, *saṃkhyāvān*, *paṇḍita*, and *kavi*. He is also termed *dhīmān*, *sūri*, *kṛtī*, *kṛṣṭi*, *labdhavarṇa*, and *vicakṣaṇa*.

*dūradarśī* (far-sighted), *dīrghadarśī* (long-sighted), *śrotriyaḥ* (learned in the Vedas), and *chāndasaḥ* (versed in the Vedas) are synonyms. (6) *rājavaṃśyaḥ* and *rājabījī* (two terms) refer to one born in a royal lineage. *Bījyaḥ* and *kulasaṃbhavaḥ* (two terms) refer to one born merely from a noble family. (2) *mahākulaḥ*, *kulīnaḥ*, *āryaḥ*, *sabhyaḥ*, *sajjanaḥ*, and *sādhuḥ*—these six are synonyms for a person of good character. [He is called] *mahākulaḥ* because he belongs to a great family (*mahat kulaṃ yasya*); *māhākulaḥ* because he is born in a great family (*mahākule bhavaḥ*). *Kulīnaḥ* means one who exists in a noble family (*kule bhavaḥ*). *Āryaḥ*, *sabhyaḥ*, *sajjanaḥ*, and *sādhuḥ* [denote the same].]

The meaning is that all four, beginning with the *brahmacārin*, are denoted by the term *āśrama*. "Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is defined as the total renunciation of sexual intercourse at all times, in all places, and in all conditions, whether by deed, mind, or speech. This is one [term]. A *vānaprastha* is one who dwells in a *vana-prastha*—that is, a forest region. Here, a *bhikṣu* is an ascetic (*yati*). (Verse 3) *Dvijāti*, *agrajanman*, *bhūdeva*, *vāḍava*, *vipra*, and *brāhmaṇa*—these six are names for a Brāhmaṇa. A *vāḍava* is one born of a *vaḍavā* (mare).

According to the *Medinī* lexicon, "vaḍavā" refers to a Brahmin woman. This Brahmin, being engaged in sacrifices and other such rites, shall be one who performs the six duties (*ṣaṭkarmā*). As it has been said: "Sacrificing, studying, giving, as well as officiating at sacrifices for others, teaching, and receiving gifts—one who is engaged in these is called a Brahmin who performs the six duties. (1) A learned man (*vidvān*) is one who possesses discernment (*vipaścit*), knows faults (*doṣajña*), and is wise (*sudhī*). He is a scholar (*kovida*), enlightened (*budha*), steadfast (*dhīra*), thoughtful (*manīṣī*), a knower (*jña*), sagacious (*prājña*), and possessed of wisdom (*prajña*). [The term] *prajña* is used in the masculine when referring to a scholar, but in the feminine when referring to intelligence.

*Medinī* states: "In the sense of a woman (*yoṣiti*). *Saṃkhyāvan*, *paṇḍita*, and *kavi* [are synonyms for a wise man]. (5) *Dhīmān*, *sūri*, *kṛtī*, *kṛṣṭi*, *labdhavarṇa*, *vicakṣaṇa*, *dūradarśī*, and *dīrghadarśī*—these twenty-two [terms] refer to a scholar (*paṇḍita*). [Dual forms: *vidvāṃsau*, *vipaścitau*, *santau*, *jñau*, *saṃkhyāvantau*, *kṛtinau*. [Etymologies: He possesses *saṃkhyā* (deliberation), thus he is *saṃkhyāvan*. He by whom praise (*varṇa*) has been obtained is *labdhavarṇaḥ*. He who sees from afar (*dūrāt*) or far ahead is *dūradarśī*.

This [section] is not found in the palm-leaf manuscript. The Second Book. "A Mīmāṃsaka is one who follows Jaimini; a Vedāntin is one who propounds Brahman. One who follows Ulūka is a Vaiśeṣika; a Saugata is one who propounds emptiness (*śūnyavādin*). (1) A Naiyāyika is Aṅkṣapāda; a Syādvādin is an Ārhaka. A Cārvāka is a Lokāyatika. The Sāṃkhya and Kāpila are those who maintain that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*). (2)" An *upādhyāya* is a teacher; furthermore, one who performs the *niṣeka* and other rites is a *guru*.

The teacher who explains the mantra is called an *ādeṣṭṛ*; in a sacrifice (*adhvara*), he is one who observes vows (*vratī*). He is both the performer (*yaṣṭṛ*) and the patron (*yajamāna*); in a Soma sacrifice, he is consecrated (*dīkṣita*). [Regarding the terms] *naiyāyika* and *śrotriya*: the latter means one learned in the Vedas (*chāndasa*), and both refer to one who studies the Veda. Some read two verses here beginning with *mīmāṃsaka*, but that is not part of this [text] and has therefore been disregarded. This following commentary is for the sake of the understanding of beginners: *mīmāṃsaka* and *jaiminīya* are two terms for one who knows the Mīmāṃsā system.

*Vedāntī* and *brahmavādī* are two terms for one who knows the Vedānta scripture. *Vaiśeṣika* and *aulūkya* are two terms for a proponent of the seven categories (*saptapadārthavādin*). Those categories are: substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence; these are the seven according to the system of Kaṇāda. *Saugata* and *śūnyavādī* are two terms for a nihilist (*nāstika*) who adheres to the doctrine that the cause of the world is emptiness (*śūnya*). *Nyāyika*, *akṣapāda*, and *ākṣapāda* are three terms for one who knows the Nyāya scripture.

*Pramāṇaprameyasaṃśayaviparyayatarka* etc., refers to the two [epithets] of Gotama, who propounds the sixteen categories (*ṣoḍaśapadārtha*). *Syādvādika* and *Ārhadika* are the two for the Jain (*āīka*), who asserts that liberation may exist, may not exist, or may both exist and not exist. *Cārvāka* and *Laukāyatika* (or *Lokāyatika*) are the two for the Buddhist (*bauddha*), who maintains that the body is the self. *Sāṃkhya* and *Kāpila* are the two for the knower of the Sāṃkhya scriptures, who believes that this very world is the effect (*kārya*). *Upādhyāya* and *Adhyāpaka* are the two for the teacher; he is called an *upādhyāya* because one approaches him (*upetya*) to study (*adhīyate*).

"One who teaches is a *adhyāpaka*. The *niṣeka* is the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*), and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the *puṃsavana* and other rites are included. The performer of these rites, such as the father, is the *guru*; this is one [definition]. An *ācārya* is the expounder of the *mantra*, that is, the Veda; as it is said: "That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*) and its secret portions (*sarahasya*), him they call an *ācārya*"; this is one [definition]. As for the definition of exposition (*vyākhyā*): "The division of words (*padaccheda*), the statement of the meaning of the words (*padārthokti*), the analysis of compounds (*vigraha*), and the syntactical connection (*vākyayojanā*)."

It has been stated: "Objection (ākṣepa) and resolution (samādhāna) constitute the sixfold method of exposition. Regarding the sacrifice (adhvara), he who is the director of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) is called a *vratī* (one observing vows). By the triad [of terms] beginning with "yaṣṭā," the *yajamāna* (sacrificer) is expressed. There is also the reading "ādiṣṭī"; thus there are two *vratinau* (those observing vows) and two *yaṣṭārau* (sacrificers). That *yajamāna*, in a Soma-sacrifice, is called the director (*ādeṣṭā*) or the initiated (*dīkṣita*). One term is for him. The two terms *ijyāśīlaḥ* and *yāyajūkaḥ* refer to one who is habitually engaged in sacrificing. "One who sacrifices again and again or intensely is a *yāyajūkaḥ*."

These two verses are not even found in the palm-leaf manuscript. [From the *Amarakośa* with commentary, *Mavarga*: One who is habituated to performing sacrifices is a *yāyajūka*; one who has performed a sacrifice according to the rules is a *yajvā*. (8) One who has performed the *Gīṣpati-iṣṭi* is a *sthapati*; one who drinks the *soma* is a *somapīthī* or *somapa*. He by whom a sacrifice (*yāga*) involving all one's possessions as the sacrificial fee (*sarvasva-dakṣiṇa*) has been performed is a *sarvavedas*. (9) One who has studied the *pravacana* along with its auxiliary branches (*sāṅga*) is an *anūcāna*; one who has received permission from his teacher is a *samāvṛtta*. One who has performed the *abhiṣava* (the pressing of soma) is a *sutvā*. (10)

*Chātra* and *antevāsī* refer to a disciple (*śiṣya*); *śaikṣāḥ* are those who are beginners (*prāthamakalpikāḥ*). Those who share the same Vedic study, vows, and conduct are called *sabrahmacāriṇaḥ* (fellow-students). However, those who have the same teacher are *satīrthyāḥ*. One who has performed a sacrifice according to the injunctions—such as the injunction prescribing the sacrifice "One should sacrifice with Soma"—is a *yajvā* (a sacrificer). [Singular: *yajvā*; [Dual: *yajvānau*. He who has sacrificed according to the procedure for the Bṛhaspatisava is called a *sthapati* (a master builder/sacrificer).

"One who has performed the *vājapeya* sacrifice should perform the *bṛhaspatisava*; this is its injunction. (1) *Somapīthin*, *somapītī*, *somapībī*, *somapaḥ*, *somapa*: these two [sets of terms] refer to one who has offered the *soma* sacrifice (*somayājin*). (2) *Somapīthināu*: "This [term applies] at all times; however, it applies to one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) for that specific occasion. (3) "One by whom the sacrifice named *viśvajit*—which has the 'all-wealth' (*sarvasva*) as its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—has been performed, he would be called *sarvavedas*. (1) "Where the entire self is the sacrificial fee (*sarvasvaṃ dakṣiṇā yatra*), he makes everything known (*sarvaṃ vedayati*); thus he is *sarvavedas*. [The root] *vid* is used in the sense of 'acquisition' (*lābhe*). (4) *Sarvavedasau*. (5) 9. [End of section]

One who has completed his study (*adhītī*) of the Veda—that is, the *pravacana* endowed with the wealth of training (*śikṣā*)—is called *anūcāna*; this is one term. He who is *anūcāna* and has received permission (*labdhānujña*) from his guru to enter another stage of life (*āśrama*), such as that of a householder, is *samāvṛta*; this is one term. When the ablution (*abhiṣava-snāna*) has been performed, he is *sutvā*. According to the rule "after the root *su-yaji-man-i* [the suffix *ni* is added]," the form *sutvan* is derived from the root *su* (to press) in the sense of the past tense. Thus: *sutvā*, *sutvānau*. The root *abhi-ṣu* is used in the senses of bathing, pressing, drinking, and the fermentation of *surā* liquor. (10)

*Chātra*, *antevāsī* (also *antavāsī*), and *śiṣya*—these three denote a pupil. *Chātra* refers to one whose character (*śīla*) is to cover (*chādana*) the faults of the teacher; since the term *śīla* is understood [in the grammatical rule], the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule "from *chatra* and others, *ṇa*" (*chatrādibhyo ṇaḥ*). *Antevāsī* refers to one whose character is to dwell (*vastuṃ*) near (*ante*) [the teacher]. *Śaikṣāḥ* and *prāthamakalpikāḥ* are two terms for young students (*baṭu*) who have commenced their studies. They are called *śaikṣāḥ* because they receive instruction (*śikṣā*). Those for whom the primary purpose (*prayojana*) is the first undertaking (*prathamakalpa*), namely the initial commencement, are called *prāthamakalpikāḥ*.

Those who share the same conduct regarding Brahman and the performance of Vedic vows—namely, those celibate students (*brahmacārin*) who study the same branch of the Veda—are called *sabrahmacārin* (fellow-students) to one another. [The form *sabrahmacārin* arises from the rule] "in the sense of *caraṇa* or a *brahmacārin*, the word *samāna* becomes *sa*" (Pāṇini 6.3.89). [Verse 11] Those who have the same teacher are *satīrthya* (fellow-disciples) to one another. [The rule is: "In the sense of *samānatīrtha*... [Pāṇini 4.4.107]. *Second Book* [ends here].

The indeclinable *itihā* signifies tradition (*aitihya*), which consists of instruction received through successive lineage (12). *Upajñā* refers to the first knowledge [of a thing]; *upakrama* is the undertaking after having understood [the purpose] (13). Sacrifice (*yajña*) is called *sava*, *adhvara*, *yāga*, *saptatantu*, *makha*, and *ṛtu*. (13) Recitation, fire-oblation (*homa*), honoring guests, libation (*tarpaṇa*), and offering (*bali*)—these five are the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), known by names such as the "Brahma-sacrifice" (*brahmayajña*). (14) *Samajyā*, *pariṣad*, *goṣṭhī*, *sabhā*, *samiti*, *saṃsad*, *āsthānī*, and *āsthāna* (neuter) denote an assembly; *sadaḥ* (feminine and neuter) has the same meaning. (15)

15 || *Prāgvaṃśaḥ* (the hall in front) is that which is before the *havirgeha* (sacrificial shed). *Sadasyāḥ* (members of the assembly) are those who witness the ritual (*sadasi vidarśinaḥ*). [The suffix] *-ya* is applied according to the rule "vāsī" etc. In the rule "tīrye ye," the substitution of *sa* for *samāna* occurs. This is one [term]. *Agnicit* (one who has piled the fire-altar) refers to one who has performed the piling of the fire-altar; this is one [term] for one who has completed the *agnicayana*. *Aitihyam* (tradition): *iti ha* is a pair [of particles] used in succession through a lineage of people; the instruction therein is *aitihyam*. *Iti ha* is an indeclinable; *iti ha* is a collection of particles, and that which arises from that is *aitihyam*. || 12 ||

That which is the initial knowledge is *upakṣā*; for example, Pāṇini’s *upakṣā* (supplementary treatise) on grammar. That which is the commencement of a teaching is *upakrama*; for example, the "commencement" (*upakrama*) of a book means a beginning preceded by knowledge. One [term]. *Yajña*, *sava*, *adhvara*, *yāga*, *satratantra*, *makha*, and *ṛtu*—these seven are names for sacrifice (*yajña*). (13). The five beginning with *pāṭha* are the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) known by such names as the *brahmayajña*. One [term].

In this context, *pāṭha* is the recitation of the Vedas and other scriptures according to the prescribed rule; that is the *brahmayajña*. *Homa* is the *vaiśvadeva* oblation; that is the *devayajña*. The honoring (*saparyā*) of guests who have come to one’s house—satisfying them with food and other necessities—is the *manuṣyayajña*. *Tarpaṇa* is the production of satisfaction for the ancestors by means of water-libations and the like; that is the *pitṛyajña*. *Bali* is the offering of the *bali*; that is the *bhūtayajña*. *Pāṭha* is the act of reciting; the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*). Manu says: "Vedic study is the *brahmayajña*, while the *tarpaṇa* is the *pitṛyajña*."

"A man is a god by virtue of his strength; the sacrifice to men is the honoring of guests. (14) *Samajyā*, *pariṣad*, *goṣṭhī*, *sabhā*, *samiti*, *saṃsad*, *āsthānī*, *āsthāna*, and *sadaḥ*—these nine are synonyms for an assembly (*samājāḥ*). [The dual forms are] *pariṣadau*, *goṣṭhyau*, *saṃsadau*, *āsthānyau*. The word *sadaḥ* ending in a visarga is neuter; however, in the feminine gender, it is *sadāḥ*. [Etymologies: They gather and go to it, hence *samajyā*. Many cows—that is, many words—stand in it, hence *goṣṭhī*. They shine together or equally in it, hence *sabhā*.

Manu defines the *sabhā*: "In whatever place learned Brahmins who know the Vedas sit, along with a learned Brahmin appointed by the king—that they know as a *sabhā*. A *samiti* is so called because people gather (*saṃganti*) there. A *saṃsat* is so called because people sit together (*saṃsīdanti*) in it. An *āsthānī* is so called because people stand upon (*ātiṣṭhanti*) it. A *sadaḥ* is so called because people sit (*sīdanti*) in it. The area to the east of the sacrificial hall (*havirgeha*), where the members of the assembly (*sadasya*) and others reside, is called the *prāgvaṃśa*; this is one term for it.

The long beam fixed between the eastern and western pillars of the sacrificial hall (yajñaśālā) is called the *yūpa* (sacrificial post). [Note: This line appears to be a fragment from a commentary or a misplaced verse number]. Those who sit in the assembly (*sabhā*) are called *sabhāsadaḥ*, *sabhāstārāḥ*, *sabhyāḥ*, and *sāmājikāḥ*. The *adhvaryu*, *udgātṛ*, and *hotṛ* are, respectively, those who know the Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Ṛgveda. Those beginning with the *āmīśra* who are to be chosen for their wealth are the *ṛtvijaḥ* (priests) and *yājakāḥ* (sacrificers). The consecrated ground is called *vediḥ*. A level piece of ground is called *sthaṇḍila* or *catvara*.

The *caṣāla* is the wooden ring at the top of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); the *kambā* is a very thick enclosure. The tip of the sacrificial post is called *tarma*; *araṇi* refers to two pieces of wood used for kindling fire. The three sacred fires are the *dakṣiṇāgni*, the *gārhapatya*, and the *āhavanīya*. This triad of fires is called *tretā*. Fire that has been consecrated by ritual preparation is termed *praṇīta*. The terms *samṛhya*, *paricāyya*, and *upacāyya* are used by those engaged in the performance of the rites. According to some, the wooden structure is called *prāgvaṃśa*. Those who oversee the ritual procedure—the collection of actions prescribed in the Vedas—during the sacrificial rite are known as *sadasyas*.

The meaning is "specific types of officiating priests" (*ṛtvig-viśeṣa*). One term: *sabhāsadaḥ*, *sabhāstārāḥ*, *sabhyāḥ*, *sāmājikāḥ*—these four refer to members of an assembly. They are called *sabhāstārāḥ* because they "strew the assembly" (*sabhāṃ stṛṇanti*); [the root] *stṛñ* means "to cover. They are *sabhyāḥ* because they are associated with the assembly (*sabhāyāṃ sādhavaḥ*). They are *sāmājikāḥ* because they protect the social gathering (*samājaṃ rakṣanti*). One term each for: the Yajurveda scholar is the *adhvaryu*; the Sāmaveda scholar is the *udgātṛ*; the Ṛgveda scholar is the *hotṛ*. Two terms for those who are to be chosen by means of wealth—that is, those who are selected as priests or sacrificers (*yajaka*) by the patron (*yajamāna*) after he has given them wealth and other gifts: *vāryāḥ* and *ṛtvijaḥ*.

Those for whom the *Āgnīdhra* is the first—by the word "first," the sixteen [priests] such as the *Udgātṛ*, *Hotṛ*, and *Adhvaryu* are meant—they who sacrifice during the ritual season are called *Ṛtvij*s (sacrificial priests). Kātyāyana, however, says: "Those who, having been chosen, perform the sacrifice are both *Ṛtvij*s and *Yājaka*s (sacrificers). (17) The ground prepared and fashioned for the sake of the sacrifice, shaped like a small drum (*ḍamaruka*), is called the *Vedi*; this is one term. *Vedī* is also used. *Sthaṇḍila* and *catvara* are two terms for a portion of ground consecrated according to its purpose. *Yūpakaṭaka*: [the base of the sacrificial post].

The *caṣāla* is a wooden ring-shaped object placed upon the head of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); it is one [term]. The enclosure or surrounding fence at the site of sacrifice is called a *vṛti*; it is one [term], used in the feminine gender. The top of the sacrificial post is called *tarma*; [the dual is] *tarmāṇī*. The wood for friction, the wood used for producing fire by rubbing, is called *araṇi*; it is one [term], used in both masculine and feminine genders. In the feminine, it is *araṇī*.

The *dakṣiṇāgni*, the *gārhapatya*, and the *āhavanīya*—these three fires are each individually called *aniviśeṣa* (specific fires). However, in some places, a *dvandva* compound of the three is recited. This triad is called *tretā*; [the suffix] *tva* has been elided (*itā*), hence *tretā*. It is feminine: *tretā*, *trete*. Fire consecrated by mantras and other rites is called *praṇīta*. The collective groups are *paricāyya* and *upacāyya*. [End of] the Second Book.

He who is brought forth from the *gārhapatya* fire and carried forward as the *dakṣiṇāgni* is Ānāyya; his beloved wife is Svāhā, the consumer of oblations. (21) The verse used for kindling the fire is called both *sāmidhenī* and *dhāyyā*. The meters, beginning with the *gāyatrī*, are employed therein. In the preparation of the sacrificial offering, the *caru* is masculine. (22) When curd is mixed with warm milk, that mixture is called *āmikṣā*. A *ghavitra* is a fan made of deer skin. (23)

*Pṛṣadājya* is clarified butter mixed with curd; *paramānna* is milk-rice (*pāyasa*). *Havya* and *kavya* refer to food offerings for the gods and the ancestors respectively; the vessels used for these are the *sruva* ladle and others. (24) These three [fires] are those in which there is the application of ritual practice. They are employed in specific locations for the purpose of pouring libations (*abhidhāraṇa*). (20) That fire which, having been brought from the *gārhapatya* and drawn out, is led forward and established as the *dakṣiṇāgni*, is called *ānāyya*. *Anāyī* is the name of the beloved wife of the consumer of oblations (*hutabhuj-priyā*); thus, there are three [terms]: [the fire], its beloved, and the sacrifice itself. This word *svāhā* is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*) because it denotes a substance; for this very reason, the usage "on the right side, [place] *svāhā*" is consistent. (21) That *ṛc* which is employed during the kindling of the fire—that is, when fire is ignited by the insertion of fuel-sticks—is called both *sāmidhenī* and *ghāyyā*. Its meter (*chandas*) may be *gāyatrī* or *uṣṇih*; [the term is] singular and neuter. When the sacrificial oblation is being offered into the mouth of the fire during its cooking, that [fuel-wood] is called *caru*; [the compound] *havyapāka* means the cooking of the sacrificial oblation (*havya*).

"The *odana* (boiled rice) cooked with its internal heat not having escaped is a *caru*, according to the ritualists (*yājñika*s). It is called *caru* because it is moved about (*caryate*) or eaten (*makṣyate*). The Mīmāṃsakas also accept that the word *caru* does not have another [primary] meaning in the section concerning the *trivṛt-caru*. However, in the *Viśvaprakāśa*, it is stated that the word has multiple meanings: "The *caru* is a vessel and sacrificial food. And the *Medinī* lexicon states: "Now, *caru* is masculine in the sense of sacrificial food and a vessel. || 22 ||

That which is boiled a hundred times, heated, and curdled by the addition of yogurt to that milk is *āmikṣā*; this is one term. That sacrificial implement made of deer-skin is *havitr̥*; this is one term. It is also called *dhuvitr̥*. (23) Ghee mixed with yogurt is *pṛṣadājya*; this is one term. [It is also] *pṛṣātaka*. Hemacandra states: "That which is ghee mixed with yogurt is called *pṛṣadājya*, while *pṛṣātaka* is [the same]. *Paramānna* and *pāyasa* are two terms for milk-rice (*kṣīrānna*).

In the rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors (*daivapitrye*), the offerings to the gods and the ancestors (*havyakavye*) should be made in their respective order. That by which the gods are offered to and gratified is *havya*. That which is offered to the ancestors is *kavya*; [the root] *ku* means "to sound. The food being given to the gods is *havya*, and the food being given to the ancestors is *kavya*—this is the meaning. Food is offered to the gods face-to-face; food is offered to the ancestors through the mouth of a Brahmin. It is also called *paitra*.

The *dhruvā*, *upabhṛt*, *juhū*, and *sruva* are types of *sruk* (ladles), which are feminine in gender. An animal that has been consecrated with mantras and slaughtered at the proper time is called *upākṛta*. *Sāṃtapanam*, *pārāka*, *prokṣaṇam*, and *avadhyārthakam* are terms for sacrificial slaughter. The words *pramīta*, *upasampanna*, and *prokṣita* denote one who has been killed, and they may take any gender (*vācyaliṅga*). *Sānnāyyam* refers to the oblation; however, that which is offered into the fire is called *hutam*, and this applies to all three genders when accompanied by the exclamation *vaṣaṭ*.

The *avabhṛtha* is the final purificatory bath at the end of a sacrifice; I, however, shall explain that sacrificial rite. Among the three types of ritual acts, *iṣṭa* refers to sacrifices, while *pūrta* refers to works such as digging wells and the like. *Amṛta* denotes both the remains of a sacrifice and the remains of a meal. [In the section on Brahman-related terms, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Each of these terms applies to one object. A vessel such as the *suvacama* and so forth is called a *pātra*. There are three types of ladles (*sruc*): the *dhruvā*, the *upabhṛt*, and the *juhū*; these are feminine. The *sruva* is singular and masculine.

In this context, just as the term *ava* is established as masculine through its distinct form, so too should the rule for femininity in the preceding [verse], *strī*, be understood. Furthermore, in the *Medinīkośa*, the word *sū* is seen to be feminine as well, according to the entry: "The word *sū* is used for both [masculine and feminine] in the sense of a sacrificial vessel (*homapātra*), and for *śallakī* and *mūrvā* in the feminine. That animal which is killed after being consecrated with mantras during the ritual season is called *upākṛta*; one [synonym]. It is called *upākṛta* because it is "brought near" (*upākriyate*) or "slaughtered" (*hiṃsyate*). || 25 ||

*Paraṃparāka*, *śamana*, and *śasana* (also *sasana*)—these three denote killing for the purpose of sacrifice; that is to say, they refer to the slaughter of sacrificial animals. *Pramīta*, *upasaṃpanna*, and *prokṣita*—these three apply to any animal killed for the sake of a sacrifice. These are adjectives (agreeing with the gender of the noun). (26) *Sāmnāyya* is the name for a specific type of oblation (*haviḥ*); there is one [term]. That which is offered into the fire, such as the *yājyā* and so forth, is called *vaṣaṭkṛta*; this is a single term used in all three genders (adjectival). The word *vaṣaṭ* is an illustration for the sacrificial mantra.

"Vaṣaṇmaśreṇa" means performed or cast [into the fire]. At a sacrifice (*yajña*), the *avabhṛtha*—the concluding rite that completes the initiation (*dīkṣā*) following the specific ritual procedures—is one [term]. That which is suitable for that rite, a substance fit for sacrificial acts such as the materials for the twice-born (*dvijadravya*), is *yakṣiya*; these three [terms] are synonyms. (27) That which is the act of a *kratu* is intended here; a *kratu* is a sacrifice, and its act is giving (*dāna*). Manu says: "That which is offered in the single fire (*ekāgni*), that which is offered in the triple fire (*tretā*), and that which is given within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*)—that is designated as *iṣṭa*."

One [term] is *khāta* (dug-out), referring to ponds, wells, and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), temples and the like are included—such work is called *pūrta*. One [verse] from the *Smṛti* states: "Lotus-pools, assembly halls, ponds, temples, and especially gardens—one should designate these as *pūrta* works. Regarding the remnants of a sacrifice, such as the *puroḍāśa* cake and so on, one [term] is *amṛta* (nectar). Regarding the remnants of a meal, that which has been eaten by gods, ancestors, and others, one [term] is *vighasa*. As Manu says: "One should always be an eater of *vighasa*, and always an eater of *amṛta*."

"That which remains after being consumed is *viṣasa*; that which is not mixed is *amṛta*. [28] **Tyāga** (Renunciation/Giving): *Tyāga*, *vihāpita*, *dāna*, *utsarjana*, *visarjana*, *viśrāṇana*, *vitaraṇa*, *sparśana*, *pratipādana*, *pradeśana*, *nirvapaṇa*, *apavarjana*, and *aṃhati* are synonyms for giving. [29] Giving on the day of death for the sake of the deceased is called *aurdhvadehika*; this term applies to all three genders. [30]

The gift to the ancestors is called *nivāpa*; the ritual for that performed according to the scriptures is *śrāddha*. The monthly offering is the *anvāhārya*, and the eighth part of the day is the *kūrtapa*, which is not feminine. (31) *Paryeṣaṇā*, *parīṣṭi*, *anveṣaṇā*, and *gaveṣaṇā* mean searching. *Sani* means solicitation; *adhyeṣaṇā* is entreaty; *yācyā*, *abhiśasti*, *yācanā*, and *arthanā* mean begging. (32) Six [terms] are used in the three genders: *arhaṇa* and *arghya* refer to water intended for the guest-offering (*argha*); *pādya* refers to water for washing the feet.

Among these, *aṃhatiḥ* is feminine. Giving for the sake of the deceased (*mṛtārtha*) on the day of death refers to the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and other rites beginning from the day of death and lasting for ten days; this constitutes the *aurdhvadehika* (post-mortem) rite. On the third day, however, there is the *auvaidehikī* rite. There is also a reading: "on that day, the giving [of gifts]" (*tadahardānam*). The giving to the ancestors (*pitṛdāna*) and the *nivāpa* (offering) refer to whatever gift is performed with reference to the ancestors. According to the scriptures, that ritual related to the ancestors is called *śrāddha*. It is called *śrāddha* because it exists through faith (*śraddhā*); the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule "from *prajñā* and *śraddhā*. Regarding the monthly *śrāddha* performed on the new moon day, it is called *anvāhārya*. Manu states: "One should perform the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* *śrāddha* month after month."

"Aho! The eighth part (aṃśa) would be the *kutapa*. *Paryeṣaṇā* and *parīṣṭi* are two terms for the service and devotion shown toward a faithful twice-born (*dvija*). *Anveṣaṇā* and *gaveṣaṇā* are two terms for the seeking of dharma and so forth. The word *ṣaṭ* (six) means that the six terms—*arghya*, *pādya*, *ātithya*, *ātitheya*, *vaiśika*, and *āgata*—are masculine in gender. *Argha* refers to the materials for worship; the water intended for that purpose is called *arghya*. Prācetasa and Maitrāvaruṇi both refer to the first poet (Vālmīki). [In the section on Brahman: Arghya is one term; pādya refers to the water intended for the feet or for the purpose of the feet.

*Ātidhya* (hospitality) is one term for *atidhyartha* (the purpose of hospitality). However, it is stated in the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*: "But *prāghuṇa* and *atithi* are used in both genders [masculine and feminine]. In the feminine, however, the form is *atithī*. According to the *Viśva* and *Medinī* lexicons: "The word *upāsana* is used in the sense of practicing archery (*śarābhyāsa*), worship (*upāsti*), and sitting (*āsana*). This refers to the fourfold set beginning with *upāsana*. Among these, the word *śuśrūṣā* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for service to a teacher (*gurusevā*). Bhāguri states: "The words *paricaryā* and *upacaryā* [are synonyms]. (35) *Vrajyā*, *aṭā*, *aṭyā*, and *paryaṭanam*—these four denote wandering. The *Ratnakośa* states: "*Aṭā* is wandering (*paryaṭana*) or roaming (*bhrama*). In the word *akhyā*, there is a conjunction of retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) and palatal (*tālavya*) sounds. Abiding in the path of yoga, such as the postures (*īryā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and silence (*mauna*), constitutes one [term], namely *caryā*. As stated in another text: "The wise know that *caryā* consists of the postures. *Upasparśa* (touching) and *ācamana* (sipping water for purification) are two [terms]. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "*Upasparśa* refers to mere contact, as well as bathing and sipping water. *Mauna* (silence) and *abhāṣaṇa* (not speaking) are two [terms]. There exists a verse beginning with "Prācetasa," etc., which contains significant meanings; therein, the group of four starting with Prācetasa refers to Vālmīki. He is also called Maitrāvaruṇa.

Vālmīki—[the form] *valmīki* is found in the *Dvirūpakośa*; [the forms] *valmīka*, *vālmīka*, and *vālmīka* also exist. (From the second book, verse 175). Vālmīki, Gādheya, Viśvāmitra, and Kauśika. Vyāsa, Dvaipāyana, Pārāśarya, and Satyavatīsuta. *Niyama* is a religious observance (*vrata*) that is not feminine; it consists of meritorious acts such as fasting (*upavāsa*) and the like. *Aupavasta*, however, is synonymous with *upavāsa*. *Viveka* is the state of being distinct or separate from the self.
