It is said that *bhindi* refers to a distance of ten *tālas*, and since it protects (*pālayati*) that [distance], it is called *bhindipāla*. *Pariṣa* and *parighātina* are two names for an iron-bound club the size of an arm. (91) *Kuṭhāra*, *svadhiti*, *paraśu*, and *paraśvadha*—the latter holds (*dadhāti*) the axe (*paraśu*).

‘Parasvadha’ and ‘svadhiti’ are two names for the axe, known in the vernacular as ‘kujhāḍa’. Among these, the word *kuṭhāra* applies to both masculine and feminine genders; in the feminine, it is *kuṭhārī*. According to the *Rathasa*, “*kuṭhāraka*, *parśu*, *ratha*, and *churikā kośakṣāmikā*” [are synonyms]. *Svadhiti* is exclusively masculine. *Śastrī*, *asiputrī*, *churikā*, and *asidhenukā*—these four refer to the small knife, known in the vernacular as ‘surī’. *Śalya* and *śaṅku* [refer to the arrowhead]. || 92 ||

The two [terms] for the tip of a *bāṇāpra*, a specific type of weapon, are *phala* (feminine) or *śalya* and *śaṅku* (masculine). *Sarvalā* and *tomara* are masculine, while *astra* is not feminine. *Prāsa* and *kunta* denote a spear; *koṇa*, *pālī*, *aśri*, and *koṭi* are feminine. *Sarvābhisāra* and *sarvoṣas* signify the complete mobilization of equipment. *Lohābhisāra* is the ritual of *nīrājanā* performed for kings who bear weapons. The act of marching with an army into a desert region is called *abhiṣeṇana*.

Yātrā, vrajyā, abhiniryāṇa, prasthāna, gamana, and gama denote a journey or departure. (95) Āsāra, prasaraṇa, and pracakra signify a forward movement or an advance. Abhikrama is the term for the advance of one who is fearless toward enemies in battle. (96) [Note on etymology: It is well-known [that *śalya* means an arrow]. It comes from the root *śal*, meaning "to go. As Śāśvata states: "The word *śaṅku* refers to a number, a pin, or a type of weapon. It is masculine (*pumān*). [Regarding *sarvalā*: It is *śarbalā*; according to the lexicon *Śabhedāt*, it is synonymous with *śārdūla*, *śarvalā*, and *śalā*.

*tomara*: [This refers to] a specific type of weapon shaped like a churning-stick, commonly known as *gurūṃja*. It is called *tomara* because one who goes (*gantā*) with it dies (*mriyate*). Some say that the four items beginning with *śalya* (arrow) are also types of *tomara*. Among these, *sarvalā* is feminine. *prāsaḥ*, *kuntaḥ*: two terms for what is known as *mālā*. *koṇaḥ*, *pāliḥ*, *aśriḥ*, *aśrīḥ*, *koṭiḥ*, *koṭī*: these four refer to the edge of a sword or similar weapon, known as *ṭaॉka*. Among these, *pālī* and the others are feminine. || 93 ||

*Sarvābhisāra* (the general advance), *sarvauṣa* (the universal assault), and *sarvasamharaṇa* (the total destruction) are the three [terms] for the mobilization of a fourfold army known as the *jāmava*. That which has the seizure of everything as its purpose is [called] *sarvābhisāra*; the advancing toward all [enemies] is *sarvābhisāra*. The ritual consisting of the presentation of weapons and other items at the time of the *nīrājanā* ceremony on the ninth or tenth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa for kings who bear arms is called *lohābhisāra*; this is one [term].

*Lohābhisāra* is that in which iron (weapons) is brought forth (*abhisāryate*) or cast forward (*prasyāpyate*). *Lohābhihāra* is also used; it means the bringing (*abhiharaṇa*) of iron, that is, weapons, toward the enemy. According to the *Amaramālā*: "That which is called *lohābhihāra* is the ritual (*vidhi*) for the king's departure. In the reading *nīrājano vidhiḥ*, it should be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is a complete (*niḥśeṣeṇa*) shining forth (*rājanam*)" [of the army]. (93) The advance of the army together with the host toward the enemy, that is, into the vicinity of the foe, is *abhiṣeṇanam*; this is one term.

*Yātrā*, *vrajyā*, *abhiniryāṇa*, *prasthāna*, *gamana*, *gama*, and *prayāṇa* (95) are synonyms for the setting out of an army. *Āsāra* and *asaraṇa*—the reading *prasaraṇī* also occurs, and *prasaraṇi* also occurs—are two terms for the spreading of an army on all sides. *Pracakra* and *calita* are two terms for an army that has set in motion; according to the *Amaramālā*, "the *pracakra* and *calita* apply to three genders. In battle, the fearless advance against enemies is called *abhikrama* (one term); *atikrama* is also used. (96)

Vaitālikas (96–99) [The Section on Kṣatriyas]: Vaitālikas, bodhakarās, ācām̐krikās, ghāṭikās, and arthakās are synonyms for bards. Māgadhās, magadhas, and bandins are those who recite praises. Saṃśatakas are those who do not retreat from battle due to a formal agreement. *Reṇu* and *dhūli* are feminine; *pāṃsu* is masculine; and *rajas* is both neuter and masculine. *Cūrṇa* and *kṣoda* mean powder. *Samutpiñja* and *piñjala* mean extremely agitated or confused.

*Patākā*, *vaijayantī*, *ketana*, and *dhvaja* (the latter being masculine or neuter) denote a banner. That battlefield which inspires great terror is called *vīrāśaṃsana*. The two terms *vaitālika* and *cāṣṭika* refer to those who awaken kings in the morning by reciting panegyrics. They move about with various rhythms and sounds; thus they are *vaitālikas*. *Cāṣṭikas* and *ghāṇṭikas* are two types of bards (*bandi*). Those who proclaim [praises] by striking a bell are *ghāṇṭikas*. As it is said regarding the time of awakening: "The artisans of the bell are indeed *ghāṇṭikas*."

"Cakrikā ghaṭikārthakāḥ" is a reading found in some places. In that context, *cakrika* refers to one who has a *cakra* (drum) as his instrument of play; [the suffix] *ṭhan* is applied here. *Ghaṭikā* means they sound the *ghaṭī*; [the root] *kai* is used in the sense of "sound. These two terms refer to those who play the *ghaṭikā* drum. *Māgadha* (variant: *Magadha*)—[according to] Mukuṭa, it is *madhuka*. The etymological analysis (*vigraha*) is: "they sound what is sweet (*madhu*). These two refer to the panegyrists (*stāvaka*) of the royal lineage standing before the king. As they say: "The *māgadhas* are born of the lineage of the *sūta*."

*Bandinaḥ* (bards) and *stutipāṭhakāḥ* (panegyrists)—these two terms refer to those who recite praises for kings and others, known as *bhāṭas*. They are called *bandinaḥ* because they possess the habit (*tacchīlāḥ*) of praising (*vandante*) or eulogizing. As it has been said: "Bards are those of pure intellect whose speech is appropriate to the occasion. Some maintain that these four [terms] have the same meaning. Those who do not retreat from battle and do not turn their backs due to a vow or an oath are called *saṃśaptakāḥ*; this is one term. *Reṇuḥ*, *dhūliḥ*, *dhūlī*, *pāṃsuḥ*, *pāṃśuḥ*, and *rajaḥ*—these four denote dust.

Regarding the word *dhūli*: [it is said] "the dust of women and men shone. *Pāṃsu* is masculine; *rajas* is neuter. (98) *Cūrṇa* and *kṣoda* are two terms for ground powder (*piṣṭasya rajasaḥ*). Some say that all six [words] refer to dust (*rajas*). *Cūrṇa* is also masculine. According to the *Medinī*: "Cūrṇa is dust, a type of alkali, and various fragrant powders used for perfuming. According to the *Śāśvata*: "Cūrṇas are fragrant mixtures; cūrṇa is dust along with sugar."

*Samutpiñja* and *piñjala*—these two terms refer to that which is extremely disordered, such as an army. *Vaijayantī*, *ketana*, and *dhvaja*—these four denote a banner (*patākā*). Some maintain that the pair beginning with *ketana* refers specifically to the flagstaff (*patākā-daṇḍa*). [Note: *Dhvaja* is masculine. (99) That battlefield which is terrifying due to mangled elephants and other creatures is called *vīrāśaṃsana*. [One term. It is so called because heroes (*vīrāḥ*) are praised (*āśaṃsyante*) therein; from the root *ā-śas* in the sense of "desire."

*Ahampūrvikā* is the state of a prior battle characterized by the insistence, "I first! I first! I shall be first! [It is formed] from the repetition *ahaṃ pūrvam ahaṃ pūrvam*, with the suffix *kan* added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) according to the rule *sup supā*, and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. *Āhopuruṣikā* is that which arises from pride and the like, consisting of self-exaltation. *Ahamahamikā*, however, is that mutual assertion of "I" [which occurs when each says], "I [will do it]! [100-101].

*Draviṇa*, *taraḥ*, *sahaḥ*, *bala*, *śaurya*, *sthāma*, and *śuṣma* denote strength, power, and valor. *Śakti*, *parākrama*, *prāṇa*, and *vikrama* denote prowess and extraordinary capability. (102) The drinking that occurs when a battle has taken place or is about to take place is called *vīrapāna*. Battle is termed *yuddha*, *āyodhana*, *janya*, *pradhana*, and *pravidāraṇa*. (103) It is also called *mṛdha*, *āskandana*, *saṃkhya*, *samīka*, and *sāṃparāyika*. The words *samarānīkaraṇa*, *kalaha*, and *vigraha* are used for conflict, but not in the feminine gender. (104)

*Saṃmardā*, *abhisaṃpāta*, *kalaha*, *saṃsphoṭa*, and *saṃyuga*—these five [terms] (100–104) denote a single thing; they are feminine. The manifestation of one’s own capability, which consists of a presumption regarding oneself, is called *ādipuruṣikā*. One who possesses the conceit "I am a man" (*ahaṃ-puruṣa*) is an *ādipuruṣika*; thus, *ādipuruṣikā* is a single term. That egoism which consists of mutual claims such as "I am capable," "I am capable" is *ahamahamikā*. The word *aham-aham* is present here; the dual number is used for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).

One [word] has six syllables: *ṣaḍakṣaram* || 101 || *Draviṇa*, *taraḥ*, *sahaḥ*, *sthāma*, *śaurya*, *syāma*, *śuṣma*, *śakti*, and *parākrama*; *āṇaḥ*—these ten are synonyms for valor (*parākrama*). [The forms] *tarasī*, *sahasī*, *sthāmanī*, and *śuṣmamadanta* [are also used]. *Saha* may also end in a long vowel (*adanta*). Rabhasa states: "In the sense of power, *sahaḥ* is masculine; it is not feminine. And the Medinī lexicon says: "*Sahaḥ* is in the sense of strength, not feminine. *Vikrama* and *atiśaktitā*—these two denote excessive valor (*atitarākrama*). || 102 ||

When a battle has occurred, the drinking of liquor by heroes for the sake of allaying that fatigue, or for the sake of increasing their enthusiasm for a future battle (*bhāvini*)—that is *īrapāna*. It is also called *vīrapāṇa*; the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs according to the rule "optionally in the sense of state (*bhāva*) or instrument (*karaṇa*"). Yuddha, āyodhana, janya, pradhana, pravidāraṇa, mṛdha, āskandana, saṃkhya, samīka, sāṃparāyika (from *saṃparāya* with the suffix *kan*), samara, anīka, raṇa, kalaha, and vigraha are synonyms for battle.

104 || *Saṃgrahaḥ*, *abhisaṃpātaḥ*, *kaliḥ*, *saṃsphoṭaḥ* (also *saṃspheṭaḥ*), *saṃyugaḥ*, *abhyāmardaḥ* (also *abhimardaḥ*). According to the *Medinī*: "*Abhimardaḥ* may be masculine in the sense of crushing (*avamarda*) and in battle (*saṃparāya*). *Samāghātaḥ*, *saṃgrāmaḥ*, *abhyāgamaḥ*, *āhavaḥ* || 105 || *Samudāyaḥ*, *saṃrat*, *samitiḥ*, *ājiḥ*, *samit*, *yut*—these thirty-one denote battle. *Saṃkhyaṃ* [is used] with a final anusvāra.

405–410 [The Section on Kṣatriyas] *Abhyāmarda*, *samāghāta*, *saṃgrāma*, *abhyāgama*, and *āhava* denote battle. *Samudāya*, *striyaḥ*, *saṃyat*, *samiti*, *āji*, *sami*, and *yudh* also refer to battle. *Niyuddha* refers to hand-to-hand combat; furthermore, *tumula* denotes a tumultuous melee in battle. *Kṣveḍā* is the lion’s roar (of warriors); *ghaṭā* is the gathering or formation of elephants. *Krandana* is the clamor of troops; *bṛṃhitam* is the trumpeting of elephants. *Visphāra* is the twanging sound of a bow; *paṭaha* and *āḍambara* are synonyms for a kettle-drum.

*Prasabham*, *balātkāraḥ*, and *haṭhaḥ* denote forceful compulsion; *skhalitam* and *chalam* denote a slip or deception. *Ajanyam*, *klībam*, and *utpātaḥ*—these three are synonyms for a calamity or portent (*upasargaḥ*). *Mūrchā*, *kaśmalam*, and *mohaḥ* denote fainting or delusion. *Avamardaḥ* and *pīḍanam* denote oppression or affliction. *Abhyavaskandanam* and *abhyāsādanam* denote a sudden assault. *Vijayaḥ* and *jayaḥ* denote victory. *Vairaśuddhiḥ*, *pratīkāraḥ*, and *vairaniryātanam* denote the settling of a feud or retaliation. [The section on] battle and so forth, ending with the triad beginning with *samarādi*, is concluded. *Samiyau* and *yudhau* mean those who have engaged in combat. *Saṃyatau* means restrained or disciplined. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the commentary continues with further definitions of battle-related terms.)

*Niyuddha* and *bāhuyuddha* are two terms for wrestling. *Tumula* is one term for a tumultuous battle; it occurs in a chaotic melee where there is mutual crowding. *Kṣveḍā* and *siṃhanāda* are two terms for the specific kind of roar of heroes that resembles the lion’s roar; *kṣveḍā* ends in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. The gathering of elephants in battle, their collision, is called *ghaṭā*. The shouting of warriors, a sound preceded by loud cries, is *krandana*; this is one term for the calling out of warriors to one another in competition.

The trumpeting of elephants is called *bṛṃhita*; these two terms refer to the same thing. (107) The sound of a bow is *visphāra*. *Paṭaha* and *āḍambara* are two words for the sound of battle. *Prasabham*, *balātkāra*, and *haṭha*—these three denote forceful compulsion. [Note: *Prasabham* is so called because it has gone beyond deliberation (*sabhā*); *balātkāra* is the act of using force. *Skhalita* and *chalam*—these two refer to the deviation from the rules of combat. (108)

*Ajanya*, *utpāta*, and *upasarga*—these three denote a portent (*utpāta*) that indicates good or evil fortune. *Ajanya* means that which is not good for the people (*jana*). *Mūrcchā*, *kaśmala*, and *moha*—these three denote fainting or stupor. *Avamarda* and *pīḍana*—these two refer to the oppression of a country rich in crops and other resources by a foreign army. (109) *Abhyaṣaskandana* and *abhyāsādana*—these two denote an attack by treachery, known as a *dhāḍa*; it is also called *chāpā*.

*Vijaya* (victory) and *jaya* (conquest) refer to the excellence gained by turning the enemy away. *Vairaśuddhi* (purification of enmity), *pratīkāra* (retribution), and *vairaniryātana* (avenging an injury)—these three denote the act of retaliating against an enemy. *Pradrāva*, *udrāva*, *saṃdrāva*, *saṃdāva*, and *vidrava*—[these are synonyms for flight]. In battle, *apakrama*, *apayāna*, *bhaṅga*, and *parājaya* denote defeat. *Pradrāva*, *udrāva*, *saṃdrāva*, *saṃdāva*, *vidrava*, and *drava*; *apakrama*, *apayāna*, *bhaṅga*, and *parājaya* [are the terms for fleeing and losing a battle]. (2.111)

*Parājita* and *parābhūta* mean defeated; *naṣṭa* and *tirohita* mean vanished or concealed. *Pramārpaṇa*, *nibarhaṇa*, *nikāraṇa*, *viśāraṇa*, *pravāsana*, *parāsana*, *niṣūdana*, *nihiṃsana*, *nirvāsana*, *saṃjñapana*, *nirganthana*, *apāsana*, *nistarhaṇa*, *nihananam*, *kṣaṇana*, *parivarjana*, *nirvāpaṇa*, *viśasana*, *māraṇa*, *pratighātana*, *uddhāsana*, *pramathana*, *krathana*, and *ujāsana* [all signify killing or destruction].

*Ālabha*, *piñja*, *viśaraghāta*, *unmātha*, and *vadha* [are synonyms for killing]. (115) *Kāladharma*, *diṣṭānta*, *pralaya*, *atyaya*, *anta*, *nāśa*, *mṛtyu*, *maraṇa*, and *nighana*—these eight are synonyms for death; *nighana* is not feminine. (116) *Parāsu*, *prāptapañcatva*, *pareta*, *preta*, and *saṃsthita* [refer to one who has reached death]. *Drava*, *apakrama*, and *apamāna*—these eight are synonyms for flight. The defeat that occurs in battle is called *parājaya* (one term). (117) *Parājita* and *parābhūta*—these two refer to one who has been conquered.

*Naṣṭaḥ* (lost) and *tirohitaḥ* (concealed)—these two denote one who is hidden (*nilīnasya*). The term *triṣu* (in three genders) applies to both cases, like the word *kāka*. The thirty names beginning with *pramāpaṇa* and ending with *vānta* are synonyms for killing (*vadhasya*). "Namely: *pramāpaṇam*, *pramāpanam*; *nibarhaṇam*, *nirbarhaṇam*; *nikāraṇam*, *viśāraṇam*, *niśāraṇam*; *pravāsanam*, *parāsanam*; *niṣūdanam*, *nidanam*. (112)

*nihiṃsana*, *nirvāsana*, *saṃjñapana*—[the root] *jñā* [is used] in the senses of killing, satisfying, and quieting; or [it comes from] *śapa* or *mica*. Also *nirgran-thana* or *nirgandhana*. *Apāsana* (driving away). ||133|| *Nistaīṇa*, *nihana-na*, *kṣaṇana*, *parivarjana*, *nirvāpaṇa*, *viśasana*, *māraṇa*, *pratighātana*. ||114|| *Udvāsana*, *pramathana*, *krathana*, *ujjāsana*. From *pramāpaṇa* up to *ujjāsana*, these are formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an action (*bhāva*).

*Ālambhaḥ*, *piñjaḥ*, *viśaraḥ*, *ghātaḥ*, *unmāthaḥ* (or *unmathaḥ*), *vadhaḥ*—these are synonyms for killing. (115) *Pañcatā*, *pañcatvam*, *kāladharmaḥ*, *diṣṭāntaḥ*, *pralayaḥ*, *atyayaḥ*, *antaḥ*, *nāśaḥ*, *mṛtyuḥ*, *maraṇam*, *nidhanaḥ*—these ten denote death. Among them, *mṛtyuḥ* is feminine and masculine; *nidhanam* is neuter. (116) *Parāsuḥ*, *prāptapañcatvaḥ*, *paretaḥ*, *pretaḥ*, *saṃsthitaḥ*, *mṛtaḥ*, *pramītaḥ*.

117–119. These three terms—*mṛta*, *pramīta*, and *cite*—are used in the masculine; *citā*, *cityā*, and *citi* are feminine. *Kabandha* (masculine and feminine) refers to a headless trunk still joined with its limbs. *Śmaśāna* and *pitṛvana* denote a cemetery. *Kuṇapa* and *śava* (not feminine) mean a corpse. *Pragraha*, *upagraha*, and *bandha* mean bonds or fetters. *Kārā* refers to a prison or a place of confinement. *Asu* and *prāṇa* (used in the plural) denote the vital breaths; likewise, *jīva* is the support of these vital breaths.

*Āyuḥ* is the duration of life; *jīvātuḥ* is the medicine for living. Thus ends the section on Kṣatriyas (Chapter 8). *Ūravyas*, *ūrujas*, *aryas*, *vaiśyas*, *bhūmispṛśas*, and *viśas* are terms for the Vaiśya caste. [The following] seven terms refer to the deceased: these are adjectives that agree in gender with the noun they qualify. *Citā*, *cityā*, and *citiḥ*—these three denote the funeral pyre, the structure upon which the corpse is burned (known as *culle*). *Saraṇaḥ* refers to the same thing. (117) A headless trunk (*apamūrdha*) devoid of a head, yet joined with the actions of a dancer—that corpse known as *bhaḍa* is called *kabandha*.

*Kabandha* refers to a headless trunk in water; it is also said to denote Rāhu and a *rākṣasa*. [The word] *kabandha* is singular. In battle, the *kabandha* that completes the number one thousand dances. This usage occurs even by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*) where there is no actual dancing. *Śmaśāna* and *pitṛvana* are two names for a cemetery (*pretabhūmi*), known as "masaṇavaṭī. It is called *śmaśāna* because a corpse (*śava*) lies therein; [the word] has two palatal *ś*s. *Kuṇapa* and *śava* are two terms for a lifeless body. [Note: "But *śava* is masculine. || 118 ||

*Pragraha*, *upagraha*, and *bandī* (also *bandir*)—these three denote the act of capturing thieves and others. *Kārā* (feminine) is the single term for a prison, also known as *mandī*, *aṭakāva*, and *kaida*. *Asavaḥ* and *prāṇāḥ*—these two refer to the vital breaths; the word *bhūmi* indicates their plurality. From the word *evaṃ* [in the lexicon], it follows that *prāṇa* is always masculine and plural. Some say that what is called *prāṇa* is simply air, intended here merely as air. *Jīva* and *asudhāraṇa*—these two denote the maintenance of life. || 119 ||

The period delimited by one's life is *āyus*; this is one [term]. In the neuter, it is *usantam*. That which is the medicine for life or the means of its preservation is *jīvātu*; this is one [term] and masculine. Thus ends the section on Kṣatriyas. (8) *Ūravyaḥ* refers to one born from the thigh (*ūru*) of Brahmā. By the rule "the suffix *yat* after body parts," there is the substitution of *guṇa* and the replacement with *ava*. *Ūrujaḥ*, *arthaḥ*, *vaiśyaḥ*, *bhūmispṛk*, and *vid*—these six denote a Vaiśya. *Ājīvaḥ*, *jīvikā*, *vārtā*, *vṛttiḥ*, *vartanam*, and *jīvanam*—these six denote livelihood in general. (1)

*Agriculture* (*kṛṣi*) means plowing. *Animal husbandry* (*pāśupālya*) is the work of a herdsman, such as the tending of cattle and so forth. *Commerce* (*vāṇijya*) is the work of merchants, such as buying and selling and so forth. [The form] "vaṇijyam" is used, and "vaṇijyā" is also correct. Thus, these are the three occupations of Vaiśyas. *Ājīva*, *jīvikā*, *vārtā*, *vṛtti*, *vartana*, and *jīvana* are synonyms for a livelihood. (Verse 1) Agriculture, animal husbandry, and commerce are the occupations (*vṛtti*) for women. (Verse 2ab) Service is the "dog's life" (*śvavṛtti*), which is untruthful; agriculture is the "gleaning of ears and grains" (*uñchaśila*), which is truthful. (Verse 2cd)

The two [terms] *yācita* (borrowed) and *ayācita* (unborrowed) correspond respectively to *mṛta* (dead/ceased) and *amṛta* (not ceased/living). *Satyānṛta* (truth-and-falsehood) is the state of a merchant (*vaṇigbhāva*). Debt (*ṛṇa*) is the clearing of an obligation (*paryudaśana*). *Uddhāra* is the application of capital; *kusīda* is living by interest. (*Maṇḍa* is neuter; it is one name for what is known as *nivalī*). *Māsara* and *ācāma* [are synonyms].

*Nilāva*, *visrāva* (according to Mukuṭa), and *nīsa* or *peja*—these three refer to the scum produced from boiled rice (*maṇḍa*). *Yavāgū*, *uṣṇikā*, *śrāṇā*, *vilepī*, and *taralā* are five names for liquid rice-gruel (*dravadodana*). [In the second section: Oil is used for washing and anointing; *kṛsara* is rice cooked with sesame seeds. The term *gravya* (meat-broth) applies to all [broths] in the three genders; *gomaya* (cow-dung) is derived from cows and is not feminine.

50 || That [cow-dung] when dried is *karīṣa* (not feminine). *Dugdha*, *kṣīra*, and *payaḥ* are synonymous. *Payasya* refers to clarified butter (*ājya*), curds (*dadhi*), and so forth. *Drapsa* refers to curds that are not thick. 51 || *Ghṛta*, *ājya*, *havis*, and *sarpiḥ* mean clarified butter. *Navanīta* is butter recently extracted. That which is clarified butter produced from the milk of a cow that has just calved is called *haiyaṅgavīna*. 52 || *Daṇḍāhata*, *kālaśeya*, and *ariṣṭa* are synonyms for *gorasa* (cow-product). *Takra* is buttermilk; it is called *udaśvit* when churned with one-fourth water, and *mathita* when churned with half water, and *nirjala* when churned without water. 53 || [This is the definition] of that which is thus known.

*Yavāgū* (gruel) is the end [of the list]. *Prakṣaṇā* is an insertion regarding the *argha* (offering). *Akṣaṇam* and *abhyañjanam* (anointing) are two terms for oil. *Kasara* is rice mixed with sesame; this is one term. Whatever milk and so forth belongs to cows—meaning that which comes from cows or is a product of cows—is called *gavya*; this is one term. It applies to three genders. *Dadhi* (curd), *dugdha* (milk), and so on [are included]. *Govit* and *gomayam* are two terms for cow dung, known as *śeṇa*. *Goviṭ* ends in a short vowel (*sī*). || 50 ||

Dried cow-dung is *gomaya* or *karīṣa*; these two refer to what is commonly known as *govar*. Milk is *dugdha*, *kṣīra*, and *payaḥ*—three terms for what is known as *dūdha*. *Payaḥ* ends in a long vowel (*-as*). That which is a derivative of milk, such as clarified butter (*ājya*), curds (*dadhi*), and so forth, is called *payasya*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), buttermilk (*takra*) and fresh butter (*navanīta*) are included. Curds that are thickened and other than thin are *drapsa*; according to the *Bharatamālā*, *drapsya* is also used, and *drapsa* may be masculine. This one term refers to what is popularly known as *pātala dahī*. || 51 ||

*Ghṛtam*, *ājyam*, *haviḥ*, and *sarpiḥ*—these four are synonyms for clarified butter (*ghṛta*). According to Hemacandra, *haviḥ* and *sarpiḥ* are used in the sense of "clarified butter to be offered in sacrifice" (*hotavyam*). *Añjanīyam* refers to clarified butter. [The suffix] *kyap* is applied after the root *ad* (to eat) preceded by *ā* when forming a name. *Navanītam* and *navoddhṛtam* (two words) refer to what is known as "loṇī. *Yakṣīnam* is fresh butter produced from milk obtained on the previous day, extracted at that very time from a cow that has just calved. One [term] refers to clarified butter produced from milk that has stood for one night.

That which originated from the milking of cows yesterday is *hyogodohika* (or *hyaṅgava*). [The rule] "heya-gavīnaṃ saṃjñāyām" applies. For *hyo godohaḥ*, the substitute *hyaṅgu* is prescribed, and the suffix *khañ* is also applied in the sense of a derivative (*vikāra*). (52) *Ariṣṭa* refers to whey (*kālaśeya*) that has been stirred with a staff (*daṇḍāhata*). According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "Ariṣṭa is used for the sun, for that [whey], for the maternity room, for auspiciousness, and for a sign of death. There are four names for the essence of cow's milk (*gorasa*) when it is a collection stirred with a staff. He states its specific varieties:

That in which water constitutes one-fourth part is called *daṇḍāhata* (beaten with a stick). That in which water constitutes one-half is called *udavit* (swollen); the analysis of the compound is: "it swells (*śvayati*) or increases (*vardhate*) by means of water. [The root] *ud* [is used] in the sense of "motion" and "increase. That which is devoid of water is *nirjala*. [This refers to] the churning of curd. (Note: This portion is also not found in the palm-leaf manuscript. [End of Vaiśya-varga, Section 53–57, with commentary from the Amarakośa. 1. This part is also not found in the palm-leaf manuscript. 2. Digitized by Google. 53–57. 224. [Section on the Vaiśyas].

The cream of curd is *maṇḍa*; *mastu* is the whey; *pīyūṣa* is fresh milk. Hunger is *aśanāyā*, *bubhukṣā*, and *kṣut*; a morsel is *grāsa* (masculine). (54) *Sapīti* (feminine) is drinking together; *sagdhi* (feminine) is eating together. (55) *Udanyā*, *pipāsā*, *tṛṭ*, and *tarṣa* are thirst. Eating is *jagdhi* and *bhojana*. (1) *Jemanam*, *leha*, *āhāra*, *nivāsa*, and *nyāda* also denote food. Satiety is *sauhitya*, *tarpaṇa*, and *tṛpti*. What is left over after eating is *phelā*. (56)

*Kāmaṃ*, *prakāmaṃ*, *paryāptaṃ*, *nikāmeṣṭaṃ*, and *yathepsitam* [mean] at will, excessively, sufficiently, according to desire, and as wished. *Gopa*, *gopāla*, *gosamkhya*, *godhuk*, *gambhīra*, and *balavān* [refer to] a cowherd; [the first] by its mere mention is said to be churned [milk]; each one [is a synonym]. *Maṇḍa* is the cream produced from curds; *mastu* is the first [layer], the whey; this is one word, used in the neuter. [It refers to] the upper part of the curds; it is also considered to be the watery portion of the curds strained through a cloth. Fresh milk—the milk of a cow that has recently calved—for a period of seven days, is called *pīyūṣa*.

According to the *Viśva* and *Medinī* lexicons: "Pīyūṣa [is used] for milk up to seven days old, and likewise for nectar. According to Mukuṭa, it is "peyūṣa"; some say that what has been described is denoted by the word *satpīyūṣa*. (This is one term). *Aśanāyā*, *bubhukṣā*, and *kṣut*—these three denote hunger. *Kṣut* is feminine and ends in the letter *dh*. "The desire for food (*aśana*) is *aśanāyā*; [it is called] *kṣudh* in another [text]. *Prāsa* and *kavala* (two terms) denote a mouthful, known as "ghāṃsa. There is also a reading meaning "that which serves as a mouthful. || 54 ||

*Sapītiḥ* (drinking together) and *tulyapānam* (equal drinking) are two terms for drinking together. *Sandhiḥ* (joining) and *sahabhojanam* (eating together) are two terms for eating together; in this context, *sandhiḥ* is feminine. *Udanyā*, *pipāsā*, *tṛṭ*, and *vṛṣaḥ*—these four denote thirst. The word *hṛt* ends in a sibilant (*ṣ*). *Tarṣaḥ* is masculine. According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *tṛṣā* is used in the feminine sense of both thirst and desire. *Jagdhiḥ* and *bhojanam* (55) [denote eating]. *Jemanam* is also found in the *Dvirūpakośa*. *Lehaḥ* (and *lepaḥ*) [denote licking]; Hemacandra states: "The word *lepaḥ* is used in the sense of smearing, as well as in the sense of eating and wine."

*Āhāraḥ*, *nighāsaḥ* (also *nighasaḥ*), and *nyādaḥ*—these seven are synonyms for food. *Jandhiḥ* is feminine. *Sauhitya*, *tarpaṇa*, and *tṛptiḥ*—these three denote satisfaction. That which was eaten previously and subsequently discarded is *bhuktasamujjhitam*, meaning that which is cast off after eating; it is called *phelā*. Jaṭādhara says it is also *phelī*; this is one term. *Kāmam*, *prakāmam*, *paryāptam*, *nikāmam*, *iṣṭam*, and *yathepsitam*—these denote according to one's desire; these are adverbs.

He [the cowherd] acts according to his will; he is a *bhṛṅga*, a *gopa*, a *gopāla*, a *gosamkhya*, and a *godhuk* (or *goduha*). According to the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*, "gopa, goduha, and ballava" are synonyms. He is also called an *ābhīra* or an *abhīra*—[the latter derived from] *abhi īrayati*, with the root *īr* meaning "to move" and so forth. *Ballava* is another term for the cowherd (*gopāla*). [The dual forms are] *goduhau*. [Note: This half-verse is not found even in the palm-leaf manuscript. [This concludes] the second book. Cattle, buffaloes, and so forth, as well as their foot-tethers, [are mentioned]; [the word *go*] refers to the lord of cows (*gavīśvara*).

A cowherd is *gomin*, while a herd of cows is *gomāyu* or *gokula*; the term *godhana* refers to a collection of cattle. *Āśitaṅgavīna* (in all three genders) denotes a place where cows have previously been fed. An ox is called *ukṣan*, *bhadra*, *balīvarda*, *ṛṣabha*, *vṛṣabha*, or *vṛṣa*. A bull is *anaḍvān*, *saurabheya*, or *gauḥ*. A herd of bulls is *aukṣaka*; a herd of cows is *gavyā* or *gotrā*. A herd of calves is *vatsakya*, and a herd of milch-cows is *ghainuka*. A large bull is *mahokṣa*, and an old bull is *jaradgava*.

An ox that has reached maturity is called an *ukṣā* or *jātokṣa*; one just born is a *tarṇaka*. A calf that excretes dung is a *vatsa*; the terms *damya* and *vatsatara* are synonymous. (57–61) The term *dhyādika* refers to the tethering by the foot; it means that which is bound by the foot or at the foot. Some read *yādavaṃ dhanam* (wealth consisting of cattle); in this regard, the authority of another lexicon states: "Wealth such as cows and the like is *yādava*. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), donkeys, goats, sheep, and so forth are included. *Gomān* and *gomī* are two words for the owner of cattle, the master of cows. [In the dual: *gomantau*.

*Gomī* (owner of cows). *Gokulam* and *godhanam*—these two denote a herd of cattle, that is, a collection of things related to cows. (58) *Āśitaṅgavīnam* is the name for a place where cows were formerly fed or nourished; it is a single term used in all three genders (*triṣu liṅgeṣu*). *Ukṣā*, *bhadraḥ*, *balīvardaḥ* (also *balīvardaḥ*), *ṛṣabhaḥ*, *vṛṣabhaḥ*, *vṛṣaḥ*, *anadvān*, and *anaḥ* (as in *anaḥ* = *śakaṭam*)—these nine names refer to a bull. [Note: *Anaḥ* is masculine here, though the *Rabhasakośa* states: "The word *anaḥ* is neuter when meaning water or sorrow, but also refers to a mother or a chariot. *Saurabheyaḥ* and *gauḥ*—these two [refer to a cow]. (59) [Total: nine names for a bull.]

*ukṣāṇau*, *anaḍvāhau*, *gāvau*. In the feminine: *anaḍvāhī*; [alternatively] after *anaḍuh*, it is optionally feminine: *anuḍuhī* as well. A collection or multitude of bulls (*ukṣan*) or breeding oxen (*vṛṣabha*) is called *aukṣakam*—this is one term. A collection of cows is *gavyā* or *gotrā*—these two. A collection of calves is *vātsakam*. A collection of milch-cows is *dhenukam*. These are the respective single terms for each. (60) A large bull is *mahokṣaḥ*—one term for a great bull; it is correctly formed by the rule *acatura-*.

*vṛddhokṣaḥ* and *jaradbhavaḥ* are two terms for an old bull (*vṛddhavṛṣabha*). As stated in the *Mālā*: "A *mahokṣaḥ* is one that is larger than an ox (*ukṣatara*); a *skāndhikaḥ* is one that carries on its shoulders; a *ṣoḍan* is a calf with six teeth; a *kūṭaḥ* is one whose horns are broken. *Jātokṣaḥ* is one term for a bull that has reached full maturity (*balīvardamātra*). A bull born on the very day is called *tarṇakaḥ*; this is one term. *Śakṛtkariḥ* and *vatsaḥ* are two terms for a calf. *Damyaḥ* and *vatsataraḥ* are two terms for one clearly in the prime of youth.

A *vatsatara* is a very young bull (*vatsatva*). A bull fit for castration is an *ārṣabhya*; he is also called *ṣaṇḍa* (or *śaṇḍha*) and *gopati*. An *itvara* is one who acts according to his own will; these three terms refer to a bull that wanders at will. An *ārṣabhya* is a bull fit for castration; he is also termed *ṣaṇḍa*, *gopati*, and *itvara*. On its shoulder region is the *vaha*; the dewlap on its neck is the *sāsnā*.

A draft animal that is not yoked is called *nasyota*; one that stands at the side of the yoke is a *praṣṭhavāṭ*. Those who carry the burden of the yoke and so forth are respectively termed *yugya*, *prāsaṅga*, and *śākaṭa*. One who digs with an instrument is called by its name; the one who carries that instrument is a *hālika* (ploughman), while the one who carries it on his head is a *sairika*. Those who bear the yoke are called *dhūr-vaha*, *dhurya*, *ghoreya*, *dhurīṇa*, and *sadhurandhara*. Both *ekadhurīṇa* and *ekadhura* refer to one who bears a single yoke. However, he who indeed bears every yoke is the *sarvadhurīṇa*. A cow is called *māheyī*, *saurabheyī*, *gauḥ*, *usrā*, *mātā*, and *bhṛṅgiṇī*.

66 || 226. Of the bull known as *pola*: *sanoti* means he gives; *garbha-ṣaṇḍaḥ*. *Iṭcaraḥ* means one who moves according to his desire (*iṣā*). || 62 || On the shoulder region of this bull, there is the *vahaḥ*, one [term] for what is known as *khāṃdā*. *Sāsnā* and *galakambalaḥ* are two [names] for the skin hanging from the neck of the ox, known as *sāṃkalī* or *kāṃbala*. *Nastitaḥ* and *nasyotaḥ* (there is also the reading *nastotaḥ*) [refer to one to whom a nose-string has been passed].

"Two [terms] for one whose nose is pierced": *vesaṇya* and *baila*—these are the names known [for such an animal]. *Nasyota* means one whose nose (*nasye*) is tied (*ūta*) with a rope through the nostril. *Praṣṭhavāṭ*: Svāmī says that *praṣṭhavāṭ* is [the same as] *paṣṭhavāṭ*, but without the *repha*. "Two [terms] for one that goes by the side of the yoke": these refer to an animal bound by a wooden yoke on its shoulder for the purpose of taming. It is called *yugapārśvaga* because it goes (*gacchati*) by the side (*pārśve*) of the yoke (*yugasya*), which is the shoulder-yoke. *Yugya* means a bearer of the yoke.

At the time of breaking in young bulls (*vatsa*), a wooden yoke is placed upon their shoulders; that is called *prāsaṅga*. One who carries it is a *prāsaṅgya*, known as a "bullock for the yoke" (*loḍhaṇyā baila*). One who carries a cart is a *śākaṭa*; these [terms] are each used singly. In the sense of "one who digs with that," there may be the words *hālika* and *sairika*. For example: one who digs with a plough (*hala*) is a *hālika*. Likewise, one who carries a plough, or belongs to the plough, is a *hālika*. Similarly, one who digs with a plough (*sīra*), or carries a plough, or belongs to the plough, is a *sairika*. *Sīra* is a synonym for the plough (*hala*).

Two [terms] for that which is known as "nāṃgacyā baila": || 64 || *Dhūrvaha*, *dhurya*, *dhaureya*, *dhurīṇa*, and *dhurandhara*—these five words denote a bull that bears the yoke (*dhurandhara-vṛṣabha*). The word *dhūrvaha* begins with a long vowel; the lengthening occurs by the rule "rvor upadhāyāḥ. However, in the case of *dhurya*, the lengthening is prohibited by the rule "na bhakurkurām."

*Ekadhurīṇaḥ*, *ekadhuraḥ*, and *ekadhurāvahaḥ*—these three terms refer to one who carries a single burden alone. He who carries even the entire burden is called *sarvadhurīṇaḥ*. [The word *māheyī* refers to a cow.]

9]. Second Book. A female Arjuna (white) cow that is excellent among cows is called a *rohiṇī* or a *naicikī*. Names such as *śabalī* (spotted) and *dhavalā* (white) arise from distinctions of color and other qualities. [67] A two-year-old cow is a *bihāyanī*; a one-year-old is an *ekahāyanī*. A four-year-old is a *caturhāyaṇī*, and likewise, a three-year-old is a *trihāyanī*. [68] A barren cow is a *vaśā*; one that has miscarried is an *avatokā*; one whose fetus is leaking is a *sravadrbhā*. A cow covered by a bull is a *sandhinī*. One that destroys the embryo is a *vehad*. [69]

A cow that comes to be with calf at the proper time is called *prajane prohī*. A young cow that has recently conceived is *bālagarbhiṇī*. One that is not fierce is *acaṇḍī*; one that is easy to manage is *sukarā*; and one that gives birth frequently is *bahusūti* or *pareṣṭukā*. (70) A female buffalo is *saurabheyī*, *mauḥ*, *usā*, *mātā*, or *śuṅgiṇī*. (66) The words *arjunī*, *anyā*, *rohiṇī*, *navaka*, *gavi*, *gāvau*, and *mātarau* refer to a cow. That which is the best among cows is called *gaurnaicikī* (one term); it is also *nicikī*. According to the *Nāmamālā*: "The cow that is equal to a *naicakī* is proclaimed as *nicikī*. (66)

The *Dvirūpakośa* states: "nīcikā and nīcikī. A cow that moves low is called *naicikī*. Due to differences in color, limbs, size, and so forth, there are names for cows such as *śabalī* (variegated) and *ghavalā* (white). *Śabalī* means having a variegated color; *śabalā* is also used. *Ghavalā* means having a white color; *dhavalī* is also used. By the word "and so forth," [names like] *kapilā* (tawny) and *pāṭalā* (pinkish-white) are included. Due to differences in limbs, there are names such as *lambakarṇā* (long-eared) and *vakraśṛṅgī* (crooked-horned). Due to differences in size, there are names such as *dīrghā* (tall), *kharvā* (dwarf), and *vāmanī* (short). [These are] one by one. (67) He now states the difference in names based on differences in age.

A cow whose measure is two years is *dvihāyanī* (one); a one-year-old cow is *ekahāyanī* (one); a four-year-old cow is *caturhāyaṇī* (one). A three-year-old cow is *trihāyaṇī* (one). [Note: "The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in *hāyana* after *tri* and *catur* should be stated. (Vārttika 68)] *Vaśā* and *vandhyā* (two) refer to a barren cow known as *vāṃśa*. *Avatokā* and *sravadgarbhā* (two) refer to one whose fetus has fallen unexpectedly; [the *Mālā* lexicon states: "she who has a dead calf is *savatsā*"].

A *sandhinī* is a cow that has been mounted by a bull for the purpose of mating; she is so called because she possesses *sandhā*, which is conception or the act of impregnation. Alternatively, a *sandhinī* is one who destroys the embryo due to the bull's approach; such a cow is called a *vehad*. Bhāguri states that *vehat* means "one who has approached [for mating]. A cow that is ready for breeding—that is, whose time for conception has arrived—is called *upasaryā*. A young cow that is pregnant is a *bālagarbhiṇī*; she is also called a *praṣṭhauhī* (though *paṣṭhauhī* is also a reading).

In this regard, there is elision of the *ra* due to its being included in the *pṛṣodarādi* group; thus, one name for a cow that does not kick is *acaṇḍī* and *sukārā*. Two names for one that is not irritable are *akopanā*. Two names for one that has many offspring are *bahusūtiḥ* and *pareṣṭukā*. *Vaṣkaraṇī* (also *vaṣkariṇī*) and *ciraprasūtā* refer to a cow that has long since calved. *Baṣkayaḥ* is a young calf. A cow that has long since calved is called *baṣkayaṇī*. A cow that has recently calved is a *ghenuḥ*. One that gives milk easily is *susratā*. One with full, swelling udders is *pīnonnī*; one with large, fleshy teats is *pīvarastanī*.

A *droṇakṣīrā* is a cow that yields a *droṇa* measure of milk; a *dhenuṣyā* is a cow held as security. A *samāṃsamīnā* is a cow that calves every year. (72) *Ūdhas*, *klība*, and *āpīna* denote the udder. *Śivaka* and *kīlaka* mean a tethering post. *Drāma* and *saṃdāna* are not masculine. *Paśurajju* and *dāmanī* refer to the rope for tying cattle. (73) The *vaiśākha*, *mantha*, *manthāna*, and *manthāna* are the churning sticks. The *kuṭhera* and *daṇḍaviṣkambha* are the supports for the stick. The *manthanī* and *gargerī* are synonymous [for the churning vessel]. It possesses this [quality]. (74)

*Maṣkaya* is a one-year-old calf, according to Śākaṭāyana. *Dve* refers to a cow that has calved twice after a long interval. *Dhenu* refers to a cow that has recently calved; *nūtanaprasūtā* also means the same. *Suvratā* and *sukhasaṃdohā* (also *sukhasaṃtuhā*) refer to a well-behaved cow, known as *nisakīna*. *Pīnodhī* and *pīvarastanī* refer to a cow with full udders. *Droṇakṣīrā* and *droṇadugdhā* refer to two cows that yield a *droṇa* measure of milk.

A *dhenuṣyā* (one word) is a cow placed as a pledge (*bandhaka*) or a mortgage (*ādhi*) in the creditor's house for the purpose of milking until the debt is cleared; that is to say, she is kept there for milking. Regarding this, the *Viśvakośa* states: "A *bandhaka* is a pledge (*vinimaya*). In the vernacular language, *bandhaka* or *ādhi* is called *gāhāṇa*. A cow that calves every year is called *samāṃsamīnā* (five syllables). (72) *Ūṣas* and *āpīnam* (two words) refer to the udder of a cow, known as *kāṃsa*. *Ūdhas* ends in a nasal (*sānta*) and is feminine.

*Śivaka* and *kīlaka* (two) refer to a wooden post driven into the ground for tethering cattle, known as *meḍha*. *Dāma* and *saṃdāna* (two) refer to a tethering rope, known as *dābeṃ*; it is called *saṃdāna* because it is bound (*saṃdīyate*). The word *dāma* ends in the letter *m*; however, in the feminine gender, the forms are *dāmā*, *dāmānau*, and so on. *Paśurañjaḥ* and *dāmanī* (the latter also read as *bandhanī*) (two) refer to a rope with many knots used to tie several bulls together, known as *dāvaṇa*.

*Aṣṭāpada* refers to a chessboard (*śāriphala*) consisting of two rows of squares upon a cloth or similar material that serves as the base for the pieces (*śārī*) and is marked with compartments—commonly known as a *sārīpaṭa*. A *śārī*, however, is a specific gaming instrument made of wood or other materials, well-known in the vernacular as an *aṅgaṭī*. *Prāṇidhūrta* is a specific type of game characterized by mutual combat among living beings such as rams or cocks; it is called *samāhvaya*. That which is performed with non-living objects is called *dyūta* (gambling) in the world.

"For that which is performed by living beings is to be known as *samāhvaya*," so it is said. [This concludes] one [verse]. Here, because there is no prescription for a distinction of gender (*liṅga-bheda*) for some [terms], he removes the objection regarding their incompleteness with the words "uktāḥ" (they have been stated). Here, within the category of Śūdras, there are derivative (*yaugika*) words such as *kumbhakāra* (potter), *mālākāra* (garland-maker), and so forth.

Because they are seen to have abundant usage in the masculine gender alone in works such as the *Kāvyas* and *Purāṇas*, those [words] mentioned or specified in one gender should—due to their sharing that property (*tāddharmyāt*), since the properties of the qualified [word] belong to the qualifier—be inferred to apply even in other genders, such as the feminine, when there is a specific application characterized by femininity and so forth. Furthermore, by the force of the word "also" (*api*), it should be understood that even conventional terms (*rūḍha*) such as *karaṇa* and *kulāla*, because they denote a genus (*jāti*), function in both the masculine and the feminine.

A word whose meaning is understood through the power of its constituent parts (*avayava-śakti*) is *yaugika* (derivative). A word whose meaning is understood solely through the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*), without regard for the power of its constituent parts, is *rūḍha* (conventional). Among these, an example of a *yaugika* word in another gender is: *kumbhakārī* (female potter) and *kumbhakāram* (potter's family). Similarly: *mālākārī* (female garland-maker) and *mālākāram* (garland-maker's family). Because it ends in the suffix *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied in the case of the female. An example of a non-*yaugika* word is: *karaṇī* (female artisan) and *kulālī* (female potter). Here, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule "after a class-name that does not denote a female... (Pāṇini 4.1.63). Thus ends the section on Śūdras (10).

The meaning is that the gender and number of the qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa) should be exactly the same as those of the qualified (viśeṣya). The womb (*jarāyu*) is the uterus; those born from it are "womb-born. Worms, insects, and the like are "sweat-born" (*svedaja*). One [category]. By the word "and so forth," bedbugs, mosquitoes, and others are included. (50)

Because they are born from moisture (*sveda*), they are called *khedaja* (moisture-born). Birds and the like are *aṇḍaja* (egg-born). [The word] "one" [is used]. Those born from eggs are *aṇḍaja*. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), fish and others are included. Thus ends the section on living beings (*prāṇivarga*). Trees, shrubs, and so forth are *udbhidaḥ* (earth-sprouts). For when they are being born, they break through the earth; thus they are called *udbhidaḥ*. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), grass and other plants are included. "One" [is used]. *Udbhit*, *udbhija*, and *udbhida*—these three [terms] refer to that which sprouts from the earth. || 51 ||

*Sundara*, *rucira*, *cāru*, *suṣama*, *sādhu*, *śobhana*, *kānta*, *manorama*, and also *manohara*; *rucya*, *manojña*, *mañju*, and *mañjula*—these twelve [terms] denote the beautiful. *Su* means excellent; it is *suṣama* because everything in it is excellent (*suṣamam*). According to the rule "after *su*, *vi*, *ni*, and *dur*, the *s* of *sama* becomes *ṣ*," the *s* of *sama* changes to *ṣ*. *Ramya*, *manorama*, *saumya*, *bhadraka*, and also *rāmaṇīyaka* [denote the same]. That which, upon being seen, brings no end to the satisfaction of the eyes and the mind.

That which, even when seen many times, produces an even greater degree of pleasure—this [verse] is also found in the *Tālapatra* manuscript (Mā 11). **The Third Book.** *Abhīṣṭa*, *abhīpsita*, *hṛdya*, *dayita*, *vallabha*, and *priya* denote that which is desired or beloved. *yāpya* (despicable), *avama* (low), *aghama* (wicked), *kupūya* (or *kapūya*—the absence of the letter *t* is due to its belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* class), *kutsita* (blameworthy), *avadya* (censurable), *kheṭa* (loathsome), *garhā* (reproachable), *aṇaka* (or *āṇaka*—these thirteen denote the low). *Kheṭa* means that which terrifies (*kheṭati*). *Arvān* ends in *n*; *arvantau* [is the dual]. Vareṇyaḥ, pravaraḥ, anavarārdhyaḥ (57), parārdhyaḥ, agraḥ, prāgraharaḥ, prābhyaḥ, anyaḥ, agrīyaḥ, apriyaḥ—these seventeen [terms] refer to that which is preeminent (*pradhāna*). *Śreyān*, *śreṣṭhaḥ*, *puṣkalaḥ*, *sattamaḥ*, and *atiśobhanaḥ* (the latter being followed by *atyanta-* etc. denote the most excellent. *Śreyān*, *śreṣṭhaḥ*, *puṣkalaḥ*, and *sattamaḥ* are used for that which is most beautiful. || 58 || In compound words, when occurring as the final member (*uttarapada*), the words *vyāghra*, *puṅgava*, *ṛṣabha*, *kuñjara*, *siṃha*, *śārdūla*, *nāga*, and so forth, are masculine and signify excellence. || 59 || *Aprāgyam* and *adayahīnam* are two terms for that which is not primary; they mean secondary or subordinate (*apradhāna*). || 59 ||

*Viśaṅkaṭa*, *pṛthu*, *bṛhat*, *viśāla*, *pṛthula*, and *mahat* mean wide, broad, large, extensive, or great. *Vaḍra*, *uru*, and *vipula* mean vast. *Pīna* and *pīva* mean fat; *sthūla* and *pīvara* mean thick or stout. *Stoka*, *alpa*, and *kṣullaka* mean small. *Sūkṣma*, *lakṣṇa*, *dabhra*, *kṛśa*, and *tanu* mean fine, subtle, thin, or slender. *Mātrā* and *truṭi* (feminine) denote a minute particle; *lava*, *leśa*, *kaṇa*, and *aṇu* (masculine) denote a tiny fragment. *Alpiṣṭha*, *alpīyaḥ*, *kanīyaḥ*, and *aṇīyaḥ* mean very small or extremely minute. These words beginning with *vyāghra* (tiger) have as their scope—that is, their referent—the meaning of "excellent" when they occur as the second member of a compound. According to the rule "That which is compared [is placed first] with words such as *vyāghra*, provided that a common quality is not expressed," the specific term is placed first, while *vyāghra* and the others function as the second member. || 59 ||

*Aprāgrya*, *apradhāna*, and *upasarjana*—these three denote that which is secondary (*apradhāna*). "That which is different from what is primary (*prāgyāt*) is *aprāgyam*. *Stoka*, *alpa*, and *kṣullaka*—these three denote the small. *Sūkṣma*, *lakṣṇa*, *dava*, *kṛśa*, and *tanu* [mean thin]. (61) *Mātrā*, *truṭi*, *lava*, *leśa*, *kaṇa*, and *aṇu*—these eleven denote the minute. Some maintain that the words from *stoka* to *aṇu* are synonymous. Among them, *mātrā* and *truṭi* are feminine (though *truṭi* is sometimes seen ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*). Words beginning with *lava* are masculine. (63) Those numbers which are to be counted (*saṃkhyeya*) and exceed a hundred or a thousand are, respectively, called *paraḥśata* and *paraḥsahasra*; the meaning is that they are "beyond a hundred" or "beyond a thousand. *Pelavam*, *viralam*, and *tanu*—these three denote that which is sparse. *Samīpaḥ*, *nikaṭaḥ*, *āsannaḥ*, *sanikṛṣṭaḥ*, *sanīḍaḥ*, *sadeśaḥ*, *abhyāsaḥ* (Mukuṭa maintains that *abhyāsaḥ* ends with a dental [d]), *savidhaḥ*, *samaryādaḥ*, *saveśaḥ*, *upakaṇṭhaḥ*, *antikaḥ*, *abhyarṇaḥ*, *abhyagraḥ*, and *abhitaḥ*—these fifteen denote proximity. That which is slightly different from its own nature due to the influence of an external condition (*upādhi*) is called *bandhura*; the meaning is that it is uneven or wavy. *Bandhura* is also a form; these two [terms] refer to one thing. In the feminine, it is *nīcī*. *Avāgram*, *avanatam*, and *ānatam*—these three denote that which is bent downwards or facing down.

*Śāśvataḥ*, *dhruvaḥ*, *nityaḥ*, *sadātanaḥ*, and *sanātanaḥ*—these five [terms] refer to that which is eternal (*nitya*). "One whose nature is to remain is *sthāsnuḥ*. The dual form is *stheyāṃsau*. That which, by virtue of its uniformity, pervades time through a single nature—such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth—is *kūṭasthaḥ*. Immovable (*sthāvara*); moving about (*janamat*), third section. Moving, wandering, creeping, trembling, active, moving and unmoving (*carācara*). Shaking, quivering, trembling, unsteady, fickle, wavering (*calācala*). Also, unstable (*cañcala*) and tremulous (*tarala*), as well as *pāriplava* and *pariplava*. Excessive, exceeding; and that which is compactly joined is *saṃhata*. Harsh, hard, cruel, rigid, harsh, firm.

*Jaṭharam* (the belly) is *mūrtimat* (embodied), *mūrta* (formed), *pravṛddham* (increased), and *prauḍhameghitam* (grown like a mature cloud). In ancient usage, *pratanu*, *anapu*, *arātanu*, and *cirantana* denote the old. *Pratyagra*, *abhinava*, *navya*, *navīna*, *nūtana*, and *nava* denote the new. *Nūta* is also used in this sense. *Sukumāram*, *komalam*, *mṛdulam*, and *mṛdu* denote what is soft. *Anvag*, *anvakṣam*, *anuga*, and *anupadam* are indeclinable (*avyaya*) neuter nouns meaning "following" or "behind. *Taraḥ* and *dvē* (two) are synonyms for that which does not move (*acara*). *Cariṣṇu*, *jaṅgamam*, *caram*, *trasam*, *iṅgam*, and *carācaram* denote that which moves.

By the *vārttika* rule "caricalipati," when the root *car* is reduplicated, the vowel of the reduplicated syllable becomes *a*. The same applies in the case of *calācalam*. There are six synonyms for one who moves. "One whose nature is to move is *cariṣṇu*. *Calanam*, *kampanam*, and *kampre*—these three refer to one whose nature is to tremble. *Calaṃ*, *lolam*, and *calācalam* [are synonyms]. (74) *Cañcalam*, *taralam*, and *pāriplavam*—these seven refer to that which is moving. *Pāriplavam* is derived from the root *pariplu*. There is also a reading: "*capalaṃ caṭulaṃ caiva*. *Atiriktaḥ* and *samadhikaḥ*—these two refer to that which is excessive or additional.

*Samyagadhika* and *samadhika* [mean the same]. *Dṛḍhasandhi* and *saṃhata*—these two refer to that which possesses firm joints. *Karkaśam*, *kavaṭam*, and *khakkhaṭam* (the latter also beginning with the second letter of the *ka*-group)—*kaṭhinam*, *krūram*, *kaṭhoram*, *niṣṭhuram*, *dṛḍham*, *jaṭharam*, and *mūrtimat*—these nine denote hardness (*kaṭhina*). 76. *Purāṇa*, *pratana*, *pratna*, *purātana*, and *cirantana*—these five are synonyms for that which is ancient (*purātanasya*). It is called *purāṇa* because it exists from of old (*purā bhavam purāṇam*); it is correct by the rule *sāyaṃ-ciraṃ-prāhṇe-prage-avyayebhyaṣ ṭyuṭyulau tuṭ ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.23), and by the specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) in the rule *purāṇaprokteṣu brāhmaṇakalpeṣu* (Pāṇini 4.3.105). *Anvak*, *anvakṣam*, *anugam*, and *anupadam*—these four are used in the sense of "following after" (*payād*). Because they are *avyayībhāva* compounds, they are neuter and indeclinable. That which is experienced by the senses is *aindriya*. *Pratyakṣam* refers to that which is perceptible to the senses; that which is beyond the senses is *atīndriyam*. *Ekatānaḥ*, *ananyavṛttiḥ*, *ekāgraḥ*, and *ekāyanaḥ* also [denote one whose mind is fixed on a single object].

Among those, the term *anta* (end) applies only to a son or a neuter child; for example, a woman who is independent (*khacchandā*) is the end of her family. *Mogha* and *nirarthaka* are two words for that which is useless; "that from which the purpose (*artha*) has departed is *nirarthakam*. *Spaṣṭa*, *sphuṭa*, *pravyakta*, and *ulbaṇa*—these four denote "the clear. *Sādhāraṇa* and *sāmānya* are two [words for commonality]. Even a single thing related to many is *sādhāraṇa*. However, *sāmānya* denoting a genus is neuter. *Ekākī*, *eka*, and *ekaka*—these three denote one who is without a companion.

*Mitra* and *anyatara*—the reading is *ekatara*—are synonyms; *eka*, *tva*, *anya*, and *itara* are six words with distinct meanings, meaning they are denoters of "one. The word *tva* is like *sarva* [in its declension]. *Tvau* and *ve*. (82) *Uccāvaca* and *naikabheda* are two words for that which is manifold. *Udak* and *avāk* form *uccāvacam*; it belongs to the class beginning with *mayūravysasaka*. *Uccaṇḍa* and *avilambita*—[Kṣīrasvāmī says it is *avilambana*]—are two words for "quickly. *Aruntuda* and *marmaspṛk* are two words for one who pierces the vital parts (*marman*).

*marmaspṛśau* (the two) mean "piercing the vital points. *Abādham* and *nirargalam* are two words for that which is "unobstructed" (*nirbādhasya*). [The derivation is: "there is no obstruction (*bādhā*) for this, thus it is *anāgham*" || 83 || *Prasavyam*, *pratikūlam*, *apasavyam*, and *apaśu*—[these are synonyms]. [End of section 1] • Third Book. *Prasavyam* and *pratikūlam* may mean "contrary" (*apasavyam*) and "unskilled" (*apaṭu*). The left side of the body is *savyam*, while the right side is *apasavyam*. || 84 || *Saṃkaṭam* (masculine), *saṃbādhaḥ*, *kalilam*, and *gahanam* are synonymous.

*Saṃkīrṇa*, *saṃkula*, and *ākīrṇa* mean crowded or filled. *Muṇḍita* and *parivāpita* mean shorn or shaved. *Granthita*, *sandita*, *dṛbdha*, *visṛta*, *vistṛta*, and *tata* mean woven, strung, or spread out. *Antargata* and *vismṛta* are synonyms for forgotten. *Mā* and *praṇihita* are the same. *Velita*, *previta*, *ādhūta*, *calita*, *ākampita*, and *dhuta* mean shaken or moved. *Nutta*, *nuna*, *asta*, *niṣṭhyūta*, *āviddha*, *kṣipta*, and *irita* are synonymous. *Parikṣipta* and *nivṛta* mean surrounded. *Bhūṣita* has the sense of being adorned. There are four synonyms for "contrary" or "opposite."

*Pragataṃ savyāt prasavyam*: that which is on the left side of the body is *savya*, one [term]; that which is on the right side of the body is *apasavya*, another. (84) *Saṃkaṭa* and *saṃbādha* are two words for a narrow space, such as a path and the like. *Nā* means "not. *Kalila* and *gahana* are two words for that which is difficult to penetrate; for example, a "dense" (*gahana*) scripture, meaning it is difficult to understand. *Saṃkīrṇa*, *saṃkula*, and *ākīrṇa* are three words for being excessively crowded with people and so forth; for example, a "crowded group" (*saṃkīrṇavarga*).

Some, however, say that these are previous synonyms, based on the connection with the phrase *saṃkīrṇam ṛṣipatnīnām* ("the wives of the sages were crowded together"). *Sṛṇḍita* and *parivāpita*—these two refer to one who has had his head shaved (*kṛtamuṇḍana*). *Granthitam*; there is also the reading *grathitam*. *Sanditam*—"there are also the readings *gumphitam* and *guphitam*"—and *dṛbdham*: these three refer to what is woven or strung together (*gumphita*). *Visṛtam*, *vistṛtam*, and *tatam*: these three refer to that which has found expansion or spread out. [The derivation is: "that which is spread out (*vistīryate*) is *vistṛtam*. *Antargatam* and *vismṛtam*: these two refer to what is forgotten (*vismṛta*).

*Visaryate* is [the term for] that which is forgotten (*vismṛtam*). *Prāptam* and *praṇihitam* are two [terms] for what has been obtained (*labdhasya*). *Prāpyate* is that which is being obtained (*prāptam*). (86) *Vellitaḥ*, *prekṣitaḥ*, *ābhūtaḥ*, *calitaḥ*, *ākampitaḥ*, and *dhutaḥ*—these six [denote] that which is slightly shaken. *Velayate* is *vellitaḥ*. [The root] *vel* means "to move. Another lexicon states: "*Presolitaḥ*, *taralitaḥ*, *ullāsitaḥ*, and *āndolitaḥ* as well. *Nuttaḥ*, *numaḥ*, *astaḥ*, and *nithyūtaḥ*—[the latter] is also written as *niṣhūtaḥ*.

*Āviddhaḥ*, *kṣiptaḥ*, and *īritaḥ*—these three denote that which has been propelled. "That which is pushed is *nuttaḥ*. (87) *Parikṣiptam* and *nivṛtam*—these two denote that which is surrounded on all sides by a fence or the like. "It is covered (*niviyate*), thus it is *nivṛtam*"; [the root] *vṛñ* is used in the sense of covering. *Bhūṣitam* and *muṣitam*—these two denote that which has been stolen; "it is plundered (*muṣyate*), thus it is *mūṣitam*. *Pravṛddham* and *prasṛtam*—these two denote that which is characterized by spreading; "it spreads (*prasarati*), thus it is *prasṛtam*. *Nyastam* and *nisṛṣṭam*—these two denote that which has been deposited.

*nisṛjyate* means that which is bestowed (*nisṛṣṭam*). [The root] *sṛj* is used in the sense of emission. *Guṇitam* (multiplied) and *āhatam* (struck) refer to that which has been multiplied by two or more. Just as four [is the result] when five are struck [by four], so too: *pravṛddha-prasṛte*, *nyasta-nisṛṣṭe*, *guṇita-āhate* || 88 || *nidigdha-upacite*, *gūḍha-gupte*, *guṇṭhita-rūṣite*, *duta-avadīrṇe*, *udbhūrṇa-udyate*, *kācita-śikyite* || 89 || [These pairs of synonyms are respectively: increased and spread out; placed and bestowed; multiplied and struck; smeared and accumulated; hidden and protected; covered and stained; moved quickly and torn asunder; raised up and lifted; weighed on a scale and suspended in a loop. || 89 ||

*Prāṇaghāta*, *digdhalita*, *samudakta*, and *uddhṛta* are synonyms for "killed. *Veṣṭita*, *valayita*, *saṃvīta*, *ruddha*, and *āvṛta* mean "encircled" or "surrounded. *Rugṇa* means "broken. Then, *nirśita*, *taikṣṇya*, and *tejita* mean "sharpened. *Pakva* means "ripe" or "ready for destruction. *Hrīṇa* and *hrīta* mean "ashamed. *Vṛtta*, *vṛta*, and *vyāvṛtta* mean "occurred. *Saṃyojita* and *upāhita* mean "joined. *Prāpya*, *gamya*, and *samāsādya* mean "attainable. *Syanna*, *rīṇa*, *śruta*, and *suta* mean "flowed" or "streamed. *Nidigdha* and *upacita* are two words for that which is abundant (*samṛddha*). It is smeared (*nidihyate*), hence it is *nidigdha*; [the root] *diha* means "to accumulate. *Gūḍha* and *gupta* are two words for that which is concealed (*gopanayukta*), as in: "A secret (*mantra*) must be kept hidden. *Guṇṭhita*—also *guṇṭhitam*—and *rūpita* are two words for that which is covered with dust (*dhūlilipta*), or for that which is known as *guṃḍālalela*. *Druta* and *avadīrṇa* are two words for that which has become liquid (*dravībhūta*). *Unūrṇa* and *udyata* are two words for a weapon or the like that has been raised (*uttolita*).

*Kāñcitam* and *śikyitam* (two) refer to that which is placed in a sling (*śikya*). *Ghrāṇam* and *ghrātam* (two) refer to a flower or the like whose fragrance has been grasped by the nose. *Digdham* and *liptam* (two) refer to that which is smeared. *Samudaktam* and *uddhṛtam* (two) refer to that which has been drawn out, such as water drawn from a well. *Veṣṭitam*, *valayitam*, *saṃvītam*, *ruddham*, and *āvṛtam* (five) refer to that which is encircled, such as a city surrounded by a river. *Rugṇam* and *bhugnam* (two) refer to that which is afflicted with pain.

Or [the term applies] to clay, wood, hands, feet, and so forth. *Niśitam* and *niśātam* are also used, due to the optional substitution of *tva* by the rule "śācchoranyatarasyām. *Kṣṇutam*, *śātam*, and *tejitam*—these four refer to a weapon or similar object that has been made sharp with a whetstone or the like. That which is sharpened is *niśātam*; from the root *śo* in the sense of "making thin. *Vināśonmukham* (facing destruction) and *pratyāsannavināśam* (with destruction imminent)—these two denote that which is *pakvam* (ripe/cooked). That which is cooked is *pakvam*. *Hrīṇaḥ*, *hrītaḥ*, and *lajjitaḥ*—these three denote one who has become ashamed. || 91 ||

*vṛttaḥ*, *vṛtaḥ*, *vyāvṛttaḥ*—some say *vāvṛttaḥ*—these three refer to one who has been chosen (*kṛtavaraṇa*). As the illustrative example (*lakṣya*) states: "The venerable Kāvya was indeed chosen by the Asuras for the office of priest (*paurohitya*). *Saṃyojitaḥ*—it appears as *saṃyogitaḥ* in the *Bharatamālā*. *Upāhitaḥ* refers to one who has been brought into association (*saṃyogaṃ prāpita*). *Prāpyam*, *gamyam*, *samāsādyam*—these three refer to what is capable of being attained (*prātuṃ śakyasya*). "That which is reached or attained is *samāsādyam*. *Sannam*, *rīṇam*, *sutam*, *srutam*—these four refer to that which is commenced (*prastutasya*).

*Syandyate* means it flows; *prakhavaṇe* (in the sense of flowing). *Saṃmūḍhaḥ* and *saṃkalitaḥ* are two terms for that which has been joined together, such as numbers and so forth—for example, two and three. *Saṃgūḍhaḥ*, *saṃkalitaḥ*, and *avagītaḥ* denote one who is censured or whose reproach is well-known. *Vividhaḥ*, *viṣamaḥ*, *nānārūpaḥ*, and *pṛthagvidhaḥ* mean of various kinds or diverse forms. *Avarīṇaḥ*, *ghikṛtaḥ*, *avadhvastaḥ*, and *avacūrṇitaḥ* are synonyms. *Phāṭam*, *khanitam*, and *dhvanitam* are identical terms for something done without effort.

94. *Baddha*, *saṃdānita*, *mūta*, *utkṣipta*, *saṃdita*, and *sita* mean bound. *Niṣpakva* refers to that which has been cooked; in the context of cooking milk, clarified butter (*ājya*), or sacrificial oblation (*havis*), it means "boiled" (*bhṛta*). 95–96. *Nirvāṇa* is used for a sage (*muni*) and for fire (*vahni*) [when extinguished]; *nirvāta* means when the wind has ceased. *Pakva* means matured (*pariṇata*); *gūna* means struck (*hata*); *mīḍha* means urinated (*mūtrita*). 96. *Puṣita* means nourished (*puṣṭa*); *kṣānta* means endured (*soḍha*); *uddhānta* means risen up (*udgata*). (Note: These ten terms ending in *-ta* are thus enumerated. *Avagīta* and *khyātagardha* are two words for one who is censured (*nindita*).

*Avagīta* means that which is reviled or censured; it has four synonyms: *vividha*, *bahuvidha*, *nānārūpa*, and *pṛthagvidha*. Regarding *nānārūpa*: "that whose form is manifold (*nānā*) is *nānārūpa*. *Avarīga* and *dhikṛta*—these two denote one who is merely censured. *Abadhvasta* and *apadhvasta*—"The word *apadhvasta* is used for what is abandoned, censured, or pulverized," according to the *Viśva* lexicon. *Avacūrṇita*—these two denote that which has been reduced to powder.

*Anāyāsakṛtam* means that which is prepared without effort; *phāṇṭam* is one such term for a specific kind of decoction (*kaṣāya-viśeṣa*). It is derived as an irregular form (*nipātita*) by the rule "kṣugh-kha-anta" etc., signifying "without effort. Bhāguri, however, states in his commentary on the Vedas that *phāṭa* refers to a substance placed [in water] prior to its reaching the state of butter (*navanīta*). *Svanitam* and *dhvanitam* are two words for that which has been sounded. *Parddham*, *saṃdānitam*, *mūtam*—[Mukuṭa says "mūrṇam"]—*udditam* (also *uditam*), *saṃditam*, and *sitam* are six synonyms.

*Baddha* [is used] for that which is bound. From the root *yūha* in the sense of binding, with the suffix *kta*, we have *baddha*. *Mṛta* [is derived from] the root *mṛ* in the sense of dying. With the prefixes *ut-* and *sam-*, the root *do* in the sense of cutting (*avakhaṇḍane*) has the meaning of binding; thus, *udita* and *saṃdita*. *Niṣpakva* and *kathita* are two terms for what is cooked in its entirety, such as a decoction (*kaṣāya*). For the cooking of milk and so forth, there is one term: *śṛta*. As in *śṛtaṃ kṣīram*, meaning "cooked milk. There is also a reading *kṣīrājyapayasām ṛtam*. (Verse 95) *Nirvāṇa* is one term used for a well-extinguished fire and so forth, but not for the wind.

For example, *nirvāṇo muniḥ* means "the sage who has emerged [from defilements]"; *nirvāṇo vahnih* means "the fire that has gone out"; by the word *ādi* (and so forth), *nirvāṇo hastī* means "the elephant that has submerged [in water]"; *nirvāṇaḥ pātaḥ* [is formed] from the root *vā* preceded by *nis*, with the suffix *kta* and the substitution of *na* for *t*. [These are] one [word each]. *Nirvātam* [means] "when the wind has gone," which is one [word]. *Pakva* and *pariṇata*—these two [refer to] that which has reached ripeness (*pāka-prāpta*). *Gūna* and *hava*—these two [refer to] one who has performed the voiding of excrement; *id* [in *ida*] means "voiding of excrement."

*mīḍha* and *mūtrita* are two terms for one who has voided urine.
