It is used in both masculine and neuter genders. *Arvā* means contemptible. *Varga* means a section or division; for example, as it was stated in the first *kāṇḍa*. *Avasara* means an occasion or introduction. *Amatra* means a vessel or container. *Mūla* refers to the capital of a merchant, and in that context, *bhāṇḍa* [is used]. *Bhūṣaṇa* refers to an ornament made of gold and other materials, as well as any ornament in general. (43) Thus end those words ending in *ḍa*. *Bhṛśam* means excessively or very much. *Pratijñā* means acceptance or a promise. *Pragāḍham* is also used in the sense of firm.

*Śakta* means capable; *samartha* means competent. *Dṛḍha* means firm in that sense. *Vinyasta* and *saṃhata* mean arrayed; *vyūḍha* means broad and thick. (44) Thus end the words ending in *ḍha*. *Bhrūṇa* refers to a child and to the fetus of a woman. *Bāṇa* refers to the son of Bali and to an arrow. *Kaṇa* refers to something extremely minute and to a portion of grain. *Gaṇa* refers to a multitude, a group of attendants (*pramatha*), and a troop. (45) *Paṇa* refers to a stake in gambling and the like, as well as wages, price, and even wealth.

*Maurya* refers to one who relies on wealth; *guṇa* denotes qualities such as courage, bravery, or diplomacy. (46) *Kṣaṇa* refers to a state of inactivity, a specific point of time, or a festival. *Varṇa* refers to the twice-born classes and so forth, or to white and other colors; however, *varṇam* (with a short *a*) refers to speech or a syllable. (47) *Aruṇa* may refer to the sun, and in its three genders it also denotes a particular color. *Sthāṇu* refers to Śiva; *droṇa* refers to a measure and also to a horse; *āja* refers to the sun; and *raṇa* refers to battle. (48) *Grāmaṇī* is masculine when referring to a barber, and in its three genders it means an excellent person or the lord of a village.

298. *Narbhava* occurs in the sense of "this" (*ayam*) and "our" (*naḥ*); *bhrūṇaḥ* refers to an embryo (*garbha*) and a child (*bāla*). *Bāṇaḥ* refers to the son of Bali (Kārttikeya) and an arrow (*śara*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *bāṇaḥ* may denote a singer, a type of Daitya, or simply a shaft. *Kaṇaḥ* refers to an extremely subtle object or a grain of rice. *Gaṇaḥ* refers to a Pramatha, a follower of Rudra. (45) *Dhūta* is a game played with dice and the like; by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), one includes combats between rams, cocks, and so forth. In that context, it refers to what is cast or placed as a wager.

The word *paṇa* refers to wages, a price, a commodity for sale, wealth, and four *kākiṇīs*. Because of the word "also" (*api*), it also refers to a stake in gambling and to vegetables such as *kathya* and *śāka*. This is stated in the *Gharṇī*: "In the *Gharṇī*, *paṇa* is used for the measure of cowries, a price, a *kārpāpaṇa* coin, wealth, a stake in gambling, vegetables for sale, a closed fist, a wager, and wages. It also refers to the string of a balance and to qualities inherent in substances, such as taste and smell.

Because the word *ādi* (and so forth) is connected with each [term], the term *guṇa* applies to *sattva*, *rajas*, and the like; to heroism, cleverness, and the like; to peace and war (*saṃdhivigraha*); to the sense organs; and to that which is stated as *adeṅ* [Pāṇini 1.1.2]. Regarding this, the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *guṇa* is used for a bowstring, a subordinate element, color and the like, a cook, a sense organ, renunciation, heroism and the like, the principles (*tattva*) and so forth, peace and the like, repetition, ropes, white and the like, and also in the case of the vowel *v*. (46)

*Tuṣṇīm* means remaining inactive or silent; *adhaḥ-sthāne* means in a low position; *kālaviśeṣe* means at a specific time; *muhūrtasya dvādaśe bhāge* means in the twelfth part of a moment (*muhūrta*); and *utsave* means on occasions such as the birth of a son. Regarding the word *varṇa*: it refers to a festival (*parvaṇi*) and to the castes such as Brahmins and Kṣatriyas; it refers to colors such as white and yellow; and it refers to praise (*stuti*) or eulogy (*stava*). It signifies a syllable (*akṣara*) or a year (*varṣa*), and is used in both the neuter and masculine genders. As the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *varṇa* is used for the twice-born [castes], white and other colors, fame, qualities, and stories; it is masculine in the sense of praise, but feminine in the sense of distinction, form, a syllable, and ointment. (47) It also denotes a reddish-brown color (*kapila*).

Due to the word *api* ("also"), [the term *aruṇa*] refers to the charioteer of the Sun; it also means "unmanifested passion" (*avyaktarāga*) and "the glow of twilight" (*saṃdhyārāga*). That is the word *aruṇa*. Due to the word *api*, *sthāṇu* occurs in the sense of a pillar (*stambha*) and so forth, as well as in the sense of a tree trunk (*yuṣi*). Due to the word *api*, *droṇa* occurs in other senses: in the sense of a father and in the sense of a specific measure (*parimāṇaviśeṣa*). *Raṇa* means battle (*ājau*), war (*yuddhe*), pleasure (*rase*), and sound (*śabde*). There is also an alternative reading: "*raṇa* also means crow (*kāke*). 48. *Śreṣṭha* means principal (*mukhya*).

*Ūrṇā* refers to the wool of sheep and the like, as well as the tuft of hair between the eyebrows. (49) *Hariṇī* may denote a female deer, a golden image, or anything that is green. In the masculine, *hariṇa* means pale or white; *sthūṇā* refers to a pillar or the support of a house. (50) *Tṛṣṇā* signifies both longing and thirst; *ghṛṇā* denotes both loathing and compassion. *Vipaṇi* refers to a marketplace, and *vāruṇī* means wine as well as the western quarter. (51)

*Kareṇu* refers to a female elephant (*strī*) or an elephant (*ibha*); *draviṇa* means strength (*bala*) or wealth (*dhana*). *Śaraṇa* denotes a house or a protector; *śrīparṇa* refers to a lotus as well. *Tīkṣṇa* is used for poison, a sword, or metal (in the neuter), and for something sharp or harsh (in the masculine). *Pramāṇa* refers to a cause, a boundary, an authority, a limit, a measure, or a witness. [The *Viśvaprakāśa* states: "A leader, a husband, a chief, and also a barber. One who leads a village is a *grāmaṇī*; the substitution of *ṇ* occurs according to the rule "from *agra* and *grāma*."

The word *ūrjā* refers to the hair on the back and the whorl between the eyebrows; it is the hair of rabbits, camels, and so forth. That same [hair], when possessed of wool (*sorṇā*), generally becomes the long, white, and praiseworthy whorl of great yogins such as Cakravartins and others—characteristic marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) that is as fine as a lotus fiber. (49) Furthermore, *haritā* is a golden image, meaning it is green or yellowish-green. As the *Medinīkośa* states: "The words *hariṇa* and *haritā* denote two types of names and a golden image."

*Pāṇḍu* refers to one of white complexion (*pāṇḍaravarṇa*) and, by the use of the word *ca*, to a species of deer; *stambha* is a pillar of a house (*veśman*). By the word *api*, it also means the illusion (*māyā*) of iron. (50) *Spṛhā* is desire (*vāñchā*); *pipāsā* is the thirst for drinking. "Disgust (*jugupsā*), censure (*nindā*), and compassion (*karuṇā*) are called *ghṛṇā*. *Vipaṇi* refers to a merchant's path (*vaṇikpatha*), a market street (*paṇyavīthī*), a shop (*āpaṇa*), and merchandise (*paṇya*). *Surā* is liquor (*madya*). *Pratyañc* is the western direction (*pratīcī dik*); both are *vāruṇya*. *Gaṇḍadūrvā* grass is also called *vāruṇī*.

According to another lexicon: *vāruṇī* refers to *gaṇḍadūrvā* grass, the western direction, and wine; it is feminine when referring to a woman. (51) *Kareṇu* is feminine when meaning an elephant female (*ibhī*); this same word is masculine when meaning an elephant male (*hastin*). *Bala* means prowess (*parākrama*). *Śaraṇa* means a house or a protector. [The lexicon states: "The word *śaraṇa* also applies to protection. Due to the word "and" (*ca*), *śrīparṇa* also refers to the *agnimantha* plant. (52) *Abhimara* means battle. *Khara* means sharp. [The lexicon states: "The word *tīkṣṇa* applies to sea salt, poison, iron, the *ajamodā* herb, and the *muṣkaka* tree."

According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *liṣ* [is used] for a eunuch, for barley-ears, for a man, for one who is sharp-natured, and for those who do not abandon [their kin]. *Hetu* means earth and so forth; *maryādā* means a boundary. *Imañcā* means delimitation. *Pramātā* means a knower. The word *pramāṇa* occurs in these senses. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *pramāṇa* is used for eternity, for a boundary, for scriptures, for a speaker of truth, for a measure (*iyattā*), for a cause, and in the singular neuter for a knower. (53) *Sādhakatama* is the most efficient cause for the accomplishment of an action.

The most effective means is called *karaṇa*—it applies to the field, the limbs, and the senses. *Saṃsaraṇa* refers to the birth of living beings and the movement of an army without obstruction. *Samugiraṇa* denotes a royal highway and the vomiting of food. From this point on, *viṣāṇa* occurs in three senses: it refers to the horn of an animal and the tusk of an elephant. *Pravaṇa* means a gradual slope; as a masculine noun, it denotes a crossroads.

*Saṃkīrṇa* means mixed; *nicita* means accumulated; *aśuddhi* means impurity; *viriṇa* means barren soil; *śūnya* means empty; *ūṣara* means saline soil. (56) ["*Varaṇa* also means a bridge, a fence, a braid of hair, a type of river, or a mass of hair. (1) Thus end the words ending in *ṇ*. *Vivasvant* refers to both the gods and the sun; *sarasvant* refers to both a river and the ocean. *Garumant* and *śakunt* refer to birds; specifically, *garumant* refers to the eagle (*garuḍa*), while *śakunt* refers to the vulture (*bhāsa*). (57) *Abhyutpāta* and *dhūmaketu* both refer to comets; *jīmūta* refers to both a cloud and a mountain. [Pāṇini has stated this in the section on words with multiple meanings.]

For example, in the expression "Vālī was killed by Rāma with an arrow," the arrow possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) because it is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) with respect to the action of killing. A field (*kṣetra*) is the place of origin for the growth of crops; as the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *karaṇa* [is used] in the sense of an instrument and a field. By the force of the word "also" (*api*), it includes the object (*karman*) and so forth. As Ajaya states: "The word *karaṇa* is used for an instrument, the body, a means of accomplishment, a sense organ, and an action; it refers to a vow performed on the body, to specific varieties of drama and song, and is declared to be masculine when denoting the son of a Śūdra father and Vaiśya mother, or a monkey, and so on."

*Prāṇinām* refers to living beings, in their arising or birth. *Asambādha* means unobstructed; it applies to the movement of an army without hindrance and to a broad highway (*ghaṇṭāpatha*). *Saṃsaraṇa* refers to a road or thoroughfare. *Vāntāna* has the appearance of being vomited or discarded. *Unnaya* refers to the lifting up of water-vessels and the like, as well as to that which is uprooted (*unmūlita*); [the term] *udbhiraṇa* [is used here]. From this point forward, the words ending in the suffix *ṇa* (ana) that will be mentioned are of three genders. *Viṣāṇa* refers to the horn of an animal (*paśu*) or the tusk of an elephant (*imadanta*); in the feminine, it is *viṣāṇī*. 54–55.

*Kramanimnā* means gradually sloping; *sā cāsāv urvī* refers to that very earth. O you who are bent at the crossroads (*catuṣpatha*), you are prone (*pravaṇaḥ*) among those who stand in the masculine state (*puṃstheṣu*). You are settled (*niṣitaḥ*), meaning pervaded (*vyāptaḥ*). You are impure (*aśuddhaḥ*), meaning a non-friend (*amitraḥ*). Regarding the word *saṃkīrṇa*, Ajaya states: "It means crowded, narrow, pervaded, or in some cases, a mixture of castes. A *śūnya* is a place devoid of support. An *ūṣara* is a type of ground; it would be called *viriṇa*. [The term] *iraṇa* is also used, as well as *īraṇa*. For it is said: "An *īraṇa* is a saline wasteland (*ūvara*) or a desolate place (*śūnya*). (56)

*Setu*, *varaṇa*, *veṇī*, and *nadībheda* (types of rivers), as well as *kacoccaya* (a mass of hair)—these are [words] whose etymological roots are unknown. Thus end those ending in *ṇ*. Now he states those ending in *t*: *Nada* is a particular type of river. *Tākṣya* is Garuḍa. *Bhāsa* is a specific bird, namely the village cock. *Pakṣin* refers to any bird in general. (57) *Utpāta* is a comet (a star consisting of smoke). It also refers to a particular planet. [Note: This word does not appear even in the Vāḍha manuscript. [End of] the Third Book.

The word *hasta* refers to the hands and also to the constellation *pāṇinakṣatra*; *marut* denotes the wind and the gods; || 58 || *yantā* means an elephant-driver and a charioteer; *bhartā* means a husband, a killer, and a nourisher; *potaḥ* refers to a vessel and an infant; *pretaḥ* refers to a deceased being; || 59 || *ketuḥ* denotes a type of planet and a banner; *sutaḥ* means a son and a king; *sthapatiḥ* refers to a particular kind of artisan; *bhūbhṛt* means a mountain and a king; || 60 || *mūrdhābhiṣiktaḥ* refers to a consecrated king; and *ṛtuḥ* refers to the menstrual flow of a woman as well as a season.

*Viṣṇu* also [means] the unconquered (*ajita*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*); *sūta* means a charioteer (*tvaṣṭṛ*, *sārathi*). *Vyakta* refers to one who is manifest (*prājña*). Both are examples seen in the illustrations of the scriptures. *Kṣattṛ* occurs in the sense of a charioteer, a doorkeeper (*dauvārika*), and a son born of a Kṣatriya woman by a Śūdra father. *Vṛttānta* may mean a context (*prakaraṇa*), a manner (*prakāra*), or news of an event (*kāryavārtā*). (Verses 58–62). *Jīmūta*: He releases water while living; thus it is *jīmūta*. It belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *jīmūta* is used for a mountain, a cloud that brings stability, a thunderbolt, and a rain-cloud."

"Dhūmaketu is known [to mean] fire, a comet, and a portentous phenomenon," according to the Viśva-kośa. *Pāṇi* means the hand. *Nakṣatra* refers to the thirteenth lunar mansion. *Pavana*, *vāyu*, *amara*, and *bhrama* are synonyms for wind. (58) *Mahāmātra* and *sārathi* both mean a charioteer. *Dhātṛ* means a supporter; it also means a master (*svāmin*) or a husband (*bhartṛ*). *Yānapātra* means a boat or a vessel. *Pota* means a house, a garment, a ship, a source, or a living being. (59) "*Ketu* means a flame, a banner, an enemy, a planet, a portent, and a mark," according to the Medinī-kośa.

*Ārthiva* means a king; *tanaya* means a son; *kāru* means an artisan or a specific type thereof; and by virtue of the word *api*, it also refers to one who wears a *kāśuka* garment or a priest who performs sacrifices for a livelihood (*jīveṣṭiyājaka*). *Sthapati* means the earth-supporter (a mountain) or a mountain (*śaila*). (60) By virtue of the word *api*, it also refers to a preeminent person or any Kṣatriya who has been consecrated (*mūrdhābhiṣikta*). *Ṛtu* refers to the menstrual flow of a woman, the dust [of battle], the winter season and so forth, and [the six] seasons. *Ajita* and *avyakta*—these two ending in *t*—also apply to Viṣṇu. By virtue of the word *api*, *avājita* also means one who is unsubdued or Śiva.

The *Viśvaprakāśa* states: "The term *avyakta* refers to Viṣṇu in his unmanifest form (*avyakta-śarīra*), as well as to the principles beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*); it may also mean the 'unmanifest' (the indistinct) when applied to that which is not clearly expressed. [The word] *tvaṣṭṛ* refers to a specific type of artisan. The *Viśvaprakāśa* states: "The word *sūta* refers to one born from a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, as well as to a charioteer and a bard. || 61 || The word *vyakta* means "clear" even when referring to something manifest. *Śāstra* refers to logic (*tarka*) and so forth. *Nidarśana* means an illustration or example. These two are the examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). *Dvāḥstha* means a doorkeeper. There is also a reading *vaiśyāyām*.

From the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *kṣat* means a *mudrā*, a woman of the *triyañja* class, and a daughter of a slave (*bhujiṣyātanaya*). (62) *Prakaraṇa* means context or subject matter; *prakāra* means mode or state; *kārtsnya* means entirety or totality; *vārtā* means public rumor or report. In the sense of a dancing place, it refers to a dance pavilion (*nṛtyamaṇḍapa*). *Ānarta* is a specific region or a particular district (*janapada-viśeṣa*), located on the western ocean. (63) *Ānarta* [is used] in the sense of battle, a dancing place, and a specific region. (63)

*Kṛtānta* refers to Yama, a philosophical doctrine, destiny, and unwholesome actions; *śleṣman* (phlegm) and the like, as well as *rasa* (fluid), *rakta* (blood), and the like, the great elements (*mahābhūtas*), and their qualities; *indriya* (the senses), a transformation of stone, and the source of sound; *vāta* (wind); *kakṣāntara* (the inner apartments) refers to the private quarters of a king that are not within the range of everyone; *śakti* means both power and a spear; *mūrti* means hardness and the body; *vratati* means both expansion and a creeper; *vasati* means both night and a dwelling; *apaciti* means both decay and worship; and *sāti* means both giving and an end.

*Arati* means pain or the tip of a bow; *jāti* means a genus or birth. (67) *Īti* refers to movement or flow; *īti* also means a riot or an epidemic. *Dvārāvatī* [is used] in the sense of a dancing hall, a person, or another country—so says Ajaya. (63) *Yama* is Dharmarāja; *daiva* is past karma; *akuśalakarma* is sin. Substances such as phlegm (*śleṣman*) are denoted by the word *dhātu*; by the word "etcetera," blood and so forth are included. *Rasa* is a specific portion produced from the transformation of food.

By the phrase "rasa, rakta, etc.," fat (vasā), marrow (majjā), and so forth are included. The "great elements" (mahābhūtāni) are earth and the others; their qualities (tadguṇāḥ) are smell and the rest. The "senses" (indriyāṇi) are the eye and the rest. "The transformation of stone" (aśmaṣikṛtiḥ) refers to the mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), and so forth. "The source of words" (śabdayoniḥ) refers to the root *bhū* in the sense of "being" (sattāyām), according to the grammatical rule: "Roots beginning with *bhū* are called *dhātavaḥ*. "In the inner chamber of the king" (nṛpasya kakṣāntare) means in a specific location within the royal palace. "Not within the range of everyone" (asarvagocare) is an epithet qualifying the inner chamber.

By the force of the word *api* (also), [the term applies] to the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*), at the end of a period of impurity (*āśaucānta*), and at the conclusion of a battle (*yuddhānta*). (65) *Kāsū*: In the Mahārāṣṭra language, this is known as *saitī*; it is a type of weapon. According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *kāsū* may denote a person of indistinct speech, a spear (*śakti*), or a life-span (*āyus*). *Kāṭhinya* means firmness or hardness. *Pallī* means a creeper. It also refers to dwelling at night or in a house. (66) *Kṣaya* means loss or decline. *Arcā* means worship; in that context, *apaciti* refers to honor, as well as expiation (*niṣkṛti*) and expenditure (*vyaya*). *Avasāna* means the end. *Dhanuṣkoṭi* means the tip of a bow. The reading is *ārti*.

The vowel *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs by the rule "upasargādṛti. *Sāmānya* means genus (*gotva*), etc.; *jāti* refers to the *mālatī* flower. According to Hemacandra: "The word *jāti* is used for genus (*sāmānya*) and lineage (*gotra*); it is also used for the *mālatī*, the *āmalakī*, the hearth, the *kampilla* plant, the nutmeg (*jātīphala*), and in Vedic meter (*chandas*). (67) *Pracāra* means popular custom (*lokācāra*). *Spanda* means flowing forth; in that context, it is *rīti*. According to the Viśva lexicon: "The word *rīti* is used for custom (*pracāra*), flow (*syanda*), iron dross, and brass. *Īti* refers to a riot (*ḍimba*) and a calamity (*prabāsa*).

*Ḍimba* means a riot; it is of seven kinds. [The seven are: excessive rain, drought, locusts, rats, parrots, foreign invasion, and famine. In the third *kāṇḍa*: *Udaya* occurs in the sense of rising and attainment (*adhigama*). *Prati* occurs in the sense of opposition (*pratidvandvitva*) and in the *tretā* age. (68) *Mahatī* refers to a type of lute (*vīṇābheda*). *Bhūti* means ashes and prosperity (*saṃpad*). *Bhogavatī* refers to a river, a city, and the world of the *nāgas*. (69) *Samiti* means a mixture (*saṅkara*), a gathering (*saṅga*), and an assembly (*sabhā*). *Kṣiti* means destruction (*kṣaya*) and the earth (*vāsa*). *Hetayaḥ* refers to the rays of the sun, weapons, and the flames of fire. (70)

*Jagatī* refers to a specific meter as well as to the earth; *paścchinda* also means the tenth [chapter]. *Āyati* refers to future time as well as to one's own nature. *Patti* means movement; however, *pakṣati* refers to the root of a wing and to the divisions of the fortnights (*pakṣa*). *Prakṛti* is used in both genders, as are the dramatic styles (*vṛtti*) such as *kaiśikī*. *Sikatā* refers to sand as well as the Veda; *śruti* refers to the ear as well as the Veda. Regarding the pestilences (*īti*), they are recorded as sevenfold: locusts, rats, parrots, one’s own army, and the enemy’s army. Thus is the classification.

*Udaya* means rising or birth; *adhigama* means acquisition or attainment. *Agnitraya* refers to the triad of fires known as the Dakṣiṇa, Gārhapatya, and Āhavanīya. *Tretā* (ending in the suffix *-ā*) denotes the second Yuga. (68) *Nāradī* is a specific type of lute (*vīṇā*). *Bhūti* refers to one who possesses greatness, such as a wife, and also to the supernatural powers (*aṇimā*, etc.). According to the *Amaraśeṣa*: "Bhūti means ashes, prosperity, a particular way of cooking meat, birth, and the ornamentation of an elephant. *Bhogavatī* refers to a river, a city of the Nāgas, or a serpent. *Samiti* refers to battle and three other things. (69)

*Vāsaḥ* means dwelling; by the inclusion of the word *api*, it also refers to the earth. *Kṣitiḥ* refers to a division of time. *Hetih* refers to the rays of the sun and so forth. (70) *Jagatī* refers to the world, the earth, a sage, and a specific meter—a poetic foot consisting of twelve syllables. By the inclusion of the word *api*, it also refers to people. *Daśamī* is a meter with ten syllables per foot. *Āvaliḥ* also means a row. *Āyatiḥ* also refers to a future time. As the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *āyatiḥ* is used in the sense of restraint, power, and the future time. (71) *Pattiḥ* refers to a type of hero and a type of military unit.

The word *pakṣabhedyoḥ* is in the genitive case. The word *pakṣa* denotes both a half-month and a wing; hence the dual number. It means at the root of the half-month—that is, on the first day (*pratipad*). Or, it means at the base, i.e., the lower part of a bird’s wing. The term *pakṣati* (the root of a wing) is derived by adding the suffix *ti* according to the rule *pakṣāttiḥ*. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "In the sense of a male [person] or a variety of directions, beginning with the east (*ādikṣu*). (171) *Matsara* is masculine when it means envy toward another's prosperity or intolerance of another's success. It is of common gender (*abhidheyaliṅgaka*) when it denotes one who possesses such envy or a miser. *Vara* is masculine when it refers to a god or a chosen object desired from a deity. It is used in the three genders (*triṣu*) in the sense of "excellent. It is neuter when meaning "slightly dear" or "somewhat desired. " *Vara* [is used] for a son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*), for a choice (*vṛti*), and for an object desired from a deity or the like. It is masculine when meaning 'tawny' (*piṅga*), and in the three genders when meaning 'excellent. But in the neuter, it refers to saffron (*kuṅkuma*).”

The word *varī* is said to denote *śatāvarī*; *varā* occurs in the sense of the *phalatrika* (the three fruits). Some say that *varam* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) meaning "slightly desired. Thus says the *Medinī*. *Karīraḥ* refers to the sprout of a bamboo (*vaṃśa*); it is used in both the masculine and neuter genders (*putrapuṃsakayoḥ*). In the masculine (*nā pumān*), it means the rear of an army (*camūjaghane*), specifically the part following the main body of troops. *Pratisaraḥ* is masculine (*nā puṃliṅgaḥ*). It refers to a protective thread worn on the hand, consecrated with mantras for the sake of auspiciousness. [It is also used] in the sense of a specific type of mantra, a garland, and a bracelet. Thus says the *Medinī*: "Pratisara may be a particular mantra, a garland, or a bracelet. *Phalatrikam* is neuter (*napuṃsakam*). It consists of the three fruits: *harītakī*, *bibhītaka*, and *āmalaka*. *Varam* is used as an indeclinable (*avyayam*) in the sense of "excellent" (*praśastam*). *Karīraḥ* is masculine (*pumān*) when referring to the shoot of a bamboo. *Pratisaraḥ* is masculine (*nā puṃsi*) when denoting a protective amulet or a thread tied to the wrist. *Varā* is feminine (*strī*) when designating the plant *śatāvarī*. *Varam* is also used as a neuter noun (*napuṃsake*) in the sense of "a boon" (*iṣṭe*). *Karīraḥ* is also masculine (*pumān*) when signifying the trunk of a tree (*vṛkṣaskandhe*). *Pratisaraḥ* is masculine (*puṃsyeva*) when meaning a "border" (*maryādāyām*). *Varī* is feminine (*strī*) when referring to the plant *śatāvarī*. *Varā* is feminine (*strī*) when denoting the *phalatrika*. *Varam* is an indeclinable (*avyayam*) meaning "slightly desired" (*manāgiṣṭe*). Some say it is also a neuter noun (*napuṃsakam*) in the same sense. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *hari* is used for the purification of a wound, the rear of an army, and a man; it is not feminine, but [is so] in the sense of a circle (*maṇḍala*), a guard, a measuring line (*karasūtra*), and one who is to be employed—these being of other genders. (173) The word *hari* occurs in fourteen senses, beginning with Yama. Among these, in thirteen senses it is masculine (*pumān*). It is of three genders (*triliṅga*) when meaning the color yellow-brown (*kapilavarṇa*). *Anila* means wind; *aṃśu* means a ray; *vājī* means a horse; *śuka* means a species of bird; *ahi* means a serpent. "In the sense of another world (*lokāntara*) and the color green (*haridvarṇa*), *hari* is feminine (*yoṣa*). (174)

The word *śarkarā* is used for sand (*sikatāsu*) in a portion of a potsherd (*karparāṃśe*), and by the force of the word "also" (*api*), it refers to sugar-candy and the like (*khaṇḍavikṛtyādau*). According to the *Medinī*: "The word *śarkarā* [denotes] sugar-candy, a stone, a piece of a potsherd, a place abounding in gravel, a type of disease, and also [the number] 'all'. The term *yāpana* refers to that by which one is sustained (*yāpyate 'nena yāpanam tasmin*). As stated: "The word *yātrā* [denotes] a means of sustenance, movement, the worship of a deity, and a festival. *Irā* signifies the earth, speech, wine, and water; *tandrī* signifies drowsiness and lassitude. (Verse 175)

*Dhātrī* may mean a foster-mother, the earth, or the *āmalaka* tree. *Kṣudrā* refers to a woman with missing limbs, an actress, a prostitute, a bee, or the *kaṇṭakārikā* plant. (176) The word *kṣudra* is used in three genders for one who is cruel, base, or small; it also denotes a measure (*mātrā*) in the sense of a retinue, a small quantity, or a specific dimension. The suffix *-mātra* signifies entirety or limitation. (177) *Citra* refers to painting and a marvel; *kalatra* means the hips or a wife; *pātra* means a worthy person or a vessel; and *patra* means a vehicle or a wing. (178)

According to the *Viśva* lexicon: *śāstra* refers to an instruction or treatise; *śastra* refers to a weapon or iron. Among the four classes of roots beginning with *bhū*, there is the word *irā*. *Surā* means liquor; *āpaḥ* means water; *pramīlā* is the dullness of all the senses due to fatigue and the like. [Note: *tandrā* also ends in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. || 175 || The word *dhātrī* occurs in the sense of a foster-mother and so forth. A foster-mother (*upamātā*) is one who provides milk. *Kṣitiḥ* means the earth. *Āmalakī* is a specific type of tree. By the use of "also" (*api*), it is implied that a mother (*jananī*) is also called *dhātrī*. The word *kṣudrā* occurs in the sense of a woman with missing limbs and so forth. A woman with missing limbs (*vyaṅgā*) is one whose body parts are deficient.

*Naṭī* means one who is habitually dancing. *Saramā* refers to a honey-bee. *Kaṇṭakārikā* is the plant *bṛhatī*. According to Hemachandra: "The word *kṣudrā* is used for the tiger, the dancer (*naṭī*), the *vyāghrī*, the *bṛhatī*, and the *saramā*; it also denotes the *cāṅgerikā* plant, violence, a mere fly, and a prostitute. (176) In the group of three beginning with "cruel," *kṣudra* is used in the three genders. According to Hemachandra: "The word *kṣudra* is used for a pauper, a miser, the base, the small, and the cruel. In the group of three beginning with "retinue," *mātrā* is feminine; in the group of two beginning with "duty," it is neuter. As an example in the sense of "retinue": [text follows].

*Mātra* [is used] in the sense of "little," as in *śākamātrā* (only vegetables). In the sense of "measure," as in *kiṃ istimātro 'ṅkuśaḥ?* (Is the goad only the size of an elephant?). In the sense of "action," as in *jīvamātraṃ na hiṃsyāt* (one should not harm even a living creature). But in the sense of "restriction," as in *payomātraṃ dehi* (give only milk). *Mātrā* [also means] wealth, an ear-ornament, and a portion of a syllable. According to Hemacandra: "The word *mātra* is used in the sense of a small pit, in its own meaning (*svārtha*), and in the sense of totality (*kārtsnya*). *Mātrā* is used for a covering, a part of a syllable, a substance, a measure, a little, an ear-ornament, time, and a choice. (177)

In the passage beginning with *ālekhyam*, it refers to the drawing of various colors. According to Hemacandra: "The word *citra* is used for the sky, a forehead mark (*tilaka*), a wonder, a painting, and a variegated thing. *Śroṇiḥ* means the hips or waist. According to Ramas: "The word *kalatra* is used for a fortress, the wives of kings and others, and the hips. Regarding the word *yogya* (fitting): a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*) is a worthy recipient of gifts (*dānapātra*). According to Viśva: "The word *pātra* is used for a vessel, a worthy person, the space between two shores, a leaf, and is also desired to mean a minister of a king. Furthermore, *parṇa* means a leaf (*patra*).

The *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *patra* refers to a vehicle, a leaf, a wing, an arrow, and a bird. (178) *Nideśa* means a command or order. *Grantha* refers to works such as grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and so forth; therein, it is the Śābara [text]. *Jaṭā* means the root of a tree. *Aṃśuka* is a specific kind of garment. According to the *Mañjarī*, *netra* is a particular type of forest. [The *Amara-kośa* with commentary states: "The word *netra* may denote honey, a quality, a division of strength, a root, a crest, a garment, and here [in this context], a field, a wife, and the body. (179)

*Potra* refers to the snout of a boar or a hog; *gotra*, however, means name and lineage. *Satra* denotes a covering, a sacrifice, constant giving, and also a forest. (180) *Ajira* means a field or a body; *ambara* means the sky or a garment. *Cakra* refers to a kingdom as well; *akṣara* means liberation as well; and *kṣīra* means water as well. (181) *Bhūri* and *candra* also mean gold; *gopura* means even a mere gate. *Gahvara* means a cave or deceit; *upa-hara* means a secret place, proximity, or a secluded spot. (182) [And *tumula* means a tumult.]

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *netrī* [is used] in the sense of a chariot, the eye, a river, a leader, and like *vāc* (speech). The *Medinī* and *Viśvaprakāśa* state: "The word *kṣetra* [is used] for the body, a field, a place of perfected ones (*siddha*), and the wife. As it says in the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*: "O son of Kuntī, this body is called the *kṣetra*. (Verse 179) *Kroḍa* means a boar; its snout, as well as that of a plow, is called *potra*.

"Potraṃ" refers to the snout at the tip of the mouth of a boar (*sūkara*) and *ila*; thus says the *Viśva*. By the word "and" (*ca*), it also means lineage (*gotra*), mountain, and family; "Gotraṃ" is used for family, name, what is to be honored, understanding, forest, field, and path; thus says the *Medinī*. "Ācchādanaṃ" means covering and strength; "sadādānaṃ" means constant giving. By the word "also" (*api*), the term "satra" also denotes deception. (Verse 180) "Viṣaya" refers to form and so forth; by the word "also" (*api*), "ajira" means a courtyard.

According to Hemacandra: "Ajira means a frog, a body, a courtyard, or wind. Regarding *vyoman*: it means the sky (*ākāśa*) or a garment (*vāsas*). According to Viśva: "Ambara means a garment, the sky, cotton, or a fragrant substance. From the word *api* (also/even), it includes an army, a chariot, and a wheel. According to Hemacandra: "Cakra means a weapon, a multitude, the tools of a potter, a kingdom, an army, a chariot, a whirlpool, or deceit. From the word *api*, it also includes wool and Brahman; "Akṣara may mean liberation (*apavarga*), the Supreme Brahman, or a letter (*varṇa*)."

According to Hemacandra’s *Abhidhānacintāmaṇi*: "In the sky, in the heat of the dharma, in the atmosphere, and in the primal cause (*mūlakāraṇa*). Furthermore, in the *Bhagavadgītā*: "There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable. The perishable consists of all beings; the one who stands at the peak (*kūṭastha*) is called the imperishable. Thus, a certain person standing at the peak, denoted by the word "imperishable" (*akṣara*), is understood. By the word "and" (*ca*), milk is included [in the category of liquids]. (181) Both the words *bhūri* and *candra* end in the letter *r*; they also apply to gold. Among these, *bhūri* is neuter when referring to gold due to a difference in form.

Because of the word *api* [it is understood that other meanings apply]. According to the *Medinī*: “The masculine *bhūri* refers to Vāsudeva, Hari, and Parameṣṭhin; it is neuter for gold, and it is used as an adjective (*vācyaliṅga*) in the sense of ‘abundant. And *candra* refers to camphor and so forth: “*Candra* [is used] for camphor, *kāmpilla*, nectar, the moon, gold, and water,” according to the *Medinī*. Not only for a city (*pūra*), but even for a mere gate is there *gopura*: “*Gopura* [is used] for a city gate, a fortress, a city, and also for the *kaivartī* and *mustaka* plants,” according to the *Medinī*.

*gahvara* means a cave, a thicket, or a ravine; *nagara* means a city; *pura* means a town. *Pura* also means "more," "above," or "on top"; *mandira* refers to a house that is not inhabited by living beings. *Rāṣṭra*, which is not feminine, denotes a kingdom, a territory, or a calamity. *Dara*, which is not feminine, means fear or a crack; *vajra* is not feminine and means a diamond or the thunderbolt. *Tatra* means principal, a final conclusion (*siddhānta*), weaving with thread, or a covering. *Auśīra* refers to a whisk made of yak-tail hair or the handle thereof; it also denotes a couch or a seat.

*Puṣkara* refers to the tip of an elephant’s trunk, the mouth of a musical instrument, water, the sky, the blade of a sword, a lotus, a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), and a specific medicinal herb. (185) *Antara* denotes space, limit, enclosure, interval, difference, and purpose. (182–185) [The *Viśva-kośa* states it also means "not dense"]. *Rahaḥ* means a secluded place. *Antikam* means proximity. These two are synonyms for *upahvara*. (182) *Puraḥ*, and so forth—these three are words denoting the sense of "front" (*agra*). Among them, *puraḥ* and *purastāt* are used as follows: *agragāmī* ("one who goes before"). *Adhika* (excessive) is used as follows: [example omitted].

In the evening, [the word *upari*] means "one hundred. Regarding its usage above: *vṛkṣāgram* (the top of a tree). According to the *Medinī*: "The neuter [*upari*] is used in the senses of 'before,' 'in front of,' 'above,' 'measure,' 'weight' (*palasya*), 'support,' 'collection,' and 'edge'; it is also used in the senses of 'excessive,' 'principal,' and 'first,' like the word to be defined. Furthermore, the pair *puraṃ* and *mandiraṃ* refer to a house, a dwelling, and a city. Dharaṇi states: "A palace on top of a house is called *puraṃ*. Haima states: "*Puraṃ* is used for the body, a city, a house, and Pāṭaliputra."

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "A temple (*mandira*) is neuter when it refers to a city. The word *rāṣṭra* denotes a province, a country, a calamity, death, and so forth; "it is both masculine and neuter. (183) *Bhra* means a pit or chasm. *Hīraka* refers to a type of gemstone. *Pava* means a cleft or fissure. In the sense of "principal," as in *svatantraḥ* (independent). In the sense of "tenet" or "conclusion," as in *tāntrikaḥ* (one versed in a system). Furthermore, the word *tatra* is used for a shuttle, an accessory, and a loom. [As the commentary notes: "The suffix *tadd* occurs in the sense of 'belonging to a family,' in the sense of 'conclusion,' and in the sense of 'an excellent medicine.'"

According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *pradhāna* is used in the sense of the primary matter (*sattvādi*), a specific branch of knowledge, a garment, another Vedic recension (*śākhāntara*), a logical reason, a purpose for both [parties], and the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*). (184) *Cāmara* is a qualifier of a particular staff; it is that which belongs to the *camara* (yak-tail). According to Svāmī, the term *auśīra* refers to a bed and a seat taken together. Subhūti, however, explained it as distinct [from those]. *Puṣkara* refers to eight things, beginning with the tip of an elephant's trunk; it is the mouth of a musical instrument, that is, the opening of a vessel used for playing music.

*Puṣkara* refers to a sword-blade, a lotus (*nalina*), a particular sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), and a specific medicinal herb used for leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). According to Hemacandra: "The word *puṣkara* denotes an island, a sacred site, a serpent, the king of birds (Garuḍa), a type of medicinal plant, the mouth of a musical instrument, the blade of a sword, the trunk-tip of an elephant, the sky, water, and a lotus. (185) The term *antara* occurs in thirteen senses, beginning with "opportunity" (*avakāśa*). As an example for "opportunity": *antare himam* ("in the midst of snow"). For "limit" (*avadhi*): [as in] "within ten days. (186–133) [From the *Nānārthavarga* of the *Amarakośa* with commentary.]

*Chidra* refers to a hole, one's own, inseparable, external, an opportunity, the middle, and the inner self (186). *Piṭhara* means a musta-grass plant; *nāgara* means ginger as well as a king; *śārvara* refers to blinding darkness; and *dhātuka* is used as an adjective (187). *Gaura* means reddish-brown, white, or yellow; *aruṣkara* means a wound or the aruṣkara tree; *jaṭhara* may mean hard as well as the belly; and *adhara* means below as well as the lower lip (188). *Ekāgra* means undisturbed as well as concentrated; *vyagra* means distracted, occupied, or agitated. For example: "to be given within a month. As for its use regarding clothing: [Example omitted per instructions]

*Antara* means garments worn between [the inner and outer layers], that is to say, undergarments (*parighānīya*). Examples according to meaning: for "between," as in *parvatāntarito raviḥ* ("the sun is hidden by a mountain"); for "difference," as in *yadantaraṃ sarvapaśailarājayoḥ* ("the difference between all other mountains and the king of mountains"); for "purpose" (*tādarthye*), as in *tvadantareṇa ṛṇam etat* ("this debt is for your sake"); for "gap" (*chidra*), as in *parāntare prahartavyam* ("one should strike in the enemy's weak point"); for "one's own," as in *ayam atyantaro mama* ("this one is very close to me"); for "without" (*vinārthe*), as in *antareṇa puruṣakāram* ("without human effort"); and for "outside," as in *antare caṇḍālagṛhāḥ*, meaning "outside the houses."

In the sense of *avasara* (opportunity), as in: "an intimate servant. In the sense of *madhya* (middle), as in: "a mountain has arisen between us two. In the sense of *antarātman* (inner self), as in: "the form of light was seen within. By the inclusion of the word *ca* (and), it is used in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*), as in: "the letter *bha* is the most similar (*antaratama*) to the letter *ha*. [186] The word *piṭhara* refers to *musta* (a type of grass) and *mustaka* (its root); by the inclusion of the word *api*, it also refers to a churning-stick (*manthāna*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The masculine *piṭhara* refers to a cooking pot; the neuter *piṭhara* refers to *musta* and a churning-stick."

*Rājakaśeru* refers to the root of an aquatic grass, known as *nāgaramothā*. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *nāgara* is used for *mustaka*, for *śuṣṭhī*, and for that which is produced in the city (*nagarodbhava*) when it is cooked. In the sense of dense darkness (*andhatamasa*), meaning deep gloom, and in the sense of a murderous or harmful being (*ghātuka*), the word *śārvara* is used. There is also a reading *dhātukame nṛliṅgakam*; the meaning is that this [word] is masculine in gender when it signifies a murderer (*dhātuka*). (Verse 187) "The word *gaura* denotes yellow, reddish, white, and pure, according to its referent (*abhidheyavat*)."

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "In the white mustard, in the moon, and in the filaments of two lotuses. *Aruṣkara* also refers to the fruit of the *bhallātaka*. According to the *Medinī*: "In the masculine, *aruṣkara* refers to the *bhallātaka*; in the three genders, it means causing a wound. There is also a reading: "*aruṣkara* [is used] even in the sense of causing a wound. *Jaṭhara* also refers to the belly; according to the *Haima*: "[It is used] for the belly and for enlargement. Regarding *avaṭu*, it refers to the lower lip; according to *Amara*: "[It is used] also in the sense of inferior. (Verse 188) *Anākula* means healthy; by the word "also," it includes being one-pointed as well.

*Vyāsakta* means divided or occupied with two things. *Ākula* refers to one whose mind is fixed on many objects; such a person is *vyagra*. The word *uttara* occurs in three senses: superior, northern, and subsequent. As for "superior," for example: *ita uttaram* (further than this). In the context of *śṛṅgārādau*, it refers to the ninefold [rasas] beginning with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), such as the heroic (*vīra*) and the pathetic (*karuṇa*). *Viṣe* means poison (*garala*).

The word *rasa* may denote vigor (*vīrya*), brilliance (*tejas*), a quality such as sweetness or sourness (*guṇa*), or fluidity (*drava*). For example, in the sense of passion (*rāga*): "the youth is a connoisseur of flavor (*rasika*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *rasa* [is used] for fragrance, water, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and others, poison, vigor, the group beginning with bitter (*tikta*), deep red color, a specific constituent of the body (*dehadhātu*), mercury (*pārada*), and salt. The two forms ending in *-s*—*uttaṃsa* and *dhāvataṃsa*—refer to an ear-ornament (*karṇapūra*), a specific type of ear-jewel, or a crest (*śekhara*), an ornament for the head. (226) As an example in the sense of a class of deity:

The word *vasu* is masculine when it refers to a deity, fire, the sun, a ray, a king, or a gem; it is neuter when it means wealth or treasure. *Vedhas* refers to Viṣṇu; it is feminine when it denotes a blessing, a benediction, a snake’s fang, longing, or eager desire. *Hiṃsā* refers to acts such as theft and other forms of violence. *Masūra* refers to the lentil (*masūrāśva*) as well; *dyau*, *yau*, *rodasī*, and *rodasī* refer to heaven and earth. *Jvālā* and *bhās* (feminine) mean flame; *arcis* and *jyotis* (neuter) mean light, splendor, or vision. *Āgas* (neuter) means sin or offense; *vayas* (neuter) means bird, age, youth, and so forth. *Tejas* (neuter) means brilliance or excrement; *mahaḥ* (neuter) means festival or luster. *Rajas* (neuter) means the quality (*guṇa*), the menses of a woman, or Rāhu; *tamas* (neuter) means darkness or the quality (*guṇa*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "In the sense of the earth or a medicinal herb, *śyāla* is masculine; in the sense of honey, it is neuter; in other senses, it is used in all three genders. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), *virijya* is also [included] as a synonym for Brahmā.

According to Hemacandra’s lexicon: "Vegha [is used] for a killer, one who knows, and Viṣṇu. *Hitāśaṃsā* is the desire for what is beneficial (*hitasyāśaṃsā*). The term *āśīḥ* ending in a long vowel (*sāntam*) refers to both the fang of a serpent (*ahi*) and its venom; thus it is said: "That [term] has three meanings. Another lexicon states: "*Āśīḥ* [is used] for the fang of a serpent, a kind word, and a wish. (227) *Prārthanā*, *yātrā*, *autsukya*, and *udyuktatā*—these two (*ume*) are *lālasā*. Furthermore, *lālasā* denotes an excess of thirst or longing. The *Medinī* lexicon states: "*Lālasa* [is used] for longing, excessive thirst, and singing; it is of two genders."

Because of the word *ca* (and), there is violence (*hiṃsā*) in both cases. By the word *ādi* (etcetera), actions such as the destruction of livelihood are included. *Aśvā* refers to a mare; *jananī* and *prasūḥ* also mean mother. As the *Medinīkośa* states: "The words *prasūḥ*, *avā*, and *jananī* apply to both [mother and source]; *kandalī* and *bīrudh* are feminine. *Rodasī* and *rodasyau* are forms ending in the long vowel and the dual case-ending, used by a single expression to denote both heaven and earth. There is also separate usage, as it is said: "The word *rodas* and *rodasī* refer separately to heaven and earth."

Even when used in conjunction: "these two Rodasīs," [referring to] heaven and earth. *Rodasī* is also an indeclinable (avyaya), as it is said: "The two worlds, heaven and earth, are *rodasyau*, *rodasī*, and *rodasī*. || 228 || *Jyotis* means flame, month, and light; it is neuter in these three senses. *Bha* means a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). *Dyota* means radiance. *Dṛṣṭi* refers to the central part of the pupil. "In the masculine, *jyotis* denotes fire and the sun. *Āgas* means sin and offense.

According to Hemacandra, *āgas* means sin (*enas*) or offense (*mantu*). By the use of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the list includes] *goṣpada* and others. (229) *Purīṣa* means excrement (*gūtha*). Regarding *barcas*, the *Medinī* states: "The neuter *barcas* is used for form, excrement, and luster; in the masculine, it refers to the son of the Moon. *Mahaḥ* is used for a festival and for luster. Regarding *guṇa*, it means a quality or a specific strand. *Rajaḥ* is used for the menstrual flow of women and for dust or pollen. This word is also vowel-ending (ending in -a). According to the *Añjaya*: "This *rajas* is feminine when used with *rajas* [as a noun], and it denotes the menstrual flow, a quality, and dust."

And *tamas* occurs in the triad beginning with Rāhu; it also means sin (*pāpa*) and sorrow (*śoka*). [230] In poetry, *chandas* refers to the Gāyatrī and other meters; it also means desire (*abhilāṣa*). [230–231] The third book (*kāṇḍa*). *Chandas* also means desire. *Tapas* refers to the Kṛcchra and other ascetic penances. *Sahas* means strength (*bala*); *sahā* means a path (*mārga*). *Nabhas*, *kham*, *śrāvaṇa*, and *nabhāḥ* all mean the sky (*ākāśa*) or the month of Śrāvaṇa. [231] *Okas*, *sadmā*, and *āśraya* mean a dwelling (*gṛha*). *Payas* means milk (*kṣīra*) and water (*ambu*). *Ojas* means luster (*dīpti*) and strength (*bala*). *Srotas* means a sense organ (*indriya*) and a stream (*nimnagāraya*). [232]

The word *tejas* is used in the sense of splendor, influence, light, strength, and semen; thus it applies to three [meanings]. *Vidvān* is used for one who knows and for one who is learned. *Bībhatso* is used for one who is loathsome and also for excessive violence. These [words ending in -as] are used in the sense of excellence. *Jyāyān* is used for the elderly and the praiseworthy. *Kanīyān* is used for the young and the small. *Varīyān* is used for the excellent and the best. *Sāṃghīyān* is used for a multitude and for that which is abundant. (234) Thus end those ending in -an. *Bahas* is used for a leaf, persistence, an eclipse, the sun, and so forth. Regarding *chandas*: "In the sense of desire, *chandas* refers to verse, the Veda, and independent conduct," according to the Medinīkośa.

*Kṛcchra* refers to ascetic vows such as the *sāntapana*; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the *cāndrāyaṇa* and others are included. *Tapaḥ* also means "in another world," as in "and *tapaḥ* in the sense of *dharma*. *Sahaḥ* is neuter when meaning "strength"; *mārgaḥ* is *mārgaśīrṣaḥ*, here in the masculine. According to another lexicon: "*Sahaḥ* is masculine when meaning strength, light, the winter season, and the month of *mārga*. *Kham* is the sky; therein *nabhaḥ* is neuter, while it is masculine when meaning the month of *śrāvaṇa*. Hema states: "*Nabhaḥ* [is used] for the sky, breath, the spider's thread, a rain-gauge, the rainy season, and the month of *śrāvaṇa*. || 231 ||

*Sarva-gṛha* (all houses). *Okaḥ* is also [used] with a short vowel; it is an irregular form (*nipātana*) according to the rule "oka ucaḥ ka. *Āśraya* means merely a place of refuge. Hema states: "The word *okaḥ* may be used in the sense of mere shelter. *Ojas* refers to brilliance and light. Hema states: "[It is used] in the sense of support, the reed (*nala*), the essence of the elements (*dhātu-tejas*). *Srotaḥ* refers to the senses and the current of a river. (Verse 232) *Tejas* refers to a group of four beginning with majesty (*prabhāva*). Hema states: "*Tejas* is used for the sun, fire, valor, fresh butter, and majesty."

From here onwards, until the end of the section on *sānta* (words ending in *s*), the terms are masculine. *Vidvān* means a knower. Because of the word *ca* (and), one who knows the Self (*ātmajña*) is also called *vidvān*. The *Viśva* lexicon states: "The term *vidvān* applies to one who knows the Self, to a wise man, and to a scholar. *Bībhatsaḥ* refers to the cruel or violent; by the force of the word *api* (also), it also denotes the *bībhatsa* (disgusting) aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). The *Haima* lexicon states: "*Bībhatsa* [is used] for the deformed, the cruel, the *bībhatsa* flavor, the base, and that which is characterized by loathing. || 233 ||

These words to be mentioned, beginning with *jyāyas* and ending with *sādhīyas*, are to be understood as expressing the excellence (*atiśaya*) of terms starting with *vṛddha* and ending with *bāḍha*. *Jyāyas* is used for one who is exceedingly old or praiseworthy and worthy of praise. *Kanīyas* is used for one who is exceedingly young or small. *Varīyas* is used for one who is exceedingly broad, great, excellent, or best. *Sādhīyas* is used for one who is exceedingly good. *Sādhīyas* is also used for that which is exceedingly firm (*bāḍham*). These words are grammatically correct when used in the sense of "exceedingly" (*atiśāyana*) with the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun*. 234.

Thus end the words ending in *s*. Now he speaks of those ending in *h*. *Baī* means a leaf (*dala*) or a petal (*patra*); from the word *api*, it also means a feather (*piccha*). Hema states: "The word *baī* is used for grass (*tarṇa*), a surrounding enclosure (*parīvāra*), and a bundle (*kalāpa*). *Nirbandha* and others are synonyms for *graha* (seizure/attachment). *Nirbandha* is a specific kind of insistence or persistence. *Nirvyūha* refers to a turret (*gopura*), a pillar (*stambha*), a joint (*sandhi*), a projection (*apīḍa*), and a decoction (*kātha-rasa*). It also denotes a peg on a wall (*nāgadantaka*). *Pragrāha* and *pragraha* both refer to the string of a balance (*tulāsūtra*) and the reins of a horse (*aśva-ādi-raśmi*).

*Parigraha* refers to a wife, attendants, the root of wealth, or a curse; *gṛha* refers to wives or the hips of an excellent woman; *āroha* refers to the hips of a beautiful woman; *vyūha* refers to a military array or a multitude; *ahi* refers to a serpent or Vṛtra; *amīndarka* refers to those who dispel darkness (the moon, Indra, and the sun); *paribarha* refers to a retinue or the possessions of a king. Thus end the words ending in *ha*. The following are words ending in *ya*: *āṅ* is used in the sense of slightness (*īṣat*), pervasion (*abhivyāpti*), or as a boundary-marker when joined with a verbal root; *indra*, *arka*, and *grahaṇa* [are included]; *graha* is used in the senses of restraint, persistence, seizing, and a battle.

The *Viśva* lexicon states: "[The term *uparāga* applies] to the sun and so forth, to *pūtana* and so forth, and to the eclipses of the moon and sun. *Āpīḍa* means a crest or head-ornament. *Kātharasa* refers to the decoction of boiled substances. *Nirvyūha* refers to a pair of wooden pegs fixed into the walls of houses and the like. [Verse 235] *Tulāsūtra* refers to the cord on which goods are weighed by the hand. *Pragrāha* and *agraha* refer to the reins of horses, bulls, and the like; as it is said: "The word *pragrāha* may denote the weighing-cord as well as the tethering-rope for bulls and other animals."

*Pragraha* means a ray, an arm, a balance-string, a tethering rope, gold, the *haripādapa* tree, a bond, or a female elephant (*banyā*)—according to Hemacandra. *Parijana* means attendants or retinue. *Ādāna* means acceptance; [as Ajaya states]: "*Parigraha* refers to a wife, as well as a root, acceptance, an oath, a retinue, and the sun in the mouth of Rāhu. [The word *gṛha*] refers to wives; by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it also includes houses, which are masculine in gender. *Āroha* refers to the lap or the hip of an excellent woman (*varastrī*).

As in the case of *barārohā*. Due to the word *api* (also/even), it applies to *avaroha* (descent) and *gajāroha* (elephant-rider). Hemacandra states: "Āroha means length, height, the waist of a woman, a type of measure, ascending, and riding an elephant. Due to the word *api*, *yūha* refers to the arrangement of troops; *ahi* refers to a snake or an asura; and *nirmāṇa*, *tarka*, and *yodha* [are also included]. *Tamopaha* refers to those who dispel darkness, such as the moon and the sun; [it also applies] to the Jina, as in "the dispeller of darkness. *Nṛpārha* refers to things worthy of a king, such as the white parasol and other royal regalia.

"Even for a king, *parivāra* refers to his retinue. *Parivāra* means "retinue" (*parivāraḥ*). Hereafter, the words beginning with *āṅ* that are about to be mentioned are called indeclinables (*avyaya*). The definition of an indeclinable is as follows: "That which remains the same across the three genders, all case-endings (*vibhakti*), and all numbers (*vacana*)—that is an indeclinable. Their inclusion here in this section is for the purpose of [demonstrating] the preceding [grammatical rules]. Thus ends the section ending in *ha*. *Āṅ* is an indeclinable used in four senses, beginning with "slightness" (*īṣadartha*).

The letter *ḍ* is its *anubandha*. As an example of its use in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadarthe*): *āpiṅgalaḥ*, meaning "slightly tawny. As an example in the sense of "limit" (*abhiṣyātau*): from Satyaloka down to Pātāla. As an example in the sense of "boundary" (*sīmārthe*): the king's punishment extends as far as the ocean. As an example in the sense arising from connection with a verbal root (*dhātuyogaje*) or connection with an action (*kriyāyogaje*): "he brings" (*āharati*), "he steps upon" (*ākrāmati*), and so forth. The third section (*kāṇḍa*). The word *ā* is a *pragṛhya* [vowel] when used in the sense of "recollection" (*smṛtau*) or in a sentence (*vākye*). It may also be used in the senses of anger (*kopapīḍayoḥ*).

*Pāpaka*, *tseṣa*, and *arthe* [are used] in the sense of reproach; *ku* is used in the sense of censure and blame (239). *Ca* is used for conjunction (*anvācaya*), collection (*samāhāra*), and mutual union (*itaretarayoga*). *Svasti* is used for benediction (*āśīḥ*), welfare (*kṣema*), merit (*puṇya*), and so forth; *ati* is used for excellence and transgression (240). *Svit* is used for the self and for deliberation (*vitarka*); *tu* may be used for distinction (*bheda*) and emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) (238–240). As for *kāpatha*: the particle *ā*, which is designated as *pragṛhya*, occurs in the senses of memory (*smṛti*), recollection (*saraṇa*), a sentence, and for completing a sentence. A *pragṛhya* vowel always remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*).

In that regard, as for *smṛti* (recollection), it is as follows: *ā evaṃ kila tat*. But in the case of a sentence (*vākya*), it is: *ā evaṃ manyase*. According to the *Medinī*: "The particle *ā* [is used] in recollection, in a sentence, in compassion, and in conjunction. However, the indeclinable *āḥ* with the visarga occurs in the sense of pain and anger. There, as an example of pain: *āḥ śītam* ("Ah, the cold!"). As an example of anger: *āḥ pāpa kiṃ vikatyase* ("Ah, you wicked one, why do you boast?"). According to another lexicon: "*Āḥ* [is used] in fleeing, in warding off, and also in anger and torment. The word *ku* [is used] in three senses, such as "wickedness" and so forth.

In the sense of evil, as in *kukarma* (evil deed). In the sense of censure, as in *īṣadartha* (slight meaning), as in *kavoṣṇam* (lukewarm). Regarding this, the *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *ku* is used for the most evil, for censure, for a slight degree, and for prohibition"; and also: "*ku* [is used] for censure and prohibition. Threatening (*nirbhartsanam*) consists of producing fear through words of harm. Mere proclamation of faults is blame (*nindā*). An example of threatening: "Fie upon you, who are habitually prone to striking and neglecting your studies! An example of blame: "Fie upon the man who goes after another's wife! (239)

The word *ya* (and) is used in four senses, beginning with *anvācaya*. When one [of two things] is subordinate (*anuṣaṅgika*), it is *anvācaya*. An example is: "Go for alms and bring a cow. *Samāhāra* (aggregation) is a collection. An example is: "Technical rules and interpretive rules" (*saṃjñāparibhāṣam*). *Itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) is the connection of things that have been combined. An example is: "The *dhava* and the *khadira*" (*dhavakhadirau*). *Samuccaya* (disjunctive conjunction) is the connection of several things to a single action where they are mutually independent. An example is: [as follows].

"Worship the Lord and the Guru. Regarding the word *ca*: the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa* states, "The particle *ca* is used for filling a verse, as an alternative, for a reason, and for determination. *Āśis* means a benediction (*āśīrvāda*). An example of this is: "May it be well with you" (*svasti te bhūyāt*), or "so that there may be safety free from calamity," or "go in safety" (*svasti gaccha*), or "one who possesses merit attains heaven" (*puṇye yathā: svastimān svargam aśnute*). According to the *Medinī*, "the word *svasti* occurs in the sense of auspiciousness, merit, and sometimes in the sense of a wish. For excellence (*prakarṣe*), as in: "Viṣṇu is the most excellent" (*atyuttamo viṣṇuḥ*).

According to Hemacandra: "The word *ati* is used in the senses of excess, leaping over, abundance, praise, and also in the sense of non-delay. *Ativelam* means "to an excessive degree," as in "the surface of the ocean. [240] The particle *khit* (i.e., *kim*) is used in the senses of inquiry and deliberation. For example, in the sense of inquiry: "Is there well-being, *khit*? Deliberation (*vitarka*) is the consideration of various alternative positions. For example: "Is it Viṣṇu’s sovereignty, or rather (*āho-khit*), that of Śiva?"

*Khittam* is used in the sense of doubt and deliberation (*vitarka*). *Sakṛt* means "once" or "simultaneously," while *ārāt* signifies both "distance" and "nearness. (241) *Paścāt* is used for the western direction, the end, and also in the senses of meaning and alternative (*vikalpa*). *Śaśvat* denotes repetition and simultaneity; *sākṣāt* signifies direct perception and equality. (242) *Baṃta* is used for weariness, compassion, contentment, and astonishment. *Hanta* is used for joy, compassion, the commencement of a sentence, and dejection. (243)

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *prati* is used in the sense of a representative (*pratinidhi*), repetition (*vīpsā*), a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*), and so forth, as well as for the purpose of completing a metrical foot (*pādapūraṇa*). As for the word *tu*, it is used in the senses of distinction (*bheda*) and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). For example: "Meat, however (*tu*), is more nourishing than milk. Or: "It is considered by the learned, however (*tu*), to be appropriate. According to the *Medinī*: "'*Tu*' is used for completing a metrical foot, for distinction, for conjunction (*samuccaya*), for restriction (*avacāraṇa*), for an alternative position (*pakṣāntara*), for injunction (*niyoga*), for praise (*praśaṃsā*), and for exclusion (*vinigraha*). In the sense of "together with" (*sahārtha*), the word *sakṛt* means "once" (*ekavāra*). For example: "They eat once (*sakṛt*). Or: "One should perform even (*api*) a single act of pilgrimage at Gayā (*sakṛt*)."

*Ārāt* means "at a distance," as in: *ārācchoḥ sadā vaset* ("One should always dwell far from the wicked"). However, when it means "nearby," one should place a friend *ārāt*. *Paścāt* means "in the western direction" (*pratīcyām*), as well as "last" or "final. For example: *patrādastaṅgato raviḥ* ("The sun has set behind the mountain"), or *paścime vayasi naimiṣaṃ vaśī* ("The self-controlled one went to Naimiṣa in his later years"). The word *api* signifies "conjunction" (*samuccaya*). In that context, the word *uta* is used for "option" (*vikalpa*), as in: *uta bhīma utārjunaḥ* ("Is it Bhīma or Arjuna? or *viṣṇuruta śivaḥ sevyaḥ* ("Should Viṣṇu or Śiva be worshipped?"). Furthermore, *uta* is used in the sense of "question" (*praśna*) and "doubt" (*vitarka*).

According to Hemacandra, [the word *uta*] is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and option (*vikalpa*). Ajaya, however, states: "*uta* and *api* are both used in the sense of *ca* (and). The word *śaśvat* is used in the sense of repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) and accompaniment (*sahārtha*), as in: "He remembers Viṣṇu repeatedly," or "The teacher is constantly served by his disciples. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *śaśvat* is seen in the sense of inquiry regarding the self (*ātmapraśna*), auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), ancient times (*purākalpa*), 'always' (*sadārtha*), and 'again' (*punarartha*). Ajaya, however, says: "*śaśvat* is used in the senses of 'together' (*saha*) and 'always' (*sadārtha*). And according to Hemacandra: "*śaśvat*, *saha*, and *nitya* [are synonyms]."

The word *sākṣāt* is used in the sense of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and being face-to-face (*tulye ca sākṣāt*). For example: "I have seen Hari directly" (*sākṣād dṛṣṭo mayā hariḥ*); "This bride is Lakṣmī herself" (*sākṣāllakṣmīriyaṃ vadhūḥ*). In the group of words expressing grief and so forth (*khedādyarthapañcake*), the word *nata* (used here as *bata*) occurs. For example: "Alas! What great misery! (*aho bata mahatkaṣṭam*); "Alas, you are penniless! (*bata niḥkho'si*); "Alas, the husband has been embraced! (*bata patirāliṅgitaḥ*); "Oh, this Dhruva has indeed attained the gods! (*aho batāyaṃ dhruva āpa devam*); "Come, friend! (*ehi bata sakhe*). Ajaya states: "The word *bata* begins with a dental labial. The word *hanta* is used in the fourfold sense of joy and so forth. As for joy (*harṣe*): [Example follows].

*Hanta* is used in the sense of gain, as in: "Ah, the profit is a hundredfold! In the sense of compassion, as in: "Alas, the wretched one must be protected! In the sense of introducing a speech, as in: "Well now, I shall tell you. In the sense of sorrow, as in: "Alas! The unborn enemy has been born first through you! According to Hemachandra: "*Hanta* is used in the senses of giving, compassion, the introduction of a speech, sorrow, certainty, and joy. (243) *Prati* signifies a representative who is similar to the principal; for example: Parīkṣit [acting] *prati* Abhimanyu.

*Vīpsā* (repetition/distribution) is the desire to pervade; for example: *tīrthaṃ tīrthaṃ prati gacchati* ("he goes to every sacred ford"). In the sense of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), for example: *vṛkṣān prati vidyotate vidyut* ("the lightning flashes toward the trees"). By "and so forth" (*ādi*), [it includes] expressions such as "being in such a state" (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*). Regarding "according to usage" (*prayogataḥ*), this refers to following the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). [This concludes] the third section, which elucidates the meanings of *hetu* (cause), *prakaraṇa* (context), *prakāśa* (manifestation), and others. *Prācī* (eastern), *purastāt*, *prathama* (first), and also *agrataḥ* denote the meaning of "in front" (*pura-artha*) or the eastern direction.

*Yāvat* and *tāvat* are used in the senses of totality (*sākalya*), limit (*avadhi*), and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). (245) *Maṅgala*, *anantara*, *ārambha*, *praśna*, and *kārya* are the meanings of *atha*. *Atha* is also used [in these senses]. *Vṛthā* is used in the senses of being useless (*nirarthaka*) and futility (*vyartha*). *Nānā* has the meanings of "various" (*aneka*) and "both" (*ubhaya*).
